In one paragraph. This is the map of the UOR-R4 documentation. UOR-R4 is an open research project building a language model that predicts text with geometry and whole-number arithmetic instead of a transformer's large grids of decimal multiplications, so that it can run fast on a laptop or in a browser. It is pre-alpha : 0 of its 8 milestones are complete, and no model built under its rules holds a useful conversation yet ( where we are ). The pages here explain what the project is, where it stands and where it is going in plain words first, then give the evidence for every claim so an expert can check it. 10.body: "Geometry" in this project means a few concrete objects, each chosen because it can be computed exactly with whole numbers. The geometry section has one illustrated chapter for each. A token's address is built from fixed points. Each of the 4,096 tokens owns 4 blocks of 8 whole numbers. Each block is always one of 16 fixed points of a famous eight-dimensional lattice called E8 . Every such point is a signed rearrangement of (2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0): two of the eight places hold 2 or −2 and the rest are zero. There are \(16^4 = 65{,}536\) possible addresses, more than the 4,096 tokens, so every token can have its own ( proof , by counting; see the model page ). The model does not yet use all 240 points of E8 ( E8, H4 and the 600-cell ). Moving means rotating. Changing a block means swapping one fixed point for another, which is a rotation from a finite set. Nothing is rounded, so a rotation can always be undone exactly ( quaternions and rotation ). Names come from primes; starting places from zeta phases. Each token can be named exactly by a prime number, and that name never collides with another. Separately, angles taken from the zeros of the Riemann zeta function (a fixed, reproducible set of numbers from mathematics) scatter the tokens' starting addresses. One such construction, PrimeZeta, gives all 4,096 tokens distinct starting addresses ( measurement , construction record ). The distinctness comes from a cell-balancing step, not from the zeta angles; whether the angles help at all is untested ( primes and zeta phases ). Near means few steps apart. Distance between two addresses is the sum of the differences between their numbers, which needs only subtraction and addition. "Nearby earlier tokens" and "the nearest word" both use this distance ( the model page ). Learning means trying the legal moves. The current model does not use calculus. To learn, it tries all 16 legal values of one block on the graphics card and keeps a change only if a whole-number score strictly improves ( training , discrete learning ).

100.body: A geometric model, not a transformer. The project calls it the UOR-R4 Geometric Language Model. Technically it is an autoregressive geometric state model with exact addressed memory: it keeps a running state, updates it with each token through rotations and table look-ups, and reads facts from an exact memory by address ( architecture ). The charter forbids the expensive parts of a transformer outright: no softmax or other squashing functions and no dense matrix multiplication, anywhere: training, evaluation, tooling and serving ( charter , sections 3.2 and 3.3). One model for every job. Conversation with durable memory comes first, then coding and reasoning, all on the same model ( charter , section 1). Fast and local. The lead metric is tokens per second on an ordinary machine, with decode and context reported separately. A small quality gap is acceptable if the model is much cheaper to run.

101.body: The deliverable is one checksum-pinned D11 integer artifact in the UORLUT01 format , released at milestone M8 ( project track , M8). D11 is the serving contract. Its five rules are: no floating point or maths library (R1); no multiply or divide instruction (R2); reading every weight for every token is an interim stage, not the end state (R3; the charter no longer treats dense table maps as an allowed stepping stone for new exports); no transformer backbone (R4); energy claimed only when measured (R5) ( D11 ). UORLUT01 is the file format. It holds an 8-byte magic string, a JSON header, 4-bit weight codes in groups with one scale byte each, and small integer tables for the few nonlinear steps ( format.rs ; proof by reading the code). The reader computes the SHA-256 hash of the whole file as it loads it, so a release can pin that hash. Details are on the releases page . Training may use decimals; serving may not. Since 18 October, offline training may use floating point, but the shipped file is integer, and every float-trained candidate must report its export gap : its served score minus its float score on the same evaluator ( D37 , charter section 3.7). The engine is crates/uor-r4-integer. It runs the file natively (the uor-chat and uor-r4-stack command-line programs) and as WebAssembly (UOR-Foundation/uor-r4#2654). The serving page shows how it multiplies without a multiply instruction.

106.body: The web client is meant to be a language model that lives in a browser tab. You open a web page once, it downloads the model file, and from then on the model runs on your own computer, inside the browser, in a sandboxed form of machine code called WebAssembly. Your prompts and the model's replies never leave the device, because there is no model server to send them to. The page you would use is the Studio, an editor-and-chat interface already in the repository. Today the pieces exist separately and are not joined: the browser engine works on a synthetic test model, the Studio still points at an older engine that was retired, the public site is frozen, and there is no trained model to download. Until milestones M7 and M8 pass, the web client is a geometry explorer and demonstration, not a product. Labels used below: proof (derived from definitions or code), measurement (a recorded run with its artifact), hypothesis (untested). See docs/formal_vocabulary.md and the glossary . A browser window with three layers. Top: the Studio page (editor, chat panel, model manager). Middle: a Web Worker box holding the WebAssembly engine with its calls loadStack, step, saveSession and restoreSession. Bottom: browser storage holding the downloaded UORLUT01 model file and saved sessions (UR4SESS1). One arrow, drawn only once and labelled "first visit: download model, check SHA-256", comes in from a static file host. A crossed-out arrow to a "model server" shows that no prompt leaves the device. One download, then everything runs in the tab. The only network traffic is fetching the static page and the model file.

107.body: Load the page. The Studio is static HTML, JavaScript and CSS. The charter places it at /studio on the project's documentation site ( charter , section 2). Download the model once. The page fetches one UORLUT01 file and checks its SHA-256 against the hash published with the release ( releases ). It then keeps the file in browser storage so later visits work offline. This cache is planned, not built (from reading the repository). Start the engine in a Web Worker. A worker is a background thread of the page, so typing stays smooth while the model computes. The worker loads the WebAssembly build of crates/uor-r4-integer and calls init, then loadStack on the model bytes. Generate. For each token the worker calls step. The engine uses only integer adds, shifts and table look-ups (the D11 contract), so the same file gives the same tokens in every browser. That is a design property; M7 has to measure it. Save and resume. saveSession writes the conversation state as a UR4SESS1 snapshot, and restoreSession brings it back byte for byte. These function names are the real exports of the WebAssembly build: init, tickClock, loadStack, step, saveSession, restoreSession, weightsPerToken, allocEvents, leakedModels ( record ; proof by reading wasm_bindgen_exports.rs ). Why serving in the browser is allowed. Research compute must run on a GPU (D24). On 15 October that rule paused the browser engine, because serving in a browser runs on the user's processor ( D36 ). The owner resolved this on 19 October: serving the exported D11 file on client devices, including browser WebAssembly, is the product, and D24 does not apply to it ( charter , section 3.6).

111.body: The model computes only on the device. No prompt or reply is sent anywhere by the engine. That is the M7 bar, and today it holds trivially, because there is no remote model to call. Network use is not yet limited to static files. The target is the page and the model file only. Today the Studio also loads third-party code and fonts from CDNs (Monaco, pdf.js and three.js from cdnjs; marked, KaTeX and the three.js controls from jsDelivr; fonts from Google Fonts), and its search feature sends the typed query to en.wikipedia.org and api.duckduckgo.com. Features that open files from GitHub talk to GitHub. None of that is model compute, but a privacy claim must not hide it: the requirement is to self-host every asset and make web search opt-in, or remove it, before M7 ( index.html , lines 11 to 25 and 5845 to 5906). Integrity, not secrecy, of the model file. The SHA-256 check proves the file is the released one. The model is public, so there is nothing to hide in it.

114.body: The desktop client is a planned app you install on your laptop. It shows the same interface as the web client, but it runs the model as native code rather than inside a browser, which should make it faster. It can open your project folders, it remembers your conversations between sessions in a durable local store, and it works with no internet connection. The target machine is an M1-class laptop. This page is a specification, not a description of working software. No desktop app project exists in the repository yet, and there is no trained model for it to run. The owner asked for a spec only in this round (decision 8, 19 October 2026). Nothing ships until a trained model passes milestones M1 to M8. Labels used below: proof (derived from definitions or code), measurement (a recorded run with its artifact), hypothesis (untested). Words in this spec such as must are requirements, not claims about existing code. See the glossary . A laptop outline split in two. Left half, "webview": the shared Studio interface (editor, chat, model manager). Right half, "Rust core": four boxes — the integer model engine (uor-r4-integer), the memory store (uor-r4-object-store), a scoped file-access layer, and a model manager with an update checker. Arrows between the halves are labelled "Tauri commands". The model file and the memory store sit on a disk icon inside the laptop. A single dashed arrow leaves the laptop, labelled "optional: check for a new model release", and nothing else crosses the border. Same interface as the web client; the engine, the memory and the file access run as native Rust inside the app. Only an optional update check uses the network.

115.body: Goals. Run the released UORLUT01 model natively, under the D11 integer contract, on an M1-class laptop. Share the web client's interface, so there is one interface to maintain. Give the model access to the user's chosen project folders, for coding help. Keep durable conversation memory on disk (the D19 line), so a conversation can be closed and resumed exactly. Work fully offline after install. Non-goals. No cloud model, no account, no telemetry, no server component, and no second model format. Training and evaluation stay on GPUs ( charter , section 3.5).

Rust is the project's default language ( charter , section 3.11), so the backend can link the project's crates directly. Component Built from Exists today? 117.body: Install. The installer carries the app and, optionally, the model file. If the model is not bundled, the first run downloads it once ( update and download ). Load. The model manager reads the file, checks its SHA-256 against the release pin, and passes the bytes to the engine. The UORLUT01 reader checks every offset and length and returns an error rather than crashing on a malformed file ( format.rs ; proof by reading the code). Chat. The interface sends the user's text to a Rust command. The engine steps token by token with integer adds, shifts and table look-ups and streams tokens back to the page. Remember. At the end of a turn, the app saves the session state as a UR4SESS1 snapshot and stores conversation bytes in the object store. The store cuts bytes into 32-byte pieces arranged in a hashed three-way tree, so repeated content is stored once and any byte range can be read back and checked ( object-store dossier ). Storing session snapshots in the store is a design note, not yet done. Resume. On reopening, the app restores the snapshot, and the conversation continues token for token. That is the M3 restore bar ( project track , M3). Work on files. When the user asks about code, the app reads files only from granted folders and passes their text to the model as context.
117.breadcrumbs: The three products » The desktop client (specification) » Data flow
117.title: Data flow

118.body: The browser runs the engine as WebAssembly in one worker. A native build can use the processor's vector units (NEON on Apple silicon) and several threads. The project already has native table kernels for NEON and AVX2, though they belong to an older, frozen engine (crates/uor-r4-simd). That native will be faster is a hypothesis. Nobody has timed WebAssembly against native on the same file. No decode speed exists for any D11 artifact. The only native D11 speeds on record are from older float models served exactly by the integer engine: 68 to 80 tokens per second on 8 threads for a 29M model, which is evaluation throughput over 64 scored windows rather than decode ( D11 serving record ), and 184.58 tokens per second on one thread for input-driven forward passes, which is not free-running generation either ( lut-serving dossier ). M5 is the milestone that measures laptop cost: ms per token, peak memory, mJ per token and weights read per token ( project track , M5). Serving on the user's laptop is allowed. The charter says serving the exported D11 file on client devices, including Apple silicon, is the product, and D24's GPU-only rule does not apply ( charter , section 3.6).

119.body: D19 makes grounded conversation and durable memory the first priority ( D19 ). The object store was split out as its own crate for this purpose on 14 October (D34). What it has shown, all on test data ( measurement ): 60 tests pass, and a pure-Python client pulled a 256 KiB object byte-identically from the Rust server ( conformance record ). A 23-byte read of a 32,768-byte object touched 8 authenticated nodes, 384 bytes ( object-store dossier ). Repeated content compresses well (7,776 bytes stored in 380), but unique content expands about 2.17 times (32,768 bytes become 70,972) ( D19 store record ). Never tested: any model reading from the store, the M3 memory bars on a real model, and storage cost on real chat logs ( object-store dossier ). The store keeps exact identity (what was said, where, in which version) separate from any geometric address, as the charter requires (section 3.12).

121.body: Model files are versioned releases. Each is one UORLUT01 file with a published SHA-256 ( releases ). The app never runs an unpinned file. First download. 125.body: A release is how a finished model reaches people: a numbered version, a file you can download, and a fingerprint (a checksum) that proves the file is exactly the one that was tested. For UOR-R4 the file is meant to be one integer-only model file in a format called UORLUT01, released at milestone M8. That release does not exist. Two old software releases are on GitHub from the summer, plus one pinned-corpus data release, but both software releases belong to an earlier engine and neither is a qualified model. The release automation still targets that older engine too. This page explains the file format, the release machinery as it is, the Hugging Face repositories, and how checksums bind them together. Nothing ships until a trained model passes M1 to M8. Labels used below: proof (derived from definitions or code), measurement (a recorded run with its artifact), hypothesis (untested). See the glossary . flowchart LR P["Trained model<br/>(GPU, offline)"] --> E["Export to UORLUT01<br/>+ export gap"] E --> H["SHA-256 of the file"] H --> R["Versioned release<br/>vX.Y, notes bind scores"] R --> W["Web client<br/>verifies, caches"] R --> D["Desktop client<br/>verifies, stores"] R --> C["uor-chat CLI"] S[("Private HF store<br/>MD5SUMS / SHA256SUMS")] -.inputs and results.-> P The planned path from a trained model to the clients. Every hop carries a checksum. The release box exists only as a plan for this model; the old pipeline served a different engine.

125.title: Releases and artifacts

126.body: UORLUT01 is the container the integer engine reads. Its layout, from the reader format.rs ( proof by reading the code): The 8-byte magic string UORLUT01, then the header length as a little-endian 64-bit integer. A JSON header with the schema name, the model's shape, the group size, numeric settings, a list of matrices and tables, the exporter's provenance (never read by the serving arithmetic), and an optional record of a trained-in rotation snap, with the SHA-256 of its root set. Zero padding to a 64-byte boundary, then the data sections at 64-byte-aligned offsets. Each weight matrix stored as 4-bit codes, two per byte, with one scale byte per row and group. The scale byte holds a 4-bit mantissa \(m\) and a 4-bit exponent step \(d_e\), meaning a group scale of \((16+m)\,2^{\,e_{\text{base}}+d_e-4}\). Small integer tables (16-bit or 32-bit) for the few nonlinear steps. Three schemas exist: lut-stack/1 (a softmax attention read), /2 (adds a pointer head) and /3 (a softmax-free flock rank read). The first two serve exp-table softmax reads, which the no-squashing rule bans. No schema fits today's rules as it stands: all three also carry SiLU and GELU tables and stream dense 4-bit weight maps through a table-based product, which the charter excludes, so a new table-native schema is likely needed ( lut-serving dossier ). A built-in fingerprint. When the reader parses a file, it computes the SHA-256 of all its bytes and keeps it with the parsed model (format.rs, line 557). A release can therefore pin that hash, and a client can refuse any file that does not match. Safe loading. Every offset, length and product of sizes is checked, so a malformed file returns an error rather than crashing. A file that declares a product-key memory is refused outright, because the integer kernel for it is not built ( format.rs ). Saved sessions use a separate format, UR4SESS1, which records a conversation's state so it can be restored byte for byte ( session_codec.rs ).

13.body: In one paragraph. A transformer is built from a handful of standard parts: a tokenizer, an embedding table, a position signal, attention, feed-forward layers, normalization, an output layer, a loss and an optimizer. UOR-R4 tries to replace each part with a geometric or exact mechanism that avoids softmax and matrix multiplication. This page puts each transformer part beside the project's replacement and says how far that replacement has got. The short version: most parts have a candidate, and several candidates are built and tested. Two parts have no candidate at all: position and normalization. No two replacements have yet been trained together into a model that beats simple word-count tables ( audit synthesis , section 1). Two columns joined by arrows. The left column lists the parts of a transformer from input to output: tokenizer, embedding, position, attention, copy heads, context memory, feed-forward, gates, normalization, output head, loss, optimizer and runtime. The right column shows the UOR-R4 mechanism for each, coloured by status: green for ACTIVE, amber for READY, grey for PARKED. Two right-hand boxes, beside "position" and "normalization", are empty, drawn with dashed red outlines and labelled "no mechanism". Each transformer part beside its replacement. Colour gives the status. The two dashed boxes are the gaps. Terms are in the glossary . Labels follow docs/formal_vocabulary.md : proof , measurement or hypothesis .

132.body: UOR-R4 turns text into a short list of whole numbers per word, looks back at a few earlier words by walking a small tree of addresses, and picks the stored word nearest to what it found. It never turns scores into probabilities and never multiplies large grids of numbers. This page follows one piece of text through that whole chain and marks each stage as built, trained, or missing. The honest summary is short. Most stages exist and pass small fixed tests. None of them has learned language yet: the best trained model so far is worse than a plain table of word counts ( K16 outcome ). The project is pre-alpha, and 0 of its 8 milestones are complete (STATUS.md). A left-to-right pipeline of nine boxes: text, tokenizer, token table, ordered context, reads (Route, Flock, Relation), shared writer with admission, rank-margin loss, discrete learning on the GPU, and export to a D11 integer artifact that is then served. Each box is coloured built, trained or missing, and four dashed empty boxes mark the slots with no mechanism: position, normalization, feed-forward on the discrete path, and an exporter for a trained model. The current pipeline. Solid boxes exist in crates/uor-r4-discrete. Dashed boxes are slots a transformer fills that this model has not filled.

133.body: Built means the source exists and passes its finite construction controls. These are small, fixed GPU tests that show the code does what it says. A control is not a language result. Trained in means the stage took part in at least one learning run with a recorded result. It does not mean the run helped. Missing means no code exists, or no mechanism has been assigned. Labels follow docs/formal_vocabulary.md . Proof means derived from definitions or code. Measurement means a recorded run. Hypothesis means an untested idea. NOT_RUN is never a pass.

134.body: The current model lives in crates/uor-r4-discrete . The code-level map is docs/architecture.md . 1. Tokenizer (built; fixed before training). Text is cut into numbered pieces by a byte-level BPE tokenizer with 4,096 pieces, identity d36d3e87. Every corpus, test panel and trained artifact is pinned to it ( tokenizer ). A 16,384-piece trainer exists as tooling only, and no model has used it. 2. Token table (built; trained in). Each of the \(V=4096\) tokens owns \(B=4\) blocks of 8 whole numbers, so its vector has width 32. Each block is always one of 16 roots from a single orbit of the E8 lattice; each root is a signed rearrangement of \((2,2,0,0,0,0,0,0)\). The model does not use all 240 E8 roots. The same table encodes a token as input, carries it as memory, and ranks it as output; that is the shared vector writer. Exact token identity is kept separately from this geometric address. There are three ways to fill the table at the start, and they matter a great deal: Start What it gives Source Seeded default At most 16 distinct vectors for 4,096 tokens ( measurement ) pilot diagnosis PrimeZeta injective 4,096 of 4,096 tokens get unique vectors ( measurement ) construction Address-structured cells (A8) 1,351 of 3,847 copy-successor targets reachable at zero training, against 127 for the injective PrimeZeta start ( measurement ) pre-flight An injective code is possible in principle, because \(16^4=65{,}536\ge 4{,}096\) ( proof , from the block and root counts). See prime-zeta-codebook and address-cells . 3. Ordered context (built; not learned). The most recent tokens form a window of at most 243 positions (\(3^5\)). Recorded runs used 192. A ternary tree built by SpiralCore, the project's exact-arithmetic geometry library, puts those positions at its leaves in order ( spiralcore-fbs ). Which position a read lands on is decided by address, not by a score over all positions. 4. Reads (built; trained in, but no read's own value is isolated). A read turns the window into one integer vector \(q\) of width 32. There are three, each a hard selection with no softmax: Route walks the tree, one nearest port per level, and returns one earlier position's vector rotated along the path. Flock keeps a few nearest earlier positions, rotates each into the current frame, sums them and snaps to a root. It was trained only inside the Relation runs. Relation is Flock plus a rerank along link types such as "the word after the earlier copy". It has trained twice, and both runs stopped before a verdict. Route is the base read of every trained artifact, yet it received only 20 learning proposals in 16,404 updates ( attention state ). Nobody has switched a read off to see what it adds. 5. Shared writer and admission (built; trained in). The writer gives each token a cell from the root numbers of its first and last block: \(c(t)=(\rho_{\text{first}}(t),\rho_{\text{last}}(t))\), so there are \(16\times16=256\) cells. It opens the \(K\) occupied cells nearest to \(q\) by L1 distance (8 in the lineage of record, at most 16), then picks the nearest token inside them. Ties go to the lowest id. No probabilities are formed. This shortlist is admission . Proof. A target outside the opened cells can never be chosen, whatever the read did. So admission caps everything upstream. Rung 0's top-1 bar was 1,941 rows, but only 1,920 targets were admitted at the end, so the bar was unreachable ( Stage A sweep ). 6. Loss (built; trained in). The score is an integer rank-margin hinge : the right token must beat its strongest rival by a fixed gap, and the loss is the shortfall. It has no likelihood, so it yields no bits per byte. 7. Discrete learning (built; trained in). One table entry is tried in all 16 legal states on the GPU, and the best is kept only if it strictly lowers the loss. See training . 8. Export (missing for any trained model). The learned table is already integers, so there is no float to round. But no exporter turns a trained snapshot into a D11 artifact, and no export gap has been measured. The existing table engine's schemas /1 and /2 serve softmax through exponent tables, and all three schemas stream dense 4-bit maps with SiLU and GELU tables, so a new table-native schema is likely needed (audit reading, lut-serving dossier; hypothesis ). 9. Serving (engine built; never used for this model). The D11 engine runs integer artifacts with no multiply instruction. Its audits pass: 44 native symbol ranges ( project track , M4) and 7 of 7 WebAssembly serving functions ( WASM runtime record ) are free of multiplies. It has served only older models, which missed the milestone bar (the 19.9M-parameter stack reached 0.933 bits per byte against 0.90, "NOT MET by 0.033"). Tokens per second for the discrete model has never been measured ( lut-serving ).

138.body: Most language models learn by working out a smooth slope for every number inside them and nudging all the numbers a little. This model does not. It takes one entry of its table, tries every legal turn that entry can make, counts the mistakes after each turn using whole numbers, and keeps the best turn only if it beats leaving the entry alone. The method is exact, cheap per step and runs on the GPU. So far it has moved some counts but has not produced better language, and every new training run needs the owner's personal release. A loop for one training batch. A batch of 64 example rows feeds a baseline pass, then 16 parallel lanes (the current state plus 15 rotations) each score every row. A chooser lights the lowest integer loss, with ties going to staying put. An apply step commits only a strict improvement, and a validate step re-checks the stored table on the GPU. A side panel shows the same loop scoring K coordinates per launch (BVG-K) and committing them as one block only if the joint loss beats the best single move. A second side panel shows the offline float path as a separate module that must end in an export-gap check. One batch of discrete learning: score every legal move on 64 rows, choose the lowest integer loss, commit only a strict gain, then verify the stored result. Labels follow docs/formal_vocabulary.md : proof is derived from definitions or code, measurement is a recorded run, hypothesis is untested. The mechanism page, discrete-learning , is the short form of this page and carries the full run history.

139.body: What is learned. The model holds three kinds of coordinate . A vector block is one of the four 8-number blocks of one token's vector. A route frame is one of 64 signed-axis rotations of 8-dimensional space, one per routing stage. A gate is a switch that takes the values \(-1\), \(0\) or \(+1\). A vector block is always one of 16 roots of an E8 orbit, so it has 16 legal states, counting "stay as it is" ( architecture ). The learning step (definition). Training visits one coordinate \(\theta\) per batch. A batch is 64 rows of training text, and which rows can count is fixed by the baseline. For each candidate move \(m\) among the identity and 15 rotations, the machine replays the read and the writer and adds up the integer rank-margin loss : \[L(m)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal R}\ell\big(x;\ \theta\leftarrow m\big),\qquad m\in\{\mathrm{id},m_1,\dots,m_{15}\}.\] It chooses \(m^*=\arg\min_m L(m)\). Ties go to the identity, then to the lowest resulting port number, then to the lowest move index. It applies \(m^*\) only if \(L(m^*)<L(\mathrm{id})\), and then re-checks the stored table on the GPU. Nothing is sampled, and no floating-point number appears in the step. Consequence (proof, from the definition). Every committed move strictly lowers the loss on its own batch, and the new state is always a legal state. The rule says nothing about rows outside the batch. A move that helps its 64 rows can push other targets out of the shortlist, and that is the failure behind the early stops in the table below. Coverage (proof, by arithmetic). One pass is 16,404 batches of 64 rows, which is 1,049,856 target rows. The training split has 2,425,925 targets, so one pass sees 43.3% of them. Each coordinate is visited about once per pass, with about 64 rows of evidence (chief architect's review §3.4).

14.body: Every mechanism has exactly one of three statuses, set on the mechanism board : ACTIVE : on the current model path, crates/uor-r4-discrete. READY : built and tested, but never trained into a model. PARKED : the forms tried so far failed or broke a rule. The mechanism stays open, and its page lists what would reopen it. There is no "retired" or "dead" status. A failed run closes one configuration, never a mechanism ( charter , section 4.1). Today the board has 10 ACTIVE, 4 READY and 13 PARKED mechanisms. A passing test shows that code does what it claims. It is not a trained capability, and a test marked NOT_RUN is not a pass.

140.body: All model compute is GPU-only; a host fallback is a defect to fix ( charter §3.5). The kernels live in discrete.cu and its generated siblings. The build checks the emitted GPU code and rejects any floating-point type, tensor-core instruction or approximate exponent (crates/uor-r4-discrete/build.rs, PTX admission audit). Ordinary counterfactual. One block of 16 threads, one thread per move. Each thread walks every row in turn and recomputes the baseline. A route proposal took 3.903 s against 37.8 ms for a plain forward pass, which projected to about 17.8 hours for one 16,404-batch pass ( measurement and projection, unverified, driver cost ). A later diagnostic put this kernel at 99.99% of a proposal ( sub-phase diagnostic ). Row-parallel counterfactual (rows_v1). It computes the baseline once per row and each virtual move once per (row, lane), then a reducer replays the ordinary loop over those records in row order. So 64 rows by 16 lanes run as 1,024 threads. It is opt-in, and it matched the ordinary kernel's losses on every finite case checked (72, 108 and 288 cases in the three tables of the rows parity record; 1,085 in all across the attempt files, per the documentation reconciliation ). Speed (measurement). At vocabulary 4096, 4 blocks, context 192, \(K=8\), 64 rows, on one RTX 5090, the median of five proposals: Read and coordinate Ordinary Row-parallel Ratio Route, vector block 3.843 s 0.0691 s 55.6 times Relation, gate 4.144 s 0.0728 s 56.9 times This is the "56 times" figure. The timing is non-gating and was not qualified (qualified=false). The A8 control arm later completed 16,404 batches in 1,967 s, or 0.12 s per batch ( A8 dose ). It used a different read, so treat that as a rough size of the gain.

141.body: BVG-K means batched verified coordinates , with \(K\) the batch size. One row-parallel launch occupies at most 8 of an RTX 5090's 170 multiprocessors, so the card sits mostly idle. BVG-K scores \(K\) coordinates in one launch (1 to 64 are supported), chooses the best move for each, and commits the whole block only if its joint loss beats the best single move. Scoring (measurement, quoted). About 16 times faster at \(K=16\) than scoring one coordinate at a time, from the first qualifier ( BVG-K scoring ). Block apply (measurement, on fixtures). 259 ms at \(K=16\) with joint verification, about 8 times faster than 16 single proposals at roughly 130 ms each ( qualifier ). As a learning law, never run. BVG-K has passed construction tests only. It is the matched discrete competitor that any float method must beat.

142.body: On 18 October the owner revised the discrete-only rule: floating point is legal in offline training . A float forward pass, gradients and an optimizer may be used. Three things still hold ( D37 ): The bans on expensive operations stand. No softmax or other squashing function, no dense matrix multiplication, GPU only, and the path must stay geometric. Float lives in a separate module. It gets its own scanned entry, added with its pre-registration. It never goes in the discrete crate or in crates/uor-r4-training. The integer artifact is the boundary. Every float candidate reports its export gap , the loss in quality when its weights become the integer file. A gap above the two-seed noise band disqualifies it, and a float score alone qualifies nothing (D39 item 5). No float sheet is registered. The order set in D39 item 4 is the read-code capacity capture (W2), then BVG-K (W3), then a single float-credit sheet only if W2 points at the learning law and W3 fails. The chief architect expects the export gap to be structurally non-zero, because the table entries are exact roots with no continuous scale ( hypothesis , docs/labs/course-correction-2026-10-18/audits/d37-reactivation-architect.md §3.3).

146.body: The model never sees letters or words. It sees a stream of numbered pieces of text, and a small program called a tokenizer cuts text into those pieces and turns them back into text. The project's data is chat-shaped text, prepared into files of piece numbers with one fixed tokenizer of 4,096 pieces. Every prepared file carries a fingerprint of that tokenizer, so a result can never be quietly compared across two different ways of cutting text. The data is small: the training set for the current model path is about 7.5 million tokens. A larger corpus, written once by an open donor model under a narrow owner exception, is planned but has not been generated. Labels used below: proof means derived from definitions or code, measurement means a recorded run, hypothesis means an untested idea. See docs/formal_vocabulary.md and the glossary . A sentence at the bottom as bytes, merge arcs lifting pairs into larger pieces, and the final piece numbers on top, with the number 84 shown as the two pieces 8 and 4. Beside it, a ladder of 3,837 merges and a strip from raw text through the tokenizer to a prepared corpus file with check marks for file hash, token count and tokenizer identity. Bytes become pieces by repeated merging, and the tokenizer's fingerprint travels with every prepared file. A two-digit number is still two pieces. flowchart LR T["text: chat and memory dialogues"] --> P["Rust corpus preparation"] TOK["tokenizer d36d3e87, 4,096 pieces"] --> P D["distill-d1: planned, one-time, not generated"] -.-> P P --> U["UORT v1 file: header, 16-bit ids, response mask"] U --> C{"driver checks file hash, token count, tokenizer"} C -->|all match| TR["training and evaluation on the GPU"] C -->|any mismatch| X["refuse to read"] From text to a model run. The dotted arrow is a plan, not a file that exists.

147.body: What it is (definition). A byte-level byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokenizer. It starts from the 256 possible bytes, so any text can be encoded. It then learns the most frequent adjacent pairs and glues them into bigger pieces. This is a standard technique and is not novel here. Layout of the pinned tokenizer. Pieces 0, 1 and 2 are start, end and unknown. Pieces 3 to 258 are the 256 single bytes. The rest are learned merges: \[3+256+3837=4096 .\] Training (definition). Count each adjacent pair over the unique pieces of text in the corpus (pre-tokens), weighted by how often each occurs. Merge the pair with the highest count into a new piece and recount only the words that contain it. Repeat until the vocabulary is full. Ties go to the pair whose left, then right, piece string sorts first, so the result is the same every time. Special tokens are atomic, and no merge crosses a special token, a pre-token boundary or an input file. Encoding then applies the merges in rank order: a table look-up with no learned arithmetic ( training.rs , lib.rs ). Identity. The tokenizer crate computes a blake3 content address of the raw tokenizer.json bytes, and the discrete driver pins each file by SHA-256. The pinned tokenizer is written d36d3e87…; its full 64-hex SHA-256 is listed in the donor-corpus sheet . A different tokenizer is therefore a different corpus. The 16,384-piece trainer. On 19 October a Rust command, train-bpe, landed for building a tokenizer of any size from 259 to 65,536 pieces ( train-bpe.rs , record ). It is deterministic, refuses to overwrite a file, and by default accepts 64 MiB of input. Checks compared its merge ranks and its segmentation with an independent exhaustive recount over 40 small test corpora, and a synthetic 8,192-document fixture reached exactly 16,384 pieces. Measurement, of the tool only. It changes no active file. No tokenizer has been swapped, and no model has been trained or scored on any tokenizer other than d36d3e87. Whether 16,384 pieces help the model is a hypothesis . Numbers are split. The vocabulary has no multi-digit piece, so 84 is the pieces 8 and 4. In an older chat model's 9 October acceptance run, memory rows with a distractor and a number as the stored value passed 1 of 11, against 9 of 23 with a word as the value. A diagnosis found no multi-digit token, and that the right value was not emitted rather than confused with a distractor. An untrained probe showed the project's number codec already stores two-digit values in order, so storage is not the cause; the failure sits in the learned read and write path. Both are measurements , on an older float model ( diagnosis , probe ). Whether digit-split numbers still hurt once the discrete read can address an exact value is open.

148.body: Format (definition). A prepared corpus (UORT v1) is a 64-byte header followed by 16-bit piece numbers, with start-of-document markers and an optional one-byte-per-token response mask. The mask marks the reply tokens, the only ones scored as targets. Context resets at each start marker. Before reading, the discrete driver checks each file's SHA-256, the token count and the tokenizer file ( corpus.rs ). A DialogueProtocol object fixes how roles and turns are written out, so training, test panels and chat all use identical token segments ( dialogue.rs ). Preparation is host-side Rust bookkeeping, not model compute ( prepare-knowledge-corpus.rs , prepare-chat-parquet.rs , mix-chat-corpus.rs ).

One open-weight donor, openai/gpt-oss-120b, may run once, offline, on one declared rented GPU, to write one corpus named distill-d1 ( D41 , record ). The target is 30,000,000 student tokens, with a floor of 20 million and a ceiling of 50 million. Each document is at most 200 tokens. The mixture is conversation 35%, question answering 20%, short code 20%, short reasoning prose 15% and general prose 10%. A pilot of about 1 million tokens (about $2) comes first, and production at 30 million tokens is projected at about $52, or $63 with retries. These costs are planning estimates, not invoices. 154.body: A finished model has to leave the lab and run on an ordinary laptop or in a web browser. The project's rule is that the file it ships contains only whole numbers, and that the program running it uses only adds, shifts and table look-ups: no decimal (floating-point) arithmetic and no multiply instruction. The program that does this exists, and a checker has counted its machine instructions. But it has only ever run older models that fell short of their targets, plus a synthetic stand-in. No model built under today's rules has been exported to it yet, so nobody can chat with the project's model on a laptop today. Labels used below: proof means derived from definitions or code, measurement means a recorded run, hypothesis means an untested idea. See docs/formal_vocabulary.md and the glossary . Four boxes left to right. A table of float weights, trained offline. A snap step that rounds each weight to a 4-bit code with a group scale. An integer table file (UORLUT01). A serving engine that answers each step with table look-ups, adds and shifts. A bracket over the first three boxes marks the export gap, the quality lost by snapping. Training may use decimals; serving may not. The snap from one to the other is where quality can be lost, and that loss is the export gap.

155.body: Offline half. Training runs on rented GPUs and may use floating point. The owner's rule (D37, 18 October) allows float forward passes, gradients and optimizers offline, with two limits that stay: no matrix multiplication and no squashing functions such as softmax ( D37 ). The project's active learning path, the discrete model in crates/uor-r4-discrete, is stricter still: it is integer from end to end ( GPU and CUDA ). Served half. What ships is "D11", the project's serving contract ( D11 , 27 September). It has five rules: Rule Plain meaning R1 No floating point and no maths library R2 No multiply or divide instruction in any served kernel. Products of runtime values use tables or exact geometry R3 Reading every stored weight for every token is an interim stage, not the end state (D5) R4 No transformer backbone R5 Energy is claimed only when measured Serving on the user's own device, including browser WebAssembly, is the product and is allowed ( charter , section 3.6). The border between the halves is the export, and it is where a float-trained candidate is judged.

156.body: The container (definition). UORLUT01 stores weights as 4-bit codes in groups of 32. Each group has a one-byte scale, built from a 4-bit mantissa and a 4-bit exponent. A few small integer tables cover the nonlinear steps: square root, decay rates, exp, SiLU, GELU and arcosh (SiLU, GELU and exp are squashing-type tables; see the compliance note under "Where it stands") ( format.rs ). A projection with no multiply (proof by construction). For a weight row \(w_{ij}=s_g\,q_{ij}\) with 4-bit code \(q_{ij}\) and group scale \(s_g\), the output is \[y_i=\sum_j s_{g(j)}\,q_{ij}\,x_j .\] Instead of multiplying \(q_{ij}\) by \(x_j\), the engine builds once per activation a 16-entry table \(T_j[q]=q\,x_j\) for \(q=0,\dots,15\). Each entry comes from the one before by adding \(x_j\). Each weight's code then selects an entry, and the group scale is applied with shifts and adds. Four output rows share each table ( kernels.rs ). Two runtime values multiplied together (proof). A score, a gate or a value mix needs a true product of two numbers that only exist at run time. The engine reads it from a table of the sixteen multiples of one operand, built by repeated addition, indexed by the radix-16 digits (base-16 digits) of the other operand and summed with shifts (stack_mul_u64 and stack_mul_u128 in kernels.rs ). Write \(b=\sum_k 16^k d_k\) with each digit \(d_k\in\{0,\dots,15\}\) and let \(T_a[q]=q\,a\), built as \(T_a[q+1]=T_a[q]+a\). Then \[ab=\sum_k 16^k\,T_a[d_k(b)] ,\] which is exact by the definition of base-16 digits, and each term is a table read followed by a shift. (An alternative that D11 rule R2 would also allow is the quarter-square identity \(ab=\lfloor (a+b)^2/4\rfloor-\lfloor (a-b)^2/4\rfloor\), which holds for all integers; the training crate uses it in addressing_arms.rs, but the serving engine does not.) Normalisation uses an integer square root, computed digit by digit, and the sampler is an integer min-p rule. That sampler filters on probability mass read from the exp tables, so it is part of the compliance gap described under "Where it stands". Exact geometry as tables. Where the model uses geometry, the tables are exact: the Cayley table of the 120-element icosian group (about 14 KiB), a 1,025-entry arcosh table for Lorentz read scores, and the Q30 Hopf observation. The integer crate's native_geometry.rs provides the typed H4 geometry and checked integer arithmetic that the qualified native build uses; no discrete-model export uses it yet ( native_geometry.rs ). A saved conversation (definition). The UR4SESS1 format saves a session's state and restores it byte for byte ( session_codec.rs ).

157.body: The audit disassembles the compiled release program and counts three kinds of instruction over the serving functions: Class I multiply, Class II divide, Class III floating point. The scripts are audit_zero_matmul_serving.py (native) and audit_zero_matmul_wasm.py (WebAssembly, with a call-graph mode). They are existing Python scripts; porting them to Rust is an open question. Native: 44 symbol ranges audited, none with a forbidden instruction ( project track , milestone M4). Measurement. WebAssembly: 7 of 7 serving functions (not modules) with multiply, divide and float counts all 0, in the runtime merged as UOR-Foundation/uor-r4#2654 ( record ). It was written by an outside contributor and hardened in review before merge. Measurement. What the audit proves is absence: those instructions are not in the audited functions. It says nothing about model quality, and it does not cover every function in the binary. The record also lists three limits. First, the WebAssembly SIMD kernels are fixtures that nothing calls; the serving path still uses the scalar table kernel. Second, the demo in docs/wasm-serving/ does not run from a clean clone until its bundle is built. Third, the serving-wasm build compiles the model, sampling and tables modules unconditionally. Compliance with the "presence counts" rule (D29) rests on the feature defaulting off plus link-time removal, an interpretation that DECISIONS.md does not record.

158.body: Definition. The export gap of a candidate is its served score minus its float score, on the same evaluator and the same positions. It is the price of snapping. The charter says a float candidate whose gap is above the two-seed noise band is disqualified ( charter , section 3.7). Past gaps come from an older float model, the "geometric stack", not from today's discrete model. Bits per byte (BPB) and nats are different units, and lower is better in both. Date What was exported Gap Source 28 Sep 7.15M stack, round-to-nearest 4-bit +0.0362 nats (gate 0.02) record 28 Sep Same stack, GPTQ rounding +0.0257 nats (gate 0.02) same record 29 Sep Same stack after 1,000 quantisation-aware updates +0.010637 nats; marked pending a re-run record 8 Oct 19.9M chat stack, identical positions 0.00883 BPB; engine difference about 1e-6 #1915 9 Oct Matched float, reference and integer runs at 512 windows 0.009288 BPB; engine 2.7e-7 pin Two readings follow, both measurements on those older models. The integer engine adds almost nothing of its own: it reproduces its reference to about a millionth. And the whole gap is weight rounding, with the output layer the largest share in the 28 September record. Two cautions apply. The 8 October pair 0.877 float and 0.933 served was never like-for-like, because it mixed 512 and 64 evaluation windows. 16.body: Gap 1: position. A transformer adds a signal that says where each token sits in the sequence. No UOR-R4 mechanism is assigned to this job, and no lawful evidence exists for one. The current model keeps the most recent tokens in order at the leaves of a small tree, so order is present in its layout, but nothing is learned about it ( the model page ). The nearest result is about carrying a running state by quaternion rotation. It beat no rotation by 0.071 and 0.077 nats (a nat is a unit of prediction error; lower is better), but in a model that still used softmax attention, a sigmoid gate and dense layers, with 332,928 fewer parameters in the comparison arm ( transport record ). So "rotation can carry order" is a hypothesis . Gap 2: normalization. A transformer rescales its signals between layers so they stay in a workable range. UOR-R4 has no designed mechanism for this. Snapping each block back to one of its fixed lattice points might play that role, but no record says so or tests it ( mechanism board ). This is also a hypothesis .

161.body: The project trains and tests its model on graphics cards (GPUs), not on the laptop's processor. The programs that run on a GPU are called kernels, and the project writes them in CUDA, NVIDIA's language for GPUs. Every kernel is compiled before it runs. For the active model, an audit reads the compiled result and refuses instructions the project has banned: decimal arithmetic, tensor-core matrix instructions and approximate exponentials. The cards are rented by the hour from a marketplace through one script, under hard limits on how many and how much. The rented GPUs are used for qualification runs and a few short training doses. No trained language model has come out of them yet. Labels used below: proof means derived from definitions or code, measurement means a recorded run, hypothesis means an untested idea. See docs/formal_vocabulary.md and the glossary . flowchart LR subgraph K["What the active kernels compute"] READ["read and write one vector (forward)"] PROP["score candidate moves (counterfactual)"] PICK["choose and apply one move"] EVAL["evaluate: top-1 and top-8 hits"] CNT["count tokens: frequency baselines"] end subgraph B["How they reach the GPU"] NVCC["nvcc builds PTX ahead of time"] AUD{"PTX admission audit"} CUBIN["cubin and resource report"] LOAD["driver loads the prebuilt module"] STOP["build fails"] end K --> NVCC --> AUD AUD -->|admitted| CUBIN --> LOAD AUD -->|rejected| STOP The kernel map. Source files compile to PTX before anything runs, and the audit sits between compiling and loading. There is no run-time compiler.

162.body: The active model is crates/uor-r4-discrete, and its kernels are integer only. The header of discrete.cu says model values use gather, sign, add and subtract, comparison and finite action-table look-ups, and that storage indexing uses integer products. It has 577 lines and 12 entry points: Kernels What they compute discrete_init, discrete_encode, discrete_export_token_cells Set up the vector table from a seed, encode token numbers as vectors, export each token's address cells discrete_forward The read (route, flock or relation) and the shared writer: predictions, losses and traces discrete_counterfactual Score candidate moves in 16 fixed lanes, without changing the model discrete_choose, discrete_apply, discrete_validate Pick the best proposal, commit one move, check the state discrete_evaluate, discrete_evaluation_aggregate Top-1 and top-8 hits, with all arithmetic and denominator checks done on the GPU discrete_count, discrete_count_score Count token frequencies and rank them: the simple count baselines a model is compared with Five more modules are generated from discrete.cu at build time, each its own source, PTX and cubin, so the earlier images stay byte for byte unchanged: a diagnostic decomposition, baseline reuse, row-parallel scoring (rows, 3 entry points), scoring several coordinates per launch (rowsk, 5) and selecting and committing a set of moves (bvgk, 8). The build also writes exact geometry tables from the core crate: AXES[512], COMPOSE[4096], INVERSE[64], 16 carrier roots, a breadth-first reachability map and 15 generators ( build.rs ). Other CUDA code in the repository is not on the active path: File Lines Status uor-r4-training/src/cuda_stack.cu (22 kernels: Hamilton gate, rate select, normalisation, quaternion and recurrence scans, margin ranking, Adam update) 859 Held. 163.body: Compile ahead of time (definition). The build script calls nvcc -ptx -std=c++17 -arch=compute_NN, where NN is the card's capability from the explicit UOR_NVCC_ARCH setting. NVIDIA's run-time compiler, NVRTC, is banned project-wide (D29, amended 13 October): what nvcc compiles at build time is exactly what the driver may load, and banned code present in a module counts even if never launched ( D29 ). Two older pages, the CUDA training runbook and the pods quickstart , still describe NVRTC. They were written before the ban. The admission audit (proof by inspection of the code). The audit reads the emitted PTX text, not the CUDA source, so a banned instruction cannot hide behind spelling. It strips comments, splits each line into tokens, and rejects the build if any token has a component named f16, f16x2, f32, f64, bf16, bf16x2, tf32, e4m3, e5m2, mma, wmma, wgmma, tcgen05, tensor or tensormap, or starts with ex2.approx. It also requires the set of .entry points to equal the declared inventory exactly: a missing, extra or duplicate entry fails. A self-test runs on every build. It must accept a clean module (floats inside comments are fine) and must reject add.f32, a .bf16 register, mma.sync, ex2.approx, an unexpected entry, a duplicate entry and missing entries. After admission, the same admitted PTX is assembled into a cubin for each of the six modules, and the build fails if the cubin is empty or its resource report is missing. What it does not say. Integer multiplies are allowed in these kernels, for example to compute indexes. This is a different rule from the serving contract, where no multiply instruction may appear at all ( serving and export ). The float training crate has no equivalent PTX audit, since float is legal there, and uses precision flags instead (-ftz=false -prec-div=true -prec-sqrt=true, and --fmad=false for the flock selector). Passing the audit shows which instructions are present. It does not show that a kernel computes the right thing. Correctness comes from separate controls on a pod. Not in continuous integration. No GitHub workflow mentions nvcc or CUDA. The standing checks compile without the cuda feature, and qualification runs on rented pods. For exact-head compile checks there is a recipe, scripts/pod/uor-cuda-check-remote . It rents one fresh RTX 5090 with CUDA 12.8 for 15 minutes (30 for the training crate), runs cargo check and then clippy, and tears the pod down ( compute guide ). It is compile and lint only, never a model run.

164.body: The rules are written in docs/labs/compute.md and printed by uor-pod itself. Rule What it says One tool Every pod action goes through scripts/pod/uor-pod. Nobody rents by hand Provider Vast.ai is the default since 13 October ( D26 ). Runpod is an emergency backup: up --wait falls back to it after 30 minutes with no Vast offer, and choosing it by hand needs --owner-approved Hosts Verified datacenter hosts only, with CUDA 12.8 or newer. Community hosts are not used, because their operator would hold the disk and the access token Ladder RTX 5090 first, then 4090, then RTX PRO 6000. A100, H100 and larger are refused without owner approval Caps At most 4 running pods and $8 an hour, counting both providers together Leases Each session leases the GPUs it uses, renews at least every 30 minutes, and releases when done. Another session's GPU is never yours, even idle; only an expired lease may be taken over Jobs One job per GPU, run detached under a lock, with a log ending in # exit=N Safety net A pod-side reaper deletes a pod with no live lease after 20 idle minutes Results down copies the run, job, pod and evaluation folders off the pod first, or uploads them to the private store. Pods are not kept as storage No fallback If no GPU is free and the caps are reached, wait or ask the owner. Never run model work on the laptop CPU The laptop does non-model work: editing, compiling CPU-only builds, static checks and grading stored outputs. All model compute is GPU work (D24). Serving a finished model on the user's own device is a separate matter and is allowed ( charter , section 3.6). Measured costs. On 13 October a verified datacenter RTX 5090 on Vast cost $0.469 an hour, against $1.19 an hour on Runpod. A fresh Vast pod took its toolchain, crate cache and binaries from the private store and was ready in 57 seconds, with nothing built ( measurement , compute guide ). The 19 October A8 dose ran on a Vast pod with two RTX 5090s at $1.816 an hour for about 62 minutes: about $1.9. That is a resource estimate, not an invoice, and storage and transfer were not measured. The owner typed the release for each arm personally ( record ). Scoring 16 candidate moves in one launch took a median 123.57 ms, against 125.51 ms for scoring one. All 5,130 coordinates matched the reference exactly, and a deliberately broken copy failed as it should. The earlier launch used only 8 of the card's 170 multiprocessors ( record ). Measurement , at that one shape. One full pass over every parameter of the discrete model is projected at about 17.8 hours for the route read and 19.2 for the flock read, roughly $16 to $17. 167.body: Most chat AIs predict the next word by multiplying very large grids of decimal numbers. UOR-R4 is a bet that a different set of tools can do the same job more cheaply: rotations in a few dimensions, exact whole-number addresses built from primes, and lookup tables. This section explains those tools one chapter at a time, with pictures. It also says which ones the model uses today and which are research that has not yet been put to work. The project is pre-alpha: 0 of its 8 milestones are complete, and no model holds a useful conversation yet ( STATUS.md ). A map of the geometric pieces and how they connect: the six-prime registry, semiprimes, the complete graph K6, the icosahedral axes, the 120 icosians, quaternions, Z[phi], octonions and the Fano plane, Cl(0,6) bivectors, E8, the Hopf map and VSA codes, with each link marked as verified maths, used in a model, pre-registered, or a labelling choice How the geometric pieces connect. Each arrow is one correspondence, and the table below says whether the link is forced by the mathematics or was chosen.
167.breadcrumbs: The geometry of UOR-R4 » The geometry of UOR-R4
167.title: The geometry of UOR-R4

168.body: The owner's rule for this project is that the core of the model is built from geometric mechanisms. The reason is a cost hypothesis. A transformer's expensive parts are dense matrix multiplication, a score for every possible next word, and storing every earlier position. Rotations, exact addresses and tables may be much cheaper on a laptop (a hypothesis: no efficiency has been measured yet). Whether they are also good enough to model language is the open question. These rules shape how the geometry is used. No softmax or squashing, no matrix multiplication. Softmax, sigmoid, tanh and softplus are banned in every executed model path ( D23 , D25), and so is matrix multiplication in training and serving (D25, D30). Attention itself is not banned: bounded geometric reads replace it. Research compute is GPU-only (D24). Serving the exported D11 integer artifact on a client device (CPU, WASM, Apple silicon) is the product and is allowed. It uses no floating point and no multiplier instruction. Floating point is for offline training only ( D37 ). Float never re-admits softmax, squashing or matrix multiplication. The active discrete path and the served model stay integer (D11), and every float-trained candidate must report its export gap, the quality lost when converting to the integer artifact. Geometry is a design priority, not a measured advantage. A failed experiment closes one configuration, never a whole mechanism ( D22 ). A passing check on a piece of mathematics does not show that the piece helps a language model. Labels on this page follow docs/formal_vocabulary.md : proof means derived from definitions or code, measurement means a recorded run, and hypothesis means an untested idea. Mechanism status is ACTIVE (on the current model path), READY (built and tested, not yet trained in) or PARKED (the tried forms failed or broke a rule, and the mechanism stays open). The mechanism board holds the full list. It replaces the older labels active, dormant and archived-negative.

169.body: This is the path the current integer model (crates/uor-r4-discrete, called M1) follows for each token. Source for each step is in the architecture table . flowchart LR tok["Token ID"] --> tab["Shared table:<br/>blocks of 8 integers"] tab --> ctx["Ordered context<br/>(ternary FBS plan)"] ctx --> read["Read:<br/>Route, Flock or Relation"] read --> wr["Shared writer:<br/>admission + exact distances"] wr --> out["Next token"] out -. "learning" .-> tab The five steps of one token. The dotted arrow is learning, which changes the shared table by exact moves. Input. A token ID selects blocks from Snapshot.table. Context. Ordered ternary FBS plans (a three-branch tree over earlier tokens; see the glossary ) preserve context order for the read. Read. Route selects one carrier per block and transports it without summing or snapping. Flock ranks eligible nodes, transports them, sums and snaps. Relation adds finite relational reranking before the Flock selection. See route read , flock read and relation read . Shared writer. Product-address admission and exact distances select a token using the same table. The writer is implemented ( admission ). Learning. The learner compares virtual exact moves on a fixed batch and accepts objective improvements through the admitted driver. rows_v1 parallelizes proposal work ( discrete learning ). Each block is 8D , and four blocks give width32 . The carrier has 16 roots , acted on by 64 signed transport actions ( build.rs ). These three counts describe different objects. The orbit is not full E8 coverage. The earlier float operator path is preserved as evidence and is not the current token path. It includes the Hamilton gates (G2), the geometric recurrence and the delivered head (OP3a). See the operator record , the head record and the historical geometry tour . Its earlier sheets are inactive until they are re-registered and reviewed under D37. The dated operator diagram illustrates those retained operators.

17.body: Having a replacement on paper is not the same as having a working model: No replacement has matched its transformer part on quality. Every attention-style read that learned well in the older decimal experiments had help from softmax during training, and the best softmax-free read was rejected ( softmax-free read ; audit synthesis (docs/labs/repo-renormalization-2026-10-19/audit/synthesis.md), section 1). No two parts have been trained together except on the current discrete path. That path has no feed-forward layer and no position mechanism, and it scores below a table of word counts ( measurement , K16 outcome ). Several other things are not built: using an exact address as the read, any consumer of the object store, an exporter that turns a trained model into a D11 file, and an output step that avoids scanning the whole vocabulary ( audit synthesis , section 1). The project does not compare its models against transformers. It compares them against count tables and earlier geometric models, and grades them with fixed, deterministic checks ( charter , sections 3.10 and 4.4).

172.body: Under D11 a served kernel has no floating point and no multiplier instruction. A product of two runtime values is read from a table instead. Build the sixteen multiples (0 to 15) of one operand by repeated addition, index that table with the radix-16 digits of the other operand, and combine the results with shifts and adds. For example, to compute \(37 \times 43\), the table holds 0, 37, 74, …, 555. Write 43 as hex 0x2B, with digits 2 and 11. Then \[37 \times 43 = (T[2] \ll 4) + T[11] = (74 \ll 4) + 407 = 1184 + 407 = 1591.\] A 4-bit weight is a single digit, so one product is one table read. Division is restoring long division, square root is digit-by-digit, and the kernels are kept opaque to the optimiser so that an add chain is not folded back into a multiply. Products are taken modulo \(2^{64}\) or \(2^{128}\) to match the earlier integer engine. The code is in crates/uor-r4-integer/src/stack/kernels.rs (stack_mul_u64, stack_div_u64, stack_isqrt), and the ARM64 audit is scripts/audit_zero_matmul_serving.py --stack. The numbers in the example are illustrative and are not taken from the code. The serving contract is described on the D11 integer serving page . It is ACTIVE as the export boundary, but no lawful trained model has been exported through it yet.

175.body: A quaternion is a number with four parts. Multiplying by a unit quaternion (one of length 1) turns a point in four dimensions without stretching it, and a sandwich of two multiplications turns a point in ordinary three-dimensional space. That makes quaternions a natural way to say "turn this state" with exact, reversible steps instead of a grid of learned decimals. This chapter explains what a quaternion does, and why turning a state keeps its length while adding a new input to it does not. Terms are also defined in the glossary . Left: a quaternion q rotates a 3D vector by conjugation, q v q-inverse. Right: quaternion left multiplication q h acts on a 4D state and keeps its length. Two different actions of the same quaternion. Conjugation turns 3D space, and left multiplication turns the whole 4D state.
175.breadcrumbs: The geometry of UOR-R4 » Quaternions and rotation » Quaternions and rotation
175.title: Quaternions and rotation

176.body: A quaternion has four real components, \(q = w + xi + yj + zk\), with \(i^2=j^2=k^2=ijk=-1\). Quaternions of length 1 form the 3-sphere \(S^3\). Multiplication does not commute: in general \(qh \neq hq\). For a pure imaginary vector \(v\) (a point in \(\mathbb{R}^3\)), the map \(v \mapsto q\,v\,q^{-1}\) is a rotation of \(\mathbb{R}^3\). A unit quaternion \(q=\cos\tfrac{\theta}{2}+\sin\tfrac{\theta}{2}\,n\) turns space by the angle \(\theta\) about the unit axis \(n\) (proof, a standard identity). The quaternions \(q\) and \(-q\) give the same 3D rotation. Left multiplication \(q\,h\) is a different thing. It is a norm-preserving linear action on the full quaternion space \(\mathbb{R}^4\), because \(|qh| = |q|\,|h|\). It does not identify \(q\) and \(-q\) as the same action: the map for \(-q\) is the negative of the map for \(q\). The retained float stack's quaternion_scan (the geometric stack , PARKED) uses left multiplication, then additive input injection ( geometric_stack.rs ). The current M1 model instead executes signed actions on 8D carrier blocks. The quaternion picture explains part of the research lineage. It is not a literal 4D state for the M1 kernel.
176.breadcrumbs: The geometry of UOR-R4 » Quaternions and rotation » Rotation: conjugation and left multiplication
176.title: Rotation: conjugation and left multiplication

177.body: A repeated quaternion transport stays on the 3-sphere. The additive recurrence generally leaves it. Pure repeated quaternion transport stays on \(S^3\). The historical additive recurrence generally does not. The figure's pure transport orbit stays on \(S^3\) when its initial state and its transport quaternion are unit. The retained float recurrence is \[h_t = \lambda_t\,(u_t\cdot h_{t-1}) + \sqrt{1-\lambda_t^2}\;a_t .\] Here \(u_t\) is a unit quaternion that turns the old state, \(a_t\) is the new input and \(\lambda_t \in [0,1]\) is a fade rate. Take \(h_{t-1}\) and \(a_t\) to be unit. Then \(|u_t h_{t-1}| = 1\), and expanding the squared norm gives \[|h_t|^2 = \lambda_t^2 + (1-\lambda_t^2) + 2\lambda_t\sqrt{1-\lambda_t^2}\;\langle u_t h_{t-1},\,a_t\rangle = 1 + 2\lambda_t\sqrt{1-\lambda_t^2}\;\langle u_t h_{t-1},\,a_t\rangle .\] The cross term is generally nonzero, so the sum need not lie on \(S^3\) (proof, by expanding the norm). The identity \(\lambda^2 + (1-\lambda^2) = 1\) alone does not normalise it. The rotation preserves the norm of the transported term. Any unit-state claim for the combined state needs an explicit normalisation or further conditions. The same split shows up in the current reads. Flock and Relation reads sum transported vectors and snap the result back to the finite carrier. Route instead transports one selected carrier per block, without summing or snapping, in discrete.cu .

181.body: There is a special set of 120 unit quaternions (each one a rotation) that are the corners of a regular solid in four dimensions called the 600-cell. Pairing that set with a golden-ratio-scaled copy of itself gives 240 points in eight dimensions, the roots of a famous lattice called E8. The project uses this structure because every rotation in it can be written with exact whole-number arithmetic, so a state can be turned and turned back with no rounding. The current model uses only a small, 16-root piece of E8, and this chapter is careful about the difference. Coxeter-plane projection of the 120 unit icosians, the vertices of the 600-cell, drawn as four rings of 30 points The 120 unit icosians as the vertices of the 600-cell, seen from a plane chosen to show the symmetry. Four rings of 30 points, 12 neighbours per vertex, 720 edges.
181.breadcrumbs: The geometry of UOR-R4 » E8, H4 and the 600-cell » E8, H4 and the 600-cell
181.title: E8, H4 and the 600-cell

182.body: The binary icosahedral group \(2I\) contains 120 unit quaternions, closed under multiplication. These are the H4 roots and the vertices of the 600-cell. They are, with coordinates in order \((w,x,y,z)\): 8 quaternions \(\pm1,\pm i,\pm j,\pm k\); 16 of the form \(\tfrac12(\pm1\pm i\pm j\pm k)\); 96 from the even permutations of \(\tfrac12(\pm\varphi,\ \pm1,\ \pm\varphi^{-1},\ 0)\). That is \(8+16+96=120\) (proof, by direct count). Each has length 1: for the last family, \(\tfrac14(\varphi^2+1+\varphi^{-2})=\tfrac14\cdot 4=1\) because \(\varphi^2+\varphi^{-2}=3\). Viewed from any one vertex, all 120 vertices, counting the vertex itself, fall into shells of 1, 12, 20, 12, 30, 12, 20, 12 and 1 vertices. The first shell has 12 neighbours at angle 36°, so there are \(120\cdot12/2=720\) edges. The figure above retains the historical icosian-snap construction. Its 120 vertices form four projected rings of 30. Snapping a learned rotation to this 120-element codebook describes a retained experiment, not the current M1 read or learning path. Icosahedral rotations. Dividing by \(\pm1\) gives \(2I/\{\pm1\}=A_5\), the 60 rotations of the icosahedron. It acts two-transitively on the six five-fold axes (proof; checked in verify_connections.py ). Each of the 15 half-turns fixes exactly one pair of the six five-fold axes. So the 15 edges of the complete graph K6 on those axes match the 15 half-turn axes. This is forced once the six axes carry the six labels. A further fact is that the icosahedron's five orthogonal frames of two-fold axes form a synthematic total of K6: five perfect matchings that together cover all 15 edges. Primes and axes. The six registered primes {5, 7, 11, 13, 17, 19} give 15 semiprime products, one per K6 edge (see SpiralCore ). Attaching the six primes to the six five-fold axes is a labelling choice . There are 720 labellings, and 12 of them are inequivalent under rotation. A design that routes primes through icosian rotations must say which one it uses. Half-turns also do not compose like bivectors: two half-turns whose K6 edges share a vertex multiply to an order-5 rotation, never a half-turn. The prime-to-half-turn match is a correspondence of sets, not of products.

183.body: The 240 E8 roots in a Coxeter-plane projection, with the 120 icosian roots and the 120 golden-scaled roots drawn in two colours The 240 roots of E8 seen in the same kind of plane. Two sets of 120 meet in one picture: the icosians and a copy scaled by \(\varphi\). The shorthand E8 = H4 ⊕ φH4 means, here, an icosian construction with a specified reduced metric . It is not an independent Cartesian product of two H4 states. Let \(x\cdot y = a + b\varphi\) in the quaternion coordinates. The construction uses \[\langle x,y\rangle = 2a ,\] the rational-part bilinear form, on the 240 elements \(2I \cup \varphi\cdot 2I\). In the eight rational coefficient coordinates these have rank 8, norm 2, the E8 inner-product counts (from any root, 1 root at inner product 2, 56 at 1, 126 at 0, 56 at −1 and 1 at −2) and reflection closure. The executable finite checks are in verify_connections.py (check E2). The primary construction paper explains the reduced inner product. The standard picture of E8's roots in a Coxeter plane has 30-fold symmetry and 240 points in eight rings of 30, which is the natural companion to the four rings of 30 above. Check E1 verifies something else: that the specified signed 8×8 matrices (all 15 Cl(0,6) bivector matrices and the six generator matrices) preserve the 240 roots in the standard coordinates of E8. E2 verifies the reduced-metric icosian root system. These checks do not supply a map between the two representations, so the claim that the action is preserved across that missing map is not established . The retained anchors.rs stores \([a_0,\dots,a_3,b_0,\dots,b_3]\) and a Galois companion for one H4 root. Its header says that this invertible coefficient representation does not establish an orthogonal Euclidean E8 embedding or independent extra state. The present carrier has its own concrete basis and orbit, built in build.rs : 16 roots of one E8 orbit, each a signed permutation of \((2,2,0,0,0,0,0,0)\), acted on by 64 signed transport actions. No basis bridge from this standard-coordinate carrier to the icosian realization above is asserted.

188.body: The coordinates of the 120 icosian rotations contain the golden ratio, an irrational number, so a computer would normally round them. There is a way to avoid rounding altogether: keep every coordinate as a pair of whole numbers \((a, b)\) that stands for \(a + b\varphi\). Adding and multiplying such pairs gives another pair, exactly. This chapter explains that arithmetic, called \(\mathbb{Z}[\varphi]\), and says where the project uses it. Terms are also defined in the glossary . Exact arithmetic in Z[phi]: pairs of integers add and multiply without rounding, and the coordinates of unit icosians are such pairs scaled by one half Exact arithmetic in \(\mathbb{Z}[\varphi]\), with the coordinates of unit icosians scaled by one half.
188.breadcrumbs: The geometry of UOR-R4 » Golden integers » Golden integers
188.title: Golden integers

189.body: The golden ratio \(\varphi = (1+\sqrt5)/2\) satisfies \[\varphi^2 = \varphi + 1 .\] The set \(\mathbb{Z}[\varphi] = \{a + b\varphi : a, b \text{ integers}\}\) is closed under addition and multiplication, so it supports exact pair arithmetic. Addition adds the pairs. Multiplication uses the rule above to remove \(\varphi^2\): \[(a+b\varphi)(c+d\varphi) = (ac+bd) + (ad+bc+bd)\,\varphi .\] This is a proof by expanding and substituting \(\varphi^2=\varphi+1\). Two worked examples: \(\varphi\cdot\varphi\) is \((0,1)\cdot(0,1) = (1,1)\), that is \(1+\varphi\). \(\varphi^{-1} = \varphi - 1\) is the pair \((-1,1)\), and \(\varphi\cdot(\varphi-1)=\varphi^2-\varphi=1\). The other root of \(x^2=x+1\) is \(1-\varphi=-\varphi^{-1}\). Swapping \(\varphi\) for it is the Galois conjugate , \(a+b\varphi \mapsto (a+b)-b\varphi\). Multiplying a number by its conjugate gives the integer norm \(N(a+b\varphi)=a^2+ab-b^2\).

190.body: The unit icosian coordinates are \((a+b\varphi)/2\), which lie in \(\tfrac12\mathbb{Z}[\varphi]\). The factor one half must be kept. Scaled integer pairs represent them without rounding. For example, the icosian \(\tfrac12(\varphi,\,1,\,\varphi^{-1},\,0)\) has doubled coordinates \((0,1)\), \((1,0)\), \((-1,1)\) and \((0,0)\), and its length checks out exactly: \(\varphi^2+1+\varphi^{-2}=4\). anchors.rs documents this scale explicitly. Its norm numerators have denominator 4. The same file stores one H4 root as \([a_0,\dots,a_3,b_0,\dots,b_3]\) plus a Galois companion, and warns that this invertible coefficient representation does not by itself establish an orthogonal Euclidean E8 embedding or independent extra state. Fixed ZPhi arithmetic and exact anchor orientation tables support the research. Chirality and polarity are exact signs on \(\mathbb{Z}[\varphi]\), held as fixed integer tables in anchors.rs. They are used by the retained native geometric learner, not by the current M1 path. A caution about addresses: equality addresses for complete tuples are not semantic distances between class numbers. Two entries being exactly equal tells you they are the same entry. It does not tell you how alike two different entries are.
