194.body: In the project's quaternion designs, a rotation state is a point on a four-dimensional sphere (the current model M1 carries 8D integer blocks instead). The Hopf map takes a three-dimensional shadow of that point. The shadow forgets one angle, so many different states cast the same shadow. This chapter explains what the map does, what the forgotten angle is, and what the project does and does not do with it. Short version: the idea is built and unit-tested as a helper, it is not part of the current model's read, and nothing yet shows that keeping the forgotten angle helps language. The mechanism's status is PARKED ( mechanism page ). Hopf observation: the map from the 3-sphere to the 2-sphere loses a circle coordinate, the fibre The Hopf map \(S^3\to S^2\) sends a whole circle of 4D points to one point of the 2-sphere. The shadow cannot tell them apart.
194.breadcrumbs: The geometry of UOR-R4 » The Hopf map and the kept fibre » The Hopf map and the kept fibre
194.title: The Hopf map and the kept fibre

195.body: Write a unit quaternion as \(q=(a,b,c,d)\) and set \(z_1=a+ib\) and \(z_2=c+id\). The Hopf map to the 2-sphere is \[h(q)=\big(2(ac+bd),\ 2(bc-ad),\ a^2+b^2-c^2-d^2\big)=\big(2\,\mathrm{Re}(z_1\bar z_2),\ 2\,\mathrm{Im}(z_1\bar z_2),\ |z_1|^2-|z_2|^2\big).\] Two facts follow by expanding the squares ( proof ). It lands on the unit sphere. \(|h(q)|^2=4(a^2+b^2)(c^2+d^2)+\big((a^2+b^2)-(c^2+d^2)\big)^2=(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)^2=1\). A common phase changes nothing in the shadow. Multiply both \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) by the same phase \(e^{i\vartheta}\). The product \(z_1\bar z_2\) and both moduli are unchanged, so \(h(q)\) stays put. But \(q\) moves around a circle, the fibre . So the shadow alone cannot be inverted. Rebuilding \(q\) needs the base point on the 2-sphere, the fibre phase and a chart convention, because there is no global identification \(S^3=S^2\times S^1\). The image alone is not an invertible representation of the input, and the project does not assume a reversible universal \(S^3\to S^2\to S^1\) pipeline. Keeping the lost angle in a separate slot is what "the kept fibre" means.
195.breadcrumbs: The geometry of UOR-R4 » The Hopf map and the kept fibre » The map
195.title: The map

196.body: For a unit quaternion \((a,b,c,d)\), UnitS3Q30::hopf computes the formula above after decoding Q30 storage to f64, then normalises and requantises the result to Q30. Q30 names the storage representation here. It does not mean the Hopf map runs in integers. prime_route_attention.rs provides rotate_common_fiber and SpinTorsionState { s3, fiber, torsion }, which keeps the S³ state, a fibre phase and a torsion term in separate fields. rotate_common_fiber also decodes to f64, uses libm::sin and cos, and normalises and requantises the rotated point. These are float-backed, offline, fixed-geometry utilities. They are not an integer model execution path. Hopf fibre tracking is not wired into the current discrete M1 read. The retained M2 Hopf metric , which tracks a cumulative phase and a geodesic distance, is separate research and belongs to the held native learner. The icosians under the map. The map sends the 120 icosians of the previous chapters onto one orbit of 30 points of the 2-sphere, every fibre of size 4 (finite enumeration in verify_connections.py ). That orbit is of two-fold type; it is not literally the axes of the chosen frame. This link is forced.

201.body: Every prime number is a unique, indivisible building block, and every whole number is a product of primes in exactly one way. UOR-R4 uses that as an exact-identity idea: a word can be named by a prime (the current model M1 itself uses explicit token IDs). Separately, the project turns each prime into a set of angles using the known frequencies of the Riemann zeta zeros, as an optional input to the model's starting table; distinct starting vectors come from the allocation passes described below. This chapter explains both ideas and keeps them apart. The first is exact identity. The second is a way to scatter starting positions, and nobody has yet shown that its zeta angles help beyond simply keeping the words distinct. Terms are also defined in the glossary . Fixed zeta-zero frequencies produce complex phases from log-prime addresses: each prime p gives an angle gamma times log p for each of several zeros Fixed zeta-zero frequencies \(\gamma_k\) turn each prime \(p\) into one angle per zero, \(\theta_k=\gamma_k\ln p\). Think of a bank of clock hands, each turning at its own speed.
201.breadcrumbs: The geometry of UOR-R4 » Primes and zeta phases » Primes and zeta phases
201.title: Primes and zeta phases

202.body: The imaginary parts \(\gamma\) of the Riemann zeta zeros are fixed numbers. The first three are about 14.1347, 21.0220 and 25.0109. Each defines a phase frequency. For a prime \(p\) the phase on channel \(k\) is \[\theta_k(p)=\gamma_k\ln p \pmod{2\pi},\qquad z_k(p)=\cos\theta_k+i\sin\theta_k .\] A worked illustration (computed from the published value, not read from the code): for \(p=2\) and the first zero, \(\theta_1 = 14.1347\times\ln 2 \approx 9.797\), which is about \(3.514\) radians after subtracting \(2\pi\). Using a finite table of these constants does not require proving the Riemann hypothesis. The optional offline prime_zeta.rs constructor uses four complex channels per block (\(\mathbb{C}^4\)) with \(\theta=\gamma\ln p\), and then: Realifies them into two 4-real tuples, \((\mathrm{Re}_0,\mathrm{Im}_0,\mathrm{Re}_1,\mathrm{Im}_1)\) and \((\mathrm{Re}_2,\mathrm{Im}_2,\mathrm{Re}_3,\mathrm{Im}_3)\). Normalises each with UnitS3Q30::from_r4 and quantises to Q30. Applies the fixed coordinate permutation and exact integer alignment scores against the 16-root 8D carrier (see E8, H4 and the 600-cell ). Allocates under writer-cell quotas and, when capacity permits, full-vector uniqueness controls. The output is Snapshot.table. So \(\mathbb{C}^4\) becomes \(\mathbb{R}^4+\mathbb{R}^4\) per block, not \(\mathbb{C}^8\) or \(\mathbb{R}^{16}\) per block. The allocation controls are part of the assignment. It is not simply an unconstrained nearest-root snap. Floating point appears only in this one-time offline step, under the October 14 zeta-zero exception, and the output is an integer table. An honest caveat (proof, by reading the code). The quota and uniqueness passes also run on both matched control tables (one shifts every \(\gamma\) by 1.0, the other permutes the primes and scrambles phases and amplitudes). So the absence of collisions comes from those passes, not from prime phases. The record is prime-zeta construction ; the mechanism page is prime-zeta codebook . The retained M2 learner used the same fixed phases in a different way: it accumulated fixed phase bins as policy inputs ( engine.rs ). That historical use is distinct from the current codebook initialisation, and it does not establish learned M1 attribution to zeta phases.

202.title: Zeta phases

203.body: Prime products and gcd preserve shared identity; ordered sequence identity needs more information Distinct primes make shared factors exact. A product records which primes are present, not their order or how many times each appears. Assign each token identity its own prime. Then shared factors are exact, by unique factorisation ( proof ). For example, with primes \(2,3,5,7\) standing for four tokens, the products \(42=2\cdot3\cdot7\) and \(105=3\cdot5\cdot7\) have \(\gcd=21=3\cdot7\), which says exactly that the two sets share tokens 3 and 7. A product of distinct primes records a set . Sequence order and multiplicity need explicit additional representation: \(2\cdot3=3\cdot2\), and \(12=2\cdot2\cdot3\) needs exponents to be told from \(6=2\cdot3\). Exact identity is not a semantic metric. Two different primes are different, and nothing more is learned from their size or product.

It does not bound selection cost: the kernel scans eligible nodes, and Relation adds graph scans. The writer also scans vocabulary occupancy and admitted-cell tokens. See the cost and source discussion . On 18 October the prime-zeta table was wired in as the model's starting table. Before that, a random start gave 4,096 words only 16 different starting vectors. 208.body: Give every word a very long string of 1s and 0s, 4,096 of them. To ask "are these two strings alike?", line them up and count the positions where they differ. That count is the Hamming distance, and it costs almost nothing on a computer: an exclusive-or (XOR) and a bit count. This chapter covers two uses of the idea. One is the older "hypervector" memory cue (VSA), which is research that was measured once and is not on the current path. The other is a Hamming tie-break that does run inside the current model's reads. In both cases the similarity is only a count of bits, and it is as meaningful as the way the codes were assigned. Terms are also defined in the glossary . A token's 4096-bit bipolar code, XOR and popcount to a Hamming distance and bipolar cosine, and where the codes come from Two codes are compared with an XOR and a bit count. The result is a Hamming distance and the matching bipolar cosine.
208.breadcrumbs: The geometry of UOR-R4 » VSA and Hamming distance » VSA and Hamming distance
208.title: VSA and Hamming distance

209.body: Each token has a 4096-bit bipolar hypervector, stored as 64 u64 words. A set bit means \(+1\) and a clear bit means \(-1\). Two codes \(A\) and \(B\) are compared with an XOR and a popcount, which gives the Hamming distance \(d\). The bipolar cosine is \[\cos(A,B) = 1 - \frac{2d}{4096} .\] A context hypervector bundles the codes of the recent tokens by a bitwise majority vote. The similarity is a statistic of the code bits, and it is only as meaningful as the way the codes were assigned. Two standard facts ( proof , from the definition of XOR) are worth knowing. XOR is its own inverse, \((A\oplus B)\oplus B=A\), which is why it works as a "glue and unglue" operation. For a bundle of \(k\) random terms, unbinding returns the stored value plus noise of standard deviation about \(\sqrt{(k-1)/D}\) with \(D=4096\). That is the textbook estimate for random codes, not a measurement on this model.

21.body: The test set is 14,287 positions in 400 held-out documents, called the DEV panel ( count tables record ). At each position the model makes one guess for the next token. A top-1 score counts how many of those guesses are right. Two plain tables, built from the same training text the model sees, set the floor: The unigram table always guesses the single most common token. It scores 1,226 ( measurement ). The next-word table (called T2) looks only at the previous token and guesses the token that most often followed it in training. It scores 6,300 ( measurement ). Both come from the count tables record . A model that cannot beat them has not yet learned anything a lookup table cannot do. The project compares against these tables, not against transformers ( charter , section 3.10).

210.body: In the older native prose learner (an offline float learner on a CPU, now barred by the GPU-only rule D24), the VSA term added vsa_scale · similarity to the root and leaf scores. Three code modes existed. Mode Code Distinct codes 0 A fixed hash of the token id. Historical: it is disconnected from the learned 120-root assignment, which is why it was described as mis-wired 4,096 1 Derived from the learned icosian-root assignment (a token's nearest of the 120 roots, a Voronoi cell over the learned embeddings). Since PR #2077 these codes are trainable and refresh during training at most 120 2 The root code bound with a readout-hash residual 4,096 Measurement (9 October, two seeds, two held-out slices, 6,795,016 training tokens per run). With the VSA term trained in and fixed token-hash codes (mode 0), held-out bits per byte improved in all four seed-and-slice pairs, by 0.0144 to 0.0226 (for example 1.8366 against 1.8574). Icosian-root codes (mode 1) did not help: the change in bits per byte against VSA off (negative is better) was +0.0003 and +0.0001 on one seed and −0.0053 and −0.0054 on the other, all four under the 0.01 threshold, and with only 120 distinct codes, tokens that share a root cannot be told apart. The root-plus-residual codes (mode 2) were worse than fixed codes in all four cells, by +0.013 to +0.028 ( native test record ; a historical float-form measurement on a CPU learner). An earlier "closed" label for mode 0 applied to a frozen-artifact swap and a wiring fault, not to this trained-in run. The link from the icosians to these bit codes is learned , not forced: the learned token-to-icosian-root assignment builds the mode 1 codes ( vsa_codes.rs , since PR #2077). Limits to keep in view: the seeds differ by about 0.015 bits per byte, the size of the effect, and the cross-arm comparison is a point estimate. The same model's exact-memory table was worth about 0.19 to 0.20 bits per byte, so VSA may duplicate evidence that other heads supply. VSA is not tied to SpiralCore ( next chapter ). The full tried-and-untested list is on the VSA mechanism page , and the mechanism's status is PARKED.

212.body: On the current path, Hamming distance is one factor among several, not the whole read. The kernel flock_vector orders candidates by: relation score, descending; L1 displacement, ascending; coordinate Hamming distance, ascending; recency, descending; node, ascending. In Flock mode the relation scores are zero. The kernel then equally sums the selected transported roots and snaps the sum to a carrier root. It does not use the historical fixed rank-table weights. Relation adds its graph reranking before this same selection and aggregation path. The Route read also uses Hamming distance, as a tie-break between ports ( route read ). Hamming distance on E8 labels is not the E8 lattice distance, and decision D32 treats XOR and Hamming comparison on ternary and E8 labels as one component of a model, not as a Hamming-only model ( ternary and XOR ).

216.body: SpiralCore is an exact-geometry source, credited to Matthew (versions v63 and v69). From the multiplication table of the octonions (an eight-part number system) it produces a small set of exact moves on eight numbers: each move shuffles the eight coordinates and flips some signs. Every move can be undone exactly. The model stores earlier words in a tree with three branches per node (the "ternary FBS" tree, the project's name for it; see the glossary ), and it carries a chosen eight-number block along a short path of these moves. No learned multiplication is involved, only swaps and sign flips. This chapter explains the moves, the tree, and how they connect to the other geometry. The integer form is the core of the current model. Terms are also defined in the glossary . A three-branch tree of stored atoms with one root-to-leaf path highlighted, beside the 16 roots of one E8 orbit drawn as nodes of a 15-edge graph. As a query point moves, the chosen atom's 8 coordinates travel along graph edges; each edge permutes axes and flips signs. A ternary tree picks one stored block. The block then travels along exact edges between the 16 roots of an E8 orbit.

216.title: SpiralCore

217.body: The table. spiralcore_operator.rs reproduces the SpiralCore v63 octonion and Cl(0,6) convention exactly. The octonions' seven oriented Fano lines are \[(124)(235)(346)(457)(561)(672)(713).\] The Clifford algebra Cl(0,6) has six generators that each square to \(-1\). Products of two distinct generators give the 15 bivectors \(B_{ij}\) (one per pair of the six, \(\binom62=15\)), with \(B_{ij}B_{jk}=-B_{ik}\). They mirror the way the semiprimes \(p_ip_j\cdot p_jp_k\to p_ip_k\) combine. The \(B_{ij}\) generate a group of order 64 that maps onto the 32 square-free even prime products, with kernel \(\pm1\). Together this gives a 64-state composition table. Each \(B\) is a signed coordinate permutation of \(\mathbb{R}^8\) with \(B^2=-I\). The orbit. One anchor orbit holds 16 roots and 64 signed operator states , and an output block's carrier is moved by the composed edge history. A breadth-first search (BFS) over the labelled edges gives an ordered history between any two roots, composed by left-composition. Exact inverse (proof). From \(B^2=-I\) it follows that \(B^4=I\) and so \(B^3=B^{-1}\). The inverse of a history is therefore the reversed sequence with each step cubed. A worked step. The projection chooses one input block \(x_{\sigma(j)}\) for each output block \(j\) and sets \(y_j=A_jx_{\sigma(j)}\), where \(A_j\) is the composed signed action. The forward pass is a gather and a sign flip. There is no learned coefficient for any input-output pair, and the adjoint is the exact inverse action \(A_j^{-1}\delta_j\) ( SpiralCore/FBS projection , proof by construction).

220.body: The Fano plane has seven points and seven lines, each line a, b, a xor b. Binding two basis units gives plus or minus the third unit on their line; signed binding changes sign on swapping distinct units and is non-associative for 168 of 210 ordered triples. A historical proposal: bind with a signed XOR whose sign depends on operand order, unlike plain XOR. On the Fano plane, \(e_a\cdot e_b=\pm e_{a\oplus b}\): a signed XOR whose sign depends on operand order, unlike plain XOR (which is commutative and associative, so it loses order and grouping). Incidence alone does not define coherent octonion signs. The design is not on the current path, and it needs its own pre-registration and a TEST FITNESS: FIT review before compute. The canonical v63 Fano table in spiralcore_operator.rs is the control for it. It has not been tested against plain XOR ( VSA mechanism page ).

221.body: Mark (N3mesis)'s supplied Octonian Substrate Architecture and discussion PDFs motivate separating state, algebra, routing and identity. The review of that draft found the following. Its literal positive cycles \((123)(145)(167)(246)(257)(347)(356)\) fail alternativity and quadratic norm multiplicativity. For example, \((e_1+e_2)(e_4+e_7)=0\) although each factor has squared length 2. Fano incidence is not a complete sign convention. For the draft's XOR labelling, an exhaustive search of all \(2^7=128\) orientations of those seven lines finds 16 that give a valid octonion algebra (the enumeration is in the historical geometry tour ; the review record states only the counterexample). One of them reverses three of the draft's lines: \((123)(145)(167)(246)(527)(437)(536)\). The sample store route discards a coordinate after right multiplication and projection, and its packing function returns empty bytes. A pre-route embed/project inverse does not establish post-route preservation. Modular \(\mathbb{Z}/2^{256}\) coefficients are neither the real normed division algebra nor a replacement for exact \(\mathbb{Z}[\varphi]\) pairs. These findings concern the supplied draft. They are not a negative language experiment and not a retirement of octonion binding. The canonical Rust table is unchanged, and any alternative convention needs a signed basis correspondence, not just the same seven lines. The orientation in the draft is inconsistent with the canonical table and must not replace it ( full review ).

225.body: Most chat AIs are built from a few standard parts: a way to look back at earlier words (attention), a block that processes each word (a feed-forward layer), big grids of multiplications, and a function that scores every possible next word. UOR-R4 is trying to replace each of those parts with something built from geometry, such as rotations, exact addresses and lookup tables. Each replacement is called a mechanism . This page lists all 27 of them and says where each one stands today. Status here means how far a mechanism has been built and tested. No mechanism has produced a useful conversation yet: the project is pre-alpha, and 0 of its 8 milestones are complete (STATUS.md). A family tree of the 27 mechanisms, coloured by status, showing which mechanism grew out of which The 22 mechanisms with a recorded parent or child, drawn as a family tree. Most of the live ones descend from earlier, parked attempts.

23.body: No model holds a conversation ( STATUS ). The detail: The best trained model is below both count tables. The last full experiment (called K16) trained two variants of the model, each on two random seeds, for 16,404 batches ( K16 outcome ; all measurement ): Variant Seed Correct first guesses Reach: positions where the right answer was among the candidates opened Cells in use (of 256) A (nearest-address margin) 1 65 2,237 209 A 2 463 3,167 192 R (occupied-cell rank) 1 101 12,089 20 R 2 230 12,466 19 Variant A is the one the record selects. Its reach fell below the required 4,894 positions on both seeds. Variant R kept a high reach only by collapsing into 19 or 20 cells, so that each guess was drawn from about 3,400 of the 4,096 tokens, nearly the whole vocabulary; that reach is not real discrimination. The registered verdict was an occupancy collapse (record code OCCUPANCY_COLLAPSE_TRIGGERED), and no run was kept. All four miss the run's own top-1 bar of 1,941 and are far below the next-word table's 6,300. The large gap between seeds (65 against 463) also shows how noisy one run is. The cause is not established. The first guess was that too few distinct starting vectors were to blame. That is ruled out as the main cause: in variant A, training raised the distinct vectors from 16 to about 275, yet top-1 stayed low ( K16 outcome , census section). The candidates still open are: The address key may be too coarse. The key is the distance that orders the drawers. It uses only the first and last block and takes only 5 values (0, 4, 8, 12 or 16) to order up to 256 cells ( proof , from the kernel source), so which drawers open is largely decided by their arbitrary numbering ( the model page , chief architect's review §3.2). Whether this causes the low score is a hypothesis . The read, the ranking capacity, or the training schedule. One full run sees fewer than half of the training targets: 1,049,856 of 2,425,925 ( measurement , audit dossier ). These remain hypotheses . The newest run stopped early. The address-cell run (A8) began with the better reach above, but training eroded it. At its first checkpoint the Relation read held 551 reachable positions, below half its starting 1,351, which triggered the registered stop (the control held 857; measurement , A8 dose ). A version that protects the reach is built; its GPU qualification is NOT_RUN ( controller record ). No model trained under today's rules has been exported or timed. No exporter turns a trained discrete model into a D11 file (the older float stacks were exported and served in October), and tokens per second for this model have never been measured ( lut-serving ). Parts are missing. The current model has no position mechanism, no normalization and no feed-forward layer ( transformer vs geometry ). Training is on hold. Each training run needs a reviewed one-page plan and a release typed by the owner personally ( charter , section 5).

235.title: Routed read (address-routed context access)

236.body: A transformer decides what to read by comparing the current word with every earlier word. This model does something cheaper. It keeps the earlier words at the ends of a small tree of geometric addresses. To read, it starts at the top of the tree and, at each level, steps toward the branch whose address is nearest to where the current state points. After a few steps it arrives at one earlier word and picks up that word's information. By construction it never scores the whole history, so the work should not grow with the context (a design property; speed was never measured). Whether this single pick is useful is still unknown, because nobody has switched it off to see.

237.body: Attention: the step that decides which earlier positions to read. There is no query-key score table and no softmax. The read makes one hard choice per step and returns one earlier position's carrier vector. A ternary tree drawn over a row of context tokens. The query enters at the top, three child ports are lit at each level with their distances to the 16 orbit roots, the nearest is highlighted, and a rotation arrow accumulates down the path until one leaf token is picked. The routed read walks a ternary tree over the context: one nearest port per level, one leaf at the end.
237.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Routed read » What it replaces in a transformer
237.title: What it replaces in a transformer

238.body: The model width is split into 8-dimensional blocks. Per block, the query is an integer vector \(q\in\mathbb{Z}^8\) taken at the last position. A ternary tree (a "BinderPlan" built by SpiralCore, the project's exact-arithmetic geometry library) is built over the context. Its leaves are earlier positions, and the context cap is 243 positions, which is \(3^5\). Definition. Let \(G\) be the group of 64 signed-axis permutations of \(\mathbb{Z}^8\). Coordinates are permuted and sign-flipped by table lookup, so no multiplication is involved. Let \(R=\{r_0,\dots,r_{15}\}\) be the 16 roots of one E8 orbit, each a signed permutation of \((2,2,0,0,0,0,0,0)\). At level \(\ell\) the model holds one learned element \(a_\ell\in G\) and chooses a port \(p\) by hard minimum, where \(r_p\) is the orbit root tied to that port (schematic): \[c_\ell=\arg\min_{p}\ \big(\lVert a_\ell q-r_p\rVert_1,\ \operatorname{Ham}(a_\ell q,r_p),\ p\big)\] At level 0 the candidates are up to 16 frontier roots; at later levels they are the 3 children. Each choice composes a precomputed transport action between orbit roots (\(\mathrm{BFS}\) is a table built by breadth-first search over exact moves), so \(T_\ell=\mathrm{BFS}[\rho_{\ell-1}\to\rho_\ell]\circ T_{\ell-1}\). The output is \(T_L\) applied to the carrier vector of the leaf reached. This is a schematic of the kernel route_vector; the exact comparator is in the code. Cost (proof, by construction). The work per block is about levels \(\times\) 16 distance comparisons. It does not depend on how many earlier positions exist. The cost of building and updating the tree, and tokens per second, were never measured in the audited records. Content-blindness (proof). Port selection never inspects which token a leaf holds. Content enters only through the geometry of the query. That is why the read cannot express "copy the word after the earlier match"; see relation-read . Learning. Training is discrete. Each route parameter is tried against its 15 generator moves in a counterfactual forward pass. The best move that strictly lowers the integer loss is applied. Nothing is differentiated ( discrete-learning ). The output vector goes to the shared writer ( admission ). Rule check. No softmax, sigmoid or tanh (D23); no matrix multiplication, because the 8x8 "rotation" is a table lookup (D30). The kernel uses gather, sign flip, compare and integer add (D11), but no D11 served export or export-gap measurement of a trained Route model exists in the records.

245.title: Flock read (starling / murmuration neighbour read)

246.body: A starling in a flock does not watch the whole flock. It watches about seven nearest neighbours and turns toward their average heading. The Flock read works the same way. At each step the model picks a handful of earlier positions that sit closest to the current one, rotates what each one knows into the current position's point of view, and takes their consensus. Then it nudges its own state toward that consensus. Nothing is normalised, no scores are exponentiated, and no weights are multiplied. Whether this beats simply reading one position is still untested on real text.
246.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Flock read » In plain words
246.title: In plain words

247.body: Attention, both halves: choosing which earlier positions to read, and mixing what was read into the current state. A transformer weights every earlier position with a softmax and sums them. Flock keeps a few by hard integer ranking and adds their rotated consensus with a three-valued dial. The 600-cell drawn as 120 vertices. One query token sits at its home vertex with the 12 adjacent vertices outlined. Its seven nearest earlier tokens inside that neighbourhood are highlighted, each with an arrow showing its vector rotated into the query's frame. The arrows sum into one consensus vector, and the query vector bends toward it. The flock read on the 600-cell: a query point, its seven nearest neighbours, their rotation into the query's frame, and the consensus they produce. The live integer version uses 16 frame roots in place of the 600-cell (inset).

247.title: What it replaces in a transformer

248.body: The float-era picture (inactive evidence). The 600-cell is a four-dimensional solid with 120 vertices, and each vertex has 12 neighbours. Each token was given a home vertex. A query read only the tokens stored at its own vertex and the 12 adjacent ones, kept the nearest seven, and moved their values into its own frame using exact icosian transport. Those experiments ran in floating point, with the selection on the host and softmax helpers during training. The live integer form. Per 8-dimensional block, context sits in a ternary tree whose leaves are earlier positions ( route-read uses the same tree). Each interior node holds the snapped sum of its three transported children. For each tree level \(\ell\) there is one learned gate \(g_\ell\in\{-1,0,+1\}\). Rank (Definition). Eligible nodes at level \(\ell\) end strictly before the query. Keep the best \(K\) (\(1\le K\le 8\)) under the lexicographic key \(\big(d_{L1}(f_n,f_q),\ d_{H}(f_n,f_q),\ -\mathrm{last}(n),\ n\big)\). Here \(f\) is a node's frame root among the 16 roots of one E8 orbit and \(d_H\) is coordinate Hamming distance. Carry. Each kept payload \(p_n\) is moved into the query's frame by the precomputed transport action between the two roots: \(c_n=\mathrm{BFS}[f_n\to f_q]\,(p_n)\). Consensus. \(m_\ell=\operatorname{snap}\big(\sum_{n\in\text{kept}}c_n\big)\), the nearest of the 16 roots. Gated add. \(v\leftarrow v+g_\ell\,m_\ell\). Trit \(+1\) adds the consensus root, \(-1\) subtracts it, \(0\) skips the level. The output is \(v\) snapped back to a root. This is built as an integer form of the Vicsek/Kuramoto alignment rule \(\Delta=K_h(\text{mean}-v_t)\) with \(K_h\in\{-1,0,+1\}\): align with the local flock, with no weights, no normalisation and no division. That correspondence is the design intent; the page makes no equivalence claim. Rule check. Hard rank by integer keys, so no softmax (D23). No matrix multiplication (D30). The kernel uses gather, compare, add and subtract, and the snap is built by repeated addition (D11). No D11 export of a trained Flock model has been built or measured. Cost (hypothesis). The tree variant should read in about \(O(\log n)\) steps. That has not been measured in the integer form.

256.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Relation read » Relation read (finite relational head)
256.title: Relation read (finite relational head)

257.body: Much of language works by copying. When you meet a word you saw earlier, the next word is often the one that followed it last time. The Flock read finds earlier positions that look like the current one, but it cannot say "take the word right after that earlier copy." Relation adds that ability. It lets the read follow simple links between positions: the word right after, a sibling in the same phrase, the same word again. Each kind of link is controlled by one three-position dial: off, boost or penalise. With every dial off, the model behaves exactly like Flock. The dials have been trained twice, but never long enough to judge them.
257.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Relation read » In plain words
257.title: In plain words

258.body: The scoring half of attention, which decides which earlier positions matter. In a transformer, copying the next word is done by "induction heads" that learn a query-key match pattern. Here the same habit is a bounded, exact rerank by link type. There is no learned score table and no softmax. The sequence x A B y z A drawn as leaves of a small tree. The earlier A is lit with match score 8. A plus-one successor dial sends a scored arrow one leaf to the right, so B also scores 8 and jumps to the top of the ranked list. A toggle sets all dials to zero and the ranking falls back to the Flock order. The copy-the-next-word read on "x A B y z A": the dial for "successor" passes the earlier A's score on to B.
258.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Relation read » What it replaces in a transformer
258.title: What it replaces in a transformer

259.body: Relation is Flock plus a reranker. The pool is every causally eligible node of the same ternary tree that Route and Flock use. Five link types come from retained structure only: # Link type What it connects 0 parent-child a node and its tree children 1 sibling neighbouring children of one parent 2 sequential successor leaf \(j+1\) follows leaf \(j\) (the copy-successor primitive) 3 same token two positions holding the same token id 4 same frame two nodes sharing an orbit-root frame Definition. For a query with frame root \(f_q\), each node \(i\) starts with a match score \(m_i=8-d_{L1}(f_q,f_i)\in\{0,4,8\}\). Each (link type \(e\), tree level) has a learned trit \(g[e,\ell]\in\{-1,0,+1\}\), which makes 25 dials for five levels. For sweeps \(t=1,\dots,S\) (\(1\le S\le5\)): \[r_i^{(t)}=r_i^{(t-1)}+\sum_{e=0}^{4}g[e,\ell(i)]\sum_{j\in\mathcal{N}_e(i)}s_j^{(t-1)},\qquad s^{(0)}=m,\ \ s^{(t-1)}=r^{(t-1)}\ (t\ge2)\] Here \(\mathcal{N}_e(i)\) are node \(i\)'s neighbours under link type \(e\). Candidates are ranked by \(r_i^{(S)}\) first, then by the Flock keys (frame distance, Hamming distance, recency, node id). The top \(K\le8\) feed the unchanged Flock transport, consensus and gated add. Worked example. In "x A B y z A" the query is the final A. The earlier A has the same frame, so \(m=8\). Set the level-0 successor trit to \(+1\) with one sweep. B receives \(r=+8\) and outranks every candidate with \(r=0\), whatever that candidate's own frame distance. B's payload is carried in. That is the copy-successor read. Two facts that follow from the code (proof). With every trit at zero, all scores are zero and the ranking is bit-identical to Flock. This is the rollback identity, and it is the control used in training. Scores are integers bounded by \(8\cdot(1+8)^5=472{,}392\), far below \(2^{31}\), so plain integer addition suffices. No multiplier, no float, no clamp. Why Route and Flock cannot do this (proof, from reading the kernel). Both rank each node by its own frame and carry that node's own payload. The successor's frame has no fixed relation to the query's frame, so neither read can promote a node because its predecessor matched. The design record makes this argument in full. The target is large (measurement). On the pinned development panel (14,287 eligible rows, context 192), the query token recurs earlier in 8,648 rows, and the target is the word after the latest earlier copy in 3,847 rows (26.9%) . This is the copy-successor sub-panel, called \(P_{succ}\) here. Its distance buckets 1-8, 9-32, 33-96 and 97-192 hold 50, 2,872, 900 and 25 rows. Learning and the bar. The trits reuse the existing gate parameter kind and are learned by counterfactual moves ( discrete-learning ) on a schedule where every eighth batch is a read batch. To count, a trained Relation must beat a context-free successor table (called T2), which scores 6,300 of 14,287 top-1 in a host re-score, while the trained Route read scored 149. Rule check. Hard top-K by integer keys (no softmax, D23); no matrix multiplication (D30); integer compare, gather, add and subtract (D11). No D11 export or export gap exists for a trained Relation artifact.

266.title: Admission (cell shortlist before the token is chosen)

267.body: Before the model picks a word, it narrows its 4,096 possible words down to those stored in a few "drawers", the drawers nearest to where its read points. A word in a drawer that was not opened can never be chosen, however good the read was. So the number of correct words whose drawer gets opened sets a ceiling on everything upstream. This ceiling was the limit on rung 0; the later K16 runs show that a high admitted count alone does not give good ranking. In several runs, learning itself pushed correct words out of the opened drawers, so the number of reachable answers fell during training. The next registered run adds a guard against that.
267.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Admission » In plain words
267.title: In plain words

268.body: The output head: a transformer scores every word in the vocabulary and normalises with a softmax. This model never scores all 4,096 words. It makes a hard shortlist of cells, then picks the nearest word inside it. There is no softmax and no normalised distribution. A 16 by 16 grid of drawers with 4,096 tokens drawn as dots. A query star lands in the grid and the 8 nearest occupied drawers are lit. The target word is shown outside the lit set. Three small copies of the grid, at the start and after 4,096 batches in two training arms, show the target's drawer drifting out of the lit set, with the count of reachable targets beside each. Admission: only words in the lit drawers can be chosen. In the A8 control run, the number of copy-successor targets in lit drawers fell from 1,351 to 857 of 3,847 within 4,096 batches.
268.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Admission » What it replaces in a transformer
268.title: What it replaces in a transformer

269.body: The writer takes the read's integer vector \(q\) (\(B=4\) blocks of 8 numbers) and picks a token in two steps. Definition (admission). Each token \(t\) has a codebook vector. Its cell is the pair \(c(t)=(\rho_{\text{first}}(t),\rho_{\text{last}}(t))\) of orbit-root labels of its first and last block, so there are \(16\times16=256\) cells. The address distance from \(q\) to a cell is the L1 distance of \(q\)'s first block to the cell's first root plus the same for the last block. The \(K\) nearest occupied cells are admitted, ties by cell number. \(K\) is 8 in the lineage of record and at most 16. Definition (ranking). Among tokens in admitted cells, the nearest by total L1 over all blocks wins. Ties go to the lowest token id. Consequence (proof). A target outside the admitted cells cannot be predicted whatever the read does. So top-1 hits \(\le\) top-8 hits \(\le\) \(N_{\text{adm}}\), the number of rows whose target cell is admitted. Rung 0 shows the force of this. Its top-1 bar was 1,941 rows, but only 1,920 targets were admitted at the end, so the bar was arithmetically unreachable. Training hinge. Learning uses an integer hinge: \(8\times\) the token margin plus \(32\times\) a cell term. The two cell terms are objective A (the margin to the nearest rival cell) and objective R (how many occupied cells outrank the target beyond \(K\)). The weights are applied by shift-and-add, with no multiplier ( rank-margin ). Why learning erodes it. Codebook moves change a token's cell. A move that improves the loss can eject a target from the shortlist. The admission-preserving rule audits a fixed anchor panel every 64 batches and rejects any interval that shrinks admission. Rule check. Hard top-K and a hinge over declared rivals: no softmax (D23). Sums of absolute differences, no matrix multiplication (D30). Integer only (D11), but no served export of an admission artifact has been measured.

277.body: A language model has to start every word somewhere. The usual start is random numbers. In this project the random start gave 4,096 words only 16 different starting positions, so many words were indistinguishable. This mechanism gives every word its own fixed address instead. A word's place in the vocabulary picks a prime (2, 3, 5, and so on), and the prime is turned into a set of angles using the known frequencies of the Riemann zeta zeros. Everything is computed once, offline, and stored as a table of small whole numbers. Whether the zeta angles help beyond simply keeping words distinct has not been tested.

278.body: The token embedding table. A transformer starts each token with a random vector and learns it. Here the starting table is constructed, fixed and made of integers. The model can still change it later through its learning moves ( discrete learning ). Left: a ladder of primes feeding eight clock dials, one per zeta zero, each hand turned by that zero's frequency times the log of the prime; an arrow drops the word onto a 16 by 16 board of cells. Right: before and after piles of 4,096 dots, 16 piles of 256 for the random start against 256 cells of 16 for this table. A word's prime sets eight dial angles, and the angles pick a cell on a 16 by 16 board. The random start put 256 words on each of 16 patterns. This table puts 16 words in each of 256 cells, all distinct.

278.title: What it replaces in a transformer

279.body: Prime address (Definition). Token \(v\) with vocabulary id \(\mathrm{id}(v)\in\{0,\dots,V-1\}\) gets the prime \(p_{\mathrm{id}(v)+1}\). The vocabulary maps one-to-one onto the first \(V\) primes, and \(p_{4096}=38873\). Zeta phases (Definition). Take the first 512 imaginary parts \(\gamma_k\) of the zeta zeros from a pinned table of published values. The phase and phasor of channel \(k\) are \[\theta_k(p)=\gamma_k\ln p \pmod{2\pi},\qquad z_k(p)=\cos\theta_k+i\sin\theta_k .\] Using a finite table of these constants does not require solving the Riemann hypothesis. Quantize and place (Definition). Four consecutive channels per 8-dimensional block form a vector in \(\mathbb{C}^4\). It is split into two \(\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{R}^4\) spinor pairs and stored as integers (PhaseQ29, UnitS3Q30). The pairs are embedded in the four orthogonal 2D root planes of a 16-root orbit of the E8 lattice. Each block takes the orbit root with the largest exact integer inner product. Cells (Definition). A token's writer cell is the pair (root of block 0, root of the last block). That makes a \(16\times16=256\) cell grid. Two passes then run: A quota pass puts exactly \(V/256=16\) tokens in each cell. A uniqueness pass gives interior blocks distinct roots, so all 4,096 full vectors differ. Where floating point lives. The logarithm, sine and cosine are confined to this one-time host step, under the October 14 zeta-zero exception. The output is an integer table loaded as the model's starting table (pinned_table_v1). The served model sees only integers. Two matched controls share the same pipeline. TangentNull shifts every \(\gamma_k\) by 1.0. NormalNull permutes the primes and moves the phases off the critical line. An honest caveat (proof, by reading the code). The quota and uniqueness passes also run on both controls. So the zero collisions come from those passes, not from prime phases. The seed does not change the PrimeZeta table: seeds 0, 1 and 2 give identical tables. Rule check. No softmax or squashing (D23). No matrix multiplication; each token is scored by a few 8-element integer inner products, once, on the host. This is data preparation: no model quantity is computed there (D24, D30). The compiled integer module contains 0 floating-point instructions (D11, D32). Float is allowed here only by the October 14 exception.

28.body: In one paragraph. The goal is a fast language model that runs on your own laptop or in your browser, holds a conversation with a durable memory, and later reasons and writes code, all on the geometric path with no transformer. The project marks progress with eight milestones, M1 to M8. None is complete yet. On 19 October 2026 the owner set a plain first bar: the model must beat two simple word-count tables, on each of two seeds, through its whole-number export. This page explains the milestones in plain words, the shortest credible path from today to a first simple conversation, and the three products at the end. The path is a plan, not a promise. Every training step still needs the owner's release, and the central question, whether a softmax-free model can learn to rank words well, is unanswered. A left-to-right road with six numbered stops, Stage 0 to Stage 5: "run what is already FIT'd", "make capacity measurable", "pick the learning law", "add the missing parts", "export and serve", "first conversation". A "you are here" pin stands at Stage 0. Gate symbols between stops are labelled "owner release". Under the road, milestone flags line up with the stages: M1 under Stages 2 to 4, M4 under Stage 4, M2 under Stage 5, and M3 marked not yet staged. Beyond Stage 5 the road continues lighter to M5 (laptop cost), M6 (reasoning and coding), M7 (browser and API) and M8 (alpha), ending at three product icons: a model file, a browser tab and a laptop app. The road from today to the products. Stage 0 is where the project stands. Each gate needs an owner release. Terms are in the glossary . Labels are proof , measurement or hypothesis ( docs/formal_vocabulary.md ).

287.body: Picture a 16 by 16 board of 256 cells. Each of the 4,096 words gets a home cell, and every cell holds 16 words. The trick is where words go. A word is placed next to the cells of the words that usually come just before it in the training text. Only about 1,350 words are placed this way; the other 2,749 of 4,096 have no placed predecessor and are placed by the prime-zeta fallback (rule 4 below). When the model has just read a word, the reader looks only at a few nearby cells. If likely next words live in those cells, the right answer is at least in view. This is a table made before training, and it changes nothing about how the reader works. It only decides what the reader can see.

288.body: The token embedding table, in the part of its job that decides which tokens the next-word step can consider. A transformer's output step scores every word in the vocabulary. This model scores only the words in the cells it opens ( admission ), so where each word lives limits what can be chosen. A 16 by 16 board of cells with 16 dots each. Heavy training bigram arrows run from a previous word's cell to its likely next words. Three board states for the random-injective table, the shuffled table and the address-structured table show the arrows growing shorter, with the eight opened cells outlined and a counter of reachable targets reading 127, 476 and 1,351 of 3,847. The same board with three placements. With the address-structured table the likely next words sit near the last word's cell, so more of them fall inside the eight opened cells.

289.body: Cells. A word's writer cell is the pair (root of block 0, root of the last block) on a 16-root E8 orbit, the same \(16\times16=256\) grid as the prime-zeta codebook . All 4,096 full vectors stay distinct. What the reader can see (Definition). The reader admits the \(K=8\) occupied cells nearest its output \(q\), by L1 distance on those two root blocks, and can rank only the words inside them. Placement therefore decides visibility. Building the table (Definition). This is host data preparation from the training split only. Count integer bigrams \(s\to t\) at the positions where the model must answer, with \(s\) the last context word. Take words by falling frequency (ties to the lower id). Put each word in the cell \(c\) that minimises \[\sum_{s\ \text{placed}} \mathrm{count}(s\to t)\; L_1\big(\mathrm{cell}(s),\,c\big)\] subject to a quota of 16 words per cell. A word with no placed predecessor goes to its prime-zeta cell if free, else the nearest cell with room. Inner blocks get distinct root pairs by rank in the cell. A recount requires 4,096 distinct vectors with every cell at quota. The control. The shuffled table (S8) runs the same greedy search with predecessor identities relabelled by a seeded permutation. It keeps frequency, quota and total mass but destroys the relation, so it separates "words placed near their predecessors" from "words packed neatly". A stated gap (proof, by reading the construction). The reader's real centre is the last word plus the consensus of the context read, not the last word's cell alone. Placement only partly predicts admission for that reason. The gap was reported, not tuned away. Rule check. The construction is integer counting and integer L1 sums, with no floating point, so there is no export gap. No softmax, no squashing, no matrix multiplication (D23, D30). Host work is data preparation only; no model quantity is computed there (D24).

297.body: Give every word a long string of 4,096 bits. To glue two things together, such as a role and a word, flip the bits of one wherever the other has a one (XOR). Applying the same glue again undoes it. To merge many strings into one summary, take a majority vote at each position. To tell whether two strings are alike, count how many positions differ. In the older prose model this gave the next-word score a cheap cue: "was this word recently in the context?" It is a lossy sketch. Exact copies still need an exact lookup.

298.body: Part of the key-value memory: the cue that says whether something stored earlier matches the current query. A transformer compares a query against every stored key with dot products. A hypervector sketch compares bit strings by counting differences, using only XOR and bit counts. Three words drawn as 64-cell bit strips, each XORed with a role strip and folded by majority vote into one summary strip. Unbinding with one role lights up the matching word, with similarity bars that fall as more items are bundled. Beside it, three code modes drawn as 4,096 dots: far apart for a random hash, 120 clumps for root codes, loosened clumps for the root-plus-residual code, each with its held-out change in bits per byte. Bind, bundle and probe on bit strips, and three ways to choose each word's code. Only the random-hash codes helped.

299.body: A hypervector has \(D=4096\) bits. Bind (Definition). Bitwise XOR. It is its own inverse: \((A\oplus B)\oplus B=A\). That follows from the definition of XOR (proof). Order (Definition). A cyclic bit rotation marks position. Bundle (Definition). A bitwise majority vote over a context window of up to 64 terms, with a fixed tie-breaker. Similarity (Definition). Hamming distance \(d_H\) from a bit count, turned into a bipolar correlation \(1-2d_H/D\) in Q1.15 fixed point. Cross-talk (standard estimate, proof for random codes). Unbinding a bundle of \(k\) random bipolar terms returns the stored value plus noise with standard deviation about \(\sqrt{(k-1)/D}\). So 64 terms in 4,096 bits leave a signal-to-noise ratio near \(\sqrt{4096/63}\approx 8\). This is the textbook figure for random codes, not a measurement on this model. How the older prose scorer used it. One additive feature per candidate word: \[\text{score}\mathrel{+}=\big(\text{vsa\_scale\_q15}\cdot \mathrm{corr}(\text{context vector},\ \mathrm{code}(\text{candidate}))\big)\gg 16 .\] The context vector bundles an associative transition context and up to four "orthogonal VSA attention" heads. The scale is trained. The codes are not. Three ways to choose a word's code. Mode Code Distinct codes 0, fixed hash A hash of the seed and the word id. Distances are about \(D/2\), so only identity carries signal 4,096 1, root A hash of the word's icosian root (a point from a 120-element rotation group) at most 120 2, learned The root code XOR a hash of a 5-dimensional readout, rebuilt every 1,000 steps 4,096 Rule check. The bit operations contain no softmax and no matrix multiplication. The Q15 scale multiply is a runtime product that has not been shown to be table-only, so it is not audited against the zero-multiplier serving rule (D11). The host learner that trained the scale was not audited against D23 here. The 9 October run used a CPU learner (the record says it was meant to run on the laptop, owner rule #2095). D24, dated 12 October, now bars CPU model compute. Binary 4,096-bit codes are not part of the current discrete path (D32). D32 welcomes XOR and Hamming comparison on ternary and E8 labels as one component of a model, not as a Hamming-only model.

30.body: M1 closes when one saved discrete model passes five conditions ( charter , section 4.8; D39 , item 1): (a) Starting reach. Before training, the right answer is among the candidates the model opens (its "reach") at no fewer than 4,894 of the 14,287 test positions (the gate called G-Pre; the "G-" names are gate codes from D39). (b) Reach kept. That reach survives training, on both seeds (G-Adm). (c) Real spread. More than 16 of the 256 word cells (the "drawers" of words) are in use, plus the further occupancy condition in D39 (G-Occ). (d) Beat the count tables (new, 19 October). Whole-number top-1, measured through the D11 export, beats both the unigram table (1,226 of 14,287) and the next-word table (6,300 of 14,287) on the same test panel, on each of two seeds, with tokens per second reported. This replaces the earlier bar of 0.90 bits per byte, which the current model cannot be scored on because its loss gives no probabilities. Bits per byte returns at a later milestone. (e) Fresh transfer. The gain holds on a fresh, sealed test panel registered in advance. For scale: the best trained model today scores 65 and 463 ( measurement , where we are ). The gap to 6,300 is large.

307.body: A rotation state in this model is a point on a four-dimensional sphere. The Hopf map looks at that point through a three-dimensional shadow. The shadow forgets one angle, so many different states cast the same shadow. This mechanism keeps the forgotten angle in a separate slot, so nothing is lost, and uses it to track drifting phase and to sort states into routing bins. A related idea, the Lorentz read, scores a match by distance in a curved, tree-friendly space instead of by a dot product. Neither has been shown to help a language model.

307.title: In plain words

308.body: Attention scoring: the rule that decides how well a query matches a stored key. A transformer uses a dot product. The Lorentz read replaces it with a curved-space distance, and the Hopf bins were meant to route a query to a small group of keys before scoring. A unit quaternion drawn as a point on a 3-sphere, its shadow on a 2-sphere, and the fibre circle through the point. A phase slider moves the point around its circle while the shadow stays put, and a second readout accumulates the winding as the kept fibre phase. Beside it, a 512-cell sector grid with 7 cells lit, and a flat dot product against a hyperbolic disk on a tree of code scopes. What the shadow forgets, and what the old routing did with it. Moving the point around the fibre changes nothing in the shadow; the kept phase records it.
308.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Hopf observation with a kept fibre » What it replaces in a transformer
308.title: What it replaces in a transformer

309.body: The map (Definition). Write a unit quaternion as \(q=(a,b,c,d)\) with \(z_1=a+ib\) and \(z_2=c+id\). The Hopf map to the 2-sphere is \[h(q)=\big(2(ac+bd),\ 2(bc-ad),\ a^2+b^2-c^2-d^2\big)=\big(2\,\mathrm{Re}(z_1\bar z_2),\ 2\,\mathrm{Im}(z_1\bar z_2),\ |z_1|^2-|z_2|^2\big).\] Two facts (proof, by expanding the squares). First, \(|h(q)|^2=(a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2)^2=1\), so \(h\) lands on the unit sphere. Second, multiplying both \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) by the same phase \(e^{i\varphi}\) leaves \(z_1\bar z_2\) and both moduli unchanged. That phase moves \(q\) around a circle (the fibre ) while \(h(q)\) stays put. So the shadow alone cannot be inverted. Rebuilding \(q\) needs the base point, the fibre phase and a chart convention, because there is no global identification \(S^3=S^2\times S^1\). Kept fibre (Definition). Holonomy tracking accumulates the wrapped change in fibre phase, plus the Fubini-Study distance, along a trajectory of states. In the integer runtime these are recorded per session and are marked telemetry only: they do not change any output. Sector routing (Definition). Three Hopf coordinates are binned \(8\times8\times8=512\) ways. When the inputs are non-negative at most 64 sectors are reachable, a fact of the binning (proof). Lorentz read (Definition). Lift query \(q\) and key \(k\) to the hyperboloid, \(q_0=\sqrt{1+|q|^2}\) and \(k_0=\sqrt{1+|k|^2}\), and set \(z=q_0k_0-q\cdot k\). The score is \(\beta\,(\delta-\operatorname{arccosh} z)\), with a learned radius \(\delta\) and scale \(\beta\). Icosian shadows (from enumeration). The 120 icosians map onto 30 points of the 2-sphere, every fibre of size 4 (checked by finite enumeration in the geometry chapter ). Rule check. D11: not yet. The integer helpers use multiplication and division, the core helpers decode to f64, and the integer runtime refuses Lorentz models until an integer arccosh table exists. D23: the map has no softmax. Every Lorentz read and attention that was actually run normalised scores with softmax, which is excluded. D30: the map is a few products, not a matrix multiplication. The float Lorentz stacks used dense query and key projections, which are barred. D32/D37: the float Hopf helpers (sine, cosine, square root) fall outside the zeta-zero exception. Under D37 a float version could be re-registered with a fresh review. The current discrete Route, Flock and Relation reads use no Hopf quantity ( the geometry chapter ).

31.body: The audit of 19 October laid out the shortest credible path as six stages ( audit synthesis , section 4). It is a proposal. The stage order follows the owner's fixed sequence in D39 item 4; changing it is the owner's decision. Stage 0. Run what is already FIT'd. A capacity test (called W2, about $0.91) is FIT-reviewed and queued, awaiting an owner release ( NOW , row 6). "Capacity" here means how many different words the addresses can tell apart. W2 decides whether the shortfall comes from the representation (the addresses cannot tell enough words apart) or the learning law (the training method cannot find good addresses). Next comes the rerun of the address-cell model with its reach protected ( controller record ). Decides: fix the addresses, or move on to Stage 2. Stage 1. Make the capacity measurable. Replace the coarse address key (today it can take only 5 different values, so it barely separates the drawers) with one that uses the whole vector, and measure it before any training. A wider code is optional and needs new GPU code. Bar: enough distinct vectors that the number of positions still winnable clears the run bar of 1,941, and a starting reach above the address-cell model's 1,351 of 3,847. Stage 2. Pick the learning law. First a faster discrete method that scores 16 coordinates at once (called BVG-K; its first stage is qualified), at about $12 for two seeds. Only if Stage 0 blames the learning law and BVG-K fails: one decimal-training run in a separate module, at about $5 to $10 plus build work. Decimal numbers are allowed in offline training only; the shipped file stays whole-number ( charter , section 3.7). Bar: beat the unigram table, then the admission-matched next-word table (the version W2 produces, not the 6,300 full-panel table), on two seeds. Stage 3. Add the missing parts. Build a trunk with a feed-forward layer (the Hamilton gate), a recurrence with quaternion rotation, and the Flock and Relation reads. None of these has been trained together, and the only supporting evidence is weak, so this stage is a hypothesis test, not reuse of proven parts. Scale and data are also open: no trained stack has used the 1.39-billion-token chat corpus the project assembled (UOR-Foundation/uor-r4#1660). Bar: beat Stage 2's best by more than the seed-to-seed noise, with a fresh-panel number. Stage 4. Export and serve. Write the missing exporter that turns a trained model into a D11 file, then measure the export gap and tokens per second on a laptop. Bar: the integer audits stay green, the gap stays within the noise band, and tokens per second is reported for both reading the prompt and writing the reply. This is where M1's bar (d) and M4 are tested. Stage 5. First simple conversation. Train on fixed example answers produced once by a donor model (not yet generated), as the owner's one-time exception D41 allows: the student sees only the answers, never the donor's probabilities. Ground replies in the exact memory and the object store. Bar: M2's bar, at least 256 of 512 saved questions and at least 40% of fresh ones, graded by fixed deterministic checks. Binding conditions on every stage. Training is held until the owner releases each reviewed plan, and the owner types each release personally ( charter , section 5). M1 can only be closed by a whole-number-trained ("discrete") model, so if Stages 3 and 4 use a trunk (the main body of the network) trained with decimals, the owner must first redefine the milestone. Under D41 , the Stage 5 student stays on the discrete path unless the owner decides otherwise ( audit synthesis , section 4). What the audit proposes to stop: rerunning the old starting table (built from a fixed random seed) that gives at most 16 distinct vectors; tuning admission objectives on the 5-value key; and reading much into any run that loses to the two count tables.

316.title: Tokenizer

317.body: The model never sees letters. It sees numbered pieces of text, and this component cuts text into those pieces and turns pieces back into text. It starts from raw bytes, so any text can be encoded. Then it learns which neighbouring pairs of pieces occur most often and glues them into bigger pieces, so common words become one piece and rare words stay in several. The project's pinned tokenizer has 4,096 pieces. This is a standard technique, not a novel one. What is distinctive here is that the tokenizer's fingerprint is recorded in every file that depends on it.
317.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Tokenizer » In plain words
317.title: In plain words

318.body: It fills the same slot as a transformer's tokenizer; it replaces no transformer part with a different mechanism. A transformer has a tokenizer too, usually byte-level BPE. This page is on the board because the tokenizer fixes the vocabulary size and id space that the prime-zeta codebook and the address-structured cells are sized by. It also pins the identity that makes results comparable. A sentence at the bottom as bytes, merge arcs lifting pairs into larger pieces, and the final piece ids on top, with the number 84 shown as the two pieces 8 and 4. Beside it, a ladder of 3,837 merges with a vocabulary slider, and a strip from raw text through the tokenizer to a prepared corpus file with check marks for file hash, token count and tokenizer identity. Bytes become pieces by repeated merging, and the fingerprint of the merge table travels with every prepared file. A two-digit number is still two pieces.
318.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Tokenizer » What it replaces in a transformer
318.title: What it replaces in a transformer

319.body: Vocabulary layout (Definition). Ids 0, 1 and 2 are start, end and unknown. Ids 3 to 258 are the 256 single bytes. The rest are learned merges. For the pinned tokenizer that is \(3+256+3837=4096\). Training (Definition). Count adjacent pairs over the unique pieces of text in the corpus (pre-tokens), each weighted by how often it occurs. Then repeat: merge the pair with the highest weighted count into a new piece, and recount only the words that contain it. Ties go to the pair with the smaller left, then right, token string, so the result is deterministic. Special tokens are atomic. No merge crosses a special token, a pre-token boundary or an input file. Encoding (Definition). Apply the merges to a text's bytes in rank order. This is a table lookup with no learned arithmetic. Identity (Definition). The tokenizer is stored as a tokenizer.json. Its raw-byte blake3 hash is the tokenizer's identity, and that hash is bound into every prepared corpus and artifact. A different tokenizer is therefore a different corpus. Prepared corpora. The UORT v1 format is a 64-byte header followed by 16-bit token ids, with start markers and an optional binary response mask. Before reading a target, the discrete driver verifies the file hash, the token count and the tokenizer identity. One dialogue encoding. A DialogueProtocol object fixes how roles and turns are written out, so training, test panels and chat use identical token segments. The need is real. Two branches once used incompatible serialisations, and even identical visible text can encode differently, because the merge rules may join a marker's trailing space to the first content token. Numbers. In the pinned vocabulary no piece made only of digits has more than one digit: it has 10 pure single-digit pieces and 0 pure multi-digit pieces (measurement, below). Mixed pieces, such as a space plus a digit, were not ruled out. 327.body: The model is a big table of small whole-number vectors, one per word, plus a few routing choices. To teach it, the machine picks one table entry and tries every allowed rotation of it, 16 options counting "leave it alone". For each option it replays a batch of training examples and counts the mistakes with whole-number arithmetic. It keeps the best option only if that is strictly better than leaving the entry alone. There are no gradients, no decimals and no matrix multiplication. Every step stays inside the values the finished model can hold. So far the method has moved some counts but has not produced better language.
327.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Discrete geometric learning » In plain words
327.title: In plain words

328.body: The optimiser. A transformer is trained by backpropagation: it computes a smooth slope for every weight and nudges all of them a little. Here nothing is smooth. Learning is a search over a short list of legal moves for one coordinate at a time, scored by a replay of real examples. A loop drawn around one table entry. Step 1, counterfactual: the entry's 16 legal states (the current state plus 15 rotations) are laid out as a 4 by 4 grid of cells, each with an integer loss bar below it. Step 2, choose: the lowest bar is lit, with ties going to staying put. Step 3, apply: the entry moves to the lit state only if its bar is strictly lower than the stay-put bar. Step 4, validate: the stored table is re-checked on the device. An arrow returns to step 1 for the next coordinate. One learning step on one table entry: try all 16 legal states, pick the cheapest, commit only on strict improvement, then check the stored result.
328.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Discrete geometric learning » What it replaces in a transformer
328.title: What it replaces in a transformer

329.body: State (definition). A shared integer codebook maps each of the \(V=4096\) tokens to \(B=4\) blocks of 8 integers. Each block is one of 16 roots of a single orbit of the E8 lattice (a fixed set of 16 integer vectors; not the full set of 240). The model also holds, for each routing stage, one of 64 signed-axis rotations of 8-dimensional space (the SpiralCore group), and optional gates that take the values \(-1\), \(0\) or \(+1\). Each of these is a coordinate : a vector block, a route frame or a gate. Read and write (definition). A read turns the token window into an integer vector \(q\). A shared writer gives each token a cell from the root numbers of its first and last block (\(16\times16=256\) cells), keeps the \(K\) nearest occupied cells to \(q\) by L1 distance ( admission ), and picks the nearest token inside them. The same table encodes input, carries memory and ranks output. Loss (definition). The loss is the integer rank-margin hinge . Per row, with \(T\) the token hinge and \(A\) the address hinge: \[\ell = \frac{8\,T + w\,A}{8w},\qquad w = 8B = 32 \text{ in the lineage of record.}\] Learning step (definition). For one coordinate \(\theta\) and a batch of rows \(\mathcal R\) whose eligibility is fixed by the baseline: \[L(m)=\sum_{x\in\mathcal R}\ell\big(x;\ \theta\leftarrow m\big),\qquad m\in\{\mathrm{id},m_1,\dots,m_{15}\}.\] The 15 non-identity moves are bivector rotations. The step picks \(m^*=\arg\min_m L(m)\). Ties go to the identity, then to the lowest resulting port number, then to the lowest enumeration index. It applies \(m^*\) only if \(L(m^*)<L(\mathrm{id})\), then re-validates the stored table on the GPU. Nothing is sampled, and no floating-point number appears anywhere in the step. Consequence (proof, from the definition). Every committed move strictly lowers the loss on its own batch , and the new state is always a legal state. The pilot's receipt audit confirmed this on every accepted move ( measurement , pilot record ). The step says nothing about rows outside the batch. A move that helps its batch could push other targets out of the shortlist; that is a hypothesis consistent with the Q1 stops below, and causal attribution was not made. Speed-ups. The row-parallel kernel (rows_v1) computes the baseline once per row and each candidate once per row and lane, instead of replaying every row serially per candidate. It reproduces the serial losses on every checked case ( measurement : Route read 3.843 s to 0.0691 s per proposal, 55.6 times faster, 64 rows; Route-mode index coverage was widened after review). BVG-K (batched verified coordinates) scores up to 64 coordinates per launch and commits a block only if its joint loss beats the best single move. Rule check. No softmax, exp, softplus, sigmoid or tanh (D23), and no matrix multiplication (D30): the choice is an integer minimum, distances are integer L1 and Hamming, and moves are table lookups. The snapshot is integer, but it has not been exported or audited against the D11 serving form, no serving engine for it exists and no export gap or tokens per second has been measured. D37 allows offline float training; that would need a separate scanned module and a reported export gap.

336.body: Most language models are scored by turning every possible next word into a probability and punishing surprise. Here the score is simpler. For each example, the right word has to beat its strongest wrong rivals by a fixed gap. If it does, the loss is zero and there is nothing to learn from that example. If it does not, the loss is the size of the shortfall. Every step is a comparison and a subtraction, with no probabilities and no logarithms.
336.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Rank-margin hinge objective » In plain words
336.title: In plain words

337.body: The loss function. A transformer minimises cross-entropy, which needs a softmax over the whole vocabulary. This objective compares the target with a few named rivals only. A number line of raw scores for one example. The target is a dot, eight rival dots sit to its left and right, and a shaded band one unit wide sits below the target. Rivals inside the band contribute a red overshoot bar whose length is the hinge loss. A second panel shows the same example after learning, with every rival outside the band and no red bars. Hinge loss on one example: only rivals that come within the margin of the target contribute, and their contribution is the length of the overshoot.
337.breadcrumbs: The mechanism board » Rank-margin hinge objective » What it replaces in a transformer
337.title: What it replaces in a transformer

338.body: Float form (definition; training only, never trained). Take the raw scores \(z\) of the head. Fix a rival count \(k\) in advance (1 or 8 in the rung-0 sheet) and let \(\mathcal R_k\) be the \(k\) highest-scoring non-target entries. \[L=\frac1k\sum_{j\in\mathcal R_k}\max\big(0,\ 1-z_t+z_j\big).\] The margin is fixed at 1. A row that already leads every rival by 1 or more contributes exactly zero gradient, and nothing is exponentiated or normalised in either direction. Integer form (definition; the live objective). The writer ( discrete-learning ) already ranks by integer distances, so the hinge works on those. With \(d\) the L1 token distance, \(\mathrm{addr}\) the address distance to a cell, and \(w=32\): \[T=\max\big(0,\ w+d(\text{target})-d(\text{best rival token})\big),\qquad A=\max\big(0,\ 8+\mathrm{addr}(\text{target})-\mathrm{addr}(\text{best rival cell})\big),\] \[\text{loss numerator}=8T+w\,A\qquad\text{over the common denominator }8w.\] This is objective A . Objective R replaces \(A\) by a rank term. Let \(r\) be one plus the number of occupied cells that come before the target's cell in the order (address distance, cell number). Then \[R=\max(0,\ r-K).\] A crowded cell counts once, and \(R=0\) exactly when the target's cell is among the \(K\) kept cells ( admission ). Rules of the comparison (definition). Which rows can count is fixed from the baseline. A missing comparison contributes zero, and the output reports how many rivals it had, so zero is never mistaken for learning. A batch with no eligible row is refused. Ties go to the smaller token or cell number. Consequence (proof, from the definition). The weights 8 and \(w=32\) are powers of two, so the numerator needs only adds, compares and shifts. Because the loss is a weighted sum, its total and the visible ranks can disagree: the pilot's token term fell while its address term rose by more. Rule check. Compliant with D23 by construction: no exp, log-sum-exp, softplus, sigmoid or tanh. The older pooled-rank run used softplus on a log-ratio and is not compliant. It is the historical precursor only. No matrix multiplication (D30). The integer form already fits the integer serving contract (D11). The float form's export gap has never been measured, and under D37 it returns only as a new pre-registration with a fresh test-fitness review and an owner release.

345.body: The usual way to train a model for a small device is to train with smooth decimals and round at the end. Rounding can quietly undo what was learned. This idea skips that. Each parameter change is chosen straight from the short list of values the final integer model can hold, so every accepted step is already in its servable form. A checker also guarantees that a set of answers the model already gets right stays right. Choosing all the changes at once is a large puzzle for a solver. The attempts that rounded a smooth step broke the safety check, and the attempts that solved the puzzle directly hit arithmetic trouble before producing a single move.

346.body: The optimiser plus the rounding step that follows it: train in decimals, then quantise, then check by hand what broke. A number line for one coefficient. The unrounded training value is a dot. Fifteen evenly spaced ticks mark the legal quarter-step values from minus 7 over 4 to plus 7 over 4. A smooth step moves the dot to a new place, and rounding lands it on the nearest tick. A small box of protected answers beside the line turns red when the landing tick is on the wrong side of a guard. A second panel shows a grid of 380 guard rows against four step sizes, with many red cells after rounding and none for the unrounded step. Why rounding breaks protection: a step that passes every guard in smooth form can fail some of them once it lands on the legal grid.

347.body: Setting (definition). The older learner for milestone M2 (answering from memory; see the milestones ) holds 1,920 coefficients as decimal masters, in two groups of 960 (called Prefix and Generate). They are served as quarter-step codes \(q/4\) with \(q\in\{-7,\dots,7\}\), which gives 15 legal destinations per coefficient. Protected transaction (definition). A change \(\delta\) commits only if three things hold: the native scoring strictly lowers the pooled loss; 17 reference cases and 380 original winners still win; and the linearised guard test holds, \(J\delta\ge-10^{-10}\lVert\delta\rVert\). Here each row of \(J\) is the slope of one protected answer's margin. Two ways to build \(\delta\) (definition). Residual feedback. Take a smooth, protected direction and round it onto the grid over 32 feedback rounds. Direct construction. Solve a mixed-integer program. For each coefficient with unrounded value \(m\) and current code \(q_0\), binaries \(l\) and \(r\) pick "keep", "go lower" or "go higher": \[l+r\le1,\quad q\ge q_0+r-(q_0+7)\,l,\quad q\le q_0-l+(7-q_0)\,r,\quad \delta=\tfrac{q-q_0}{4}+(l+r)\Big(\tfrac{q_0}{4}-m\Big).\] Minimise the original gradient \(g\cdot\delta\) subject to the 380 unit-normalised guard rows \(\hat J\delta\ge0\). That is 1,960 variables, 440 constraints and a 4,096-node branch-and-bound cap, run offline in a pure-Rust solver (microlp). Numerical repair (definition). Replace the solver's fixed pivot threshold by a scale-aware one, \(\tau_j=32\,n\,u\,\max_i|a_{ij}|\) (with \(n\) the matrix size and \(u\) the unit round-off), and check the residual of every fresh factorisation. Consequence (proof, from the definition). Any committed move is a legal code and, by the commit rule, strictly lowers the loss. Whether the guards also survive is not guaranteed when a smooth move is rounded afterwards. The rounding runs below measure that. Rule check. Aligned with D11: every accepted step is already in the servable code set. The solver is offline float arithmetic and is not a serving part. The pooled-ranking loss behind the M2 learner used softmax and softplus forms that D23 bans, so a rerun needs a compliant objective. Not yet assessed against D30 (the guard test forms a 380-by-1,960 Jacobian product and the solver does dense LU), so a rerun would have to be classified or run on the GPU. The float solver was frozen by D32 and can return under D37 as an offline float sheet with a fresh review, an owner release, a separately scanned module and a reported export gap.

355.body: When a model reads a memory and then writes an answer, the lesson from a mistake should reach the pieces that actually carried the information, not only the last few scoring numbers. This idea pushes the error signal back through those carriers: the geometric objects that hold the read, and the prototypes the answer is chosen from. A later version also ties input, memory and output to one shared table of vectors. The runs so far have not shown a benefit. The arm with carrier credit and the arms without it all lost every answer the starting model had right, so the runs cannot blame the credit rule or clear it.

356.body: Backpropagation's job of blame assignment. In a transformer, the error flows back through every layer by the chain rule. Here the path is a chain of hard choices (which memory, which key, which answer) and geometric carriers, so the credit has to be designed rather than inherited. A pipeline strip from left to right: query, compiler spans, exact store, E8 index, H4 carriers, Generate prototypes, answer. Two arrows run backwards beneath it. The upper arrow, labelled frozen-carrier fit, reaches only the last scoring coefficients. The lower arrow, labelled unified fit, reaches the H4 carriers and the prototypes as well. The layers that changed in the executed runs are shaded. Where the error signal lands: the frozen-carrier fit changes only the final coefficients, while the unified fit also moves the carriers and prototypes.
