586.body: August. A source-free integer n-gram table predicted 22.26% of held-out targets against 5.41% for unigram, and one exact tie-break added 0.95 points ( table , tie-break ). The skip-mix lane beat base by +28.45 per mille top-1 ( record ). A vector (SIMD) scan sped one path up 1.60 times against a 2 times bar ( record ). 8 Sep. The alpha publication was withdrawn: the scorecard had used constant or flag evidence ( record ). 9 to 10 Oct: the gap is the model. The published 0.877 float against 0.933 served compared different numbers of windows. On a matched retrain the pair is 0.8776 against 0.8868 bits per byte ( protocol pin ). The recorded criterion is still "not met and not claimable", and the matched float model sits at 0.924 on the attribution record's own table. At identical positions quantization cost 0.0041 and the engine cost -0.0000008 ( attribution ). The integer engine matched float exactly (maximum logit difference 0) while three served models scored 1.20, 1.24 and 1.24 against the 0.90 target ( D11 serving ). 10 to 11 Oct: lawful pieces. Replacing the served softmax read with rank-weight tables cost 0.017 to 0.26 bits per byte more across four arms, all missing a 0.01 bar ( softmax-free read ). Weights built from two icosian table entries and a 2-bit mantissa reached 1.5148 against 1.4944 for float quaternions and 1.5136 for dense of equal size ( icosian mantissa ). The integer engine refuses product-key memory entirely, so the speed case there is unmeasured ( port ). 18 Oct. An outside contributor's WebAssembly integer runtime was merged after hardening: 165 tests pass and 7 of 7 serving symbols show no multiply, divide or float. The vector (SIMD) kernels are not integrated and the demo is not runnable from a clean clone ( record ).

6.body: In one paragraph. UOR-R4 is an attempt to build a language model, the kind of program behind chat assistants, that is cheap enough to train and run on an ordinary laptop or inside a web browser. Today's language models are transformers . They spend most of their effort multiplying very large grids of decimal numbers. UOR-R4 bets that a different toolkit can do the same job for far less: rotations of a geometric object, exact whole-number addresses built from primes, small lookup tables, and an exact memory. This page explains that bet in about five minutes. It is a research project and it is pre-alpha . None of its 8 milestones is complete, and no model built under its rules holds a useful conversation yet ( STATUS , NOW ). Four panels read left to right. Panel 1: the words "the cat sat on the" split into numbered pieces. Panel 2: each piece becomes an address, drawn as a point on a ring of evenly spaced points (a stand-in for the geometric object), labelled "4 blocks of 8 whole numbers". Panel 3: the newest piece looks at only a few nearby earlier points, which are highlighted, while the rest of the history stays grey. Panel 4: a few labelled drawers open near what was read, and the nearest word inside them, "mat", is picked. A band under all four panels reads "whole numbers only: adds, compares and table look-ups". How UOR-R4 predicts the next word. Each step uses only whole numbers. The picture shows the design; it does not show a model that already works well. Words in bold are defined in the glossary . Claims are labelled proof (follows from definitions or code), measurement (from a recorded run) or hypothesis (an untested idea), as in docs/formal_vocabulary.md .

604.body: Baselines and the recurrent learner (24 to 25 Sep). A neural reference reached 1.574 nats against 2.392 for the best 5-gram-plus-cache baseline ( baselines ). Both float recurrent arms reached about 2.11 nats and passed the engineering gate, but the quaternion arm trailed the ordinary control, so no geometric advantage was shown ( result ). Integer forms (25 to 27 Sep). Four-bit quantization-aware training missed its +0.05-nat retention gate (+0.059 and +0.080) ( result ). Learned rounding passed (2.114 and 2.111 nats) and an integer bridge kept every source answer, about 28 times slower than float ( learned rounding , bridge ). A standalone integer command reproduced all 4,096 saved distribution hashes and ran 4.5 to 6.6 times faster after one optimization ( serving ). Continued language training lowered loss but produced 0 of 5 acceptable stories ( continuation ). Geometric reads (26 to 28 Sep). A Lorentz (hyperbolic) read beat a dot-product read by 0.018 nats on code in 3 of 4 seeds, then lost to the matched dot reset when adapted (+0.046 and +0.013 nats) ( cycle 3 , adaptation ). The stack matched a 7M-parameter transformer on repository code (1.998 against 2.011 nats), but generated code was useless ( cycle 4 ). An exact relation store was perfect in distribution but its learned read trigger fired 0 of 826 times on held-out phrasing ( exact relation store probe, D2 ). Quantization (28 to 29 Sep). Round-to-nearest 4-bit export cost +0.0362 nats against a 0.02 gate ( representation measurements ). Quantization-aware training brought the integer engine within +0.0106 nats of its float model, bit-identical to a NEON reference ( QAT ). Contest and withdrawals (6 to 11 Oct). In the D20 contest, a three-seed test of the geometric read against a parameter-matched control found no winner: the geometric arm scored 0.0073, 0.9995 and 1.0000 in class against about 0.25 for the control ( D20 run ). A claimed 12-times faster fused kernel was withdrawn because the pod never ran it ( record ).

610.body: Attention in geometric coordinates (27 Aug to 3 Sep). Small positive tests changed a decoded continuation: for example real 2/2 against 0/2 when the binding was permuted ( paragraph test ). Not all passed. Full H4 causal attention scored 3/12 while plain fixed-tangent attention scored 12/12 ( direct causal test ), and a gauge-covariance test scored 13/24 against an 18 gate ( V4 ). A recall control (Zoology) reached 99.17% (11,900/12,000) with an ordinary softmax cell, which showed the earlier binding failures came from the training recipe ( record ). A parameter-free readout ladder failed. Four variants of reading retained state all missed the frozen prompt-gain floor of 0.0433 (best 0.0390) ( block-delta ). Rust engine and exact memory (4 to 13 Sep). Dozens of narrow positives on authored panels, for example 50/50 against 12/50 for a contextual phrase start and 64/64 against 0/64 for fresh historical targets ( contextual start , historical query ). Each is scoped to a familiar grammar. The fixed geometric readout alone scored 0.13% against 21.5% with geometry disabled ( recovery ). Joint fits failed (12 to 13 Sep). Eight negative records on calibrated emission, block learning and tied sampling each broke earlier behaviour or missed a gate. A 64-update addressed-attention pilot produced no useful answers ( pilot ). Learned readers (19 to 25 Sep). A competing-source reader beat exact recurrence on a built panel but harmed natural text by +1.29 bits per token against a +0.05 tolerance ( result ). H4 shared transitions scored 186/288 where an ordinary finite table scored 288/288 ( result ). Four integrated-attention trials (A1 to A4) lifted correct source admission from 1/24 to 17/24 but never produced a complete correct answer (0/12 per arm) ( A3 ). End of the line (25 to 28 Sep). Bounded admission lost the first noun in 11 and 8 cases against a maximum of 2 ( result ). Icosian direction codes changed the dense read's top choice at 41 to 46 percent of positions and were rejected as address codes ( audit ).

628.body: Import. The standalone wire compression and transport code (Python, Rust and an interposer) was imported as a self-contained side exploration with loopback benchmarks. On a Rust peer, a 1.25 MiB compressed exchange took 2.86 ms on average (range 2.10 to 3.30) against 1.92 ms for plain TCP; for 1 KiB, a round trip took 41.8 microseconds against 55.1. So on loopback the wire layer was faster for the 1 KiB round trip and slower for the 1.25 MiB exchange ( import ). Review fixes. Four findings from Codex's review of the merged transport were repaired: a receive lock, stream cleanup, a workspace path and committed build outputs. Smoke tests pass; no model compute ran ( fixes ). A second round repaired a file-descriptor reuse race, stream registration order and half-close handling, with four smoke tests passing ( round two ). A fix that broke something. Adding a socket shutdown on close woke a blocked reader but broke fork safety, and the next record replaced it. The final interposer closes a shared socket after a fork without killing the parent's connection; fork and negative-control smoke tests pass on macOS and a Linux guest ( round three , fork-safe ). Counters and reproducibility. A one-character bug made a reused route report only its last connection's bytes. The fix reports two connections, 3,357 wire bytes and a ratio of 0.0041 against 0.0030 for the last connection alone, and a regression test fails without it ( counter fix ). The interoperability matrix was made reproducible off the owner's machine, with 18 passing legs and none failing, and claims that cited nonexistent verify tools were withdrawn ( matrix ).

657.body: Each notebook lives at docs/research/notebook/<line>.md. A line is one sustained question, such as "how the discrete model reads context". The charter sets this format (CHARTER.md, section 5.6), and the owner chose it in answer to question 4 of the 19 October 2026 review. Every result is one row with six columns: Column What goes in it Date The ISO date the result was recorded (YYYY-MM-DD). What ran One or two plain sentences: the test or check, on what, with what budget. Number The measured value, with its denominator and the baseline it is read against. Bar The pass line that was fixed before the run, or "none registered" when the run was a diagnostic or a qualification check. Verdict One of the five words below, with a short qualifier. Artifact A link to the record or the sealed evidence folder that holds the proof. Rules for keeping a notebook: Append at the bottom. The newest row is last. Rows from one day appear in the order the work ran where the records show it. One row per result. A repeat of an earlier run gets its own row. A change of plan, a review or a tooling step is not a result and gets no row. A dated evidence folder only when a run seals artifacts (checkpoints, receipts, logs with checksums). The row links to it. A result with nothing to seal needs no folder. Numbers are measurements from a recorded run, unless the row says proof or hypothesis, as defined in formal_vocabulary.md . A passing control is not a language result, and NOT_RUN is not a pass. Rows are never edited to change a verdict. If a later run corrects an earlier one, add a new row that names the earlier one.
657.breadcrumbs: How research is done now » Research notebooks » The format
657.title: The format

658.body: Verdict Meaning positive The run met the bar or passed the controls it registered, at the scope stated in the row. negative The run missed a registered bar. It closes that exact configuration (recipe, dose, window, objective) and never the mechanism (D22). inconclusive The run produced a number, but no bar was decided, or the evidence cannot separate the explanations. diagnostic stop A registered stop rule or the owner ended the run early so the cause could be found. It is not a negative. blocked A fault in the tooling, the machine or the source stopped the run before it could measure. It is not a negative, and it is not a result about the model.

663.body: DEV panel. The open development panel of 14,287 rows. Each row is a context and the true next token. P_succ (the copy-successor subset) is 3,847 of those rows; it is the subset where the answer follows an earlier occurrence of the same token. Admission. The read can only choose among a shortlist of candidate cells (K of them, usually K=8). A row is admitted when the true next token's cell is on the shortlist. A token outside it can never be chosen, so admission is a ceiling on top-1. Top-1 / top-8. The true token ranked first / within the first eight. Batches. Training steps. A full registered dose is 16,404 batches. FIT. An independent review of a run's pre-registration sheet before spending compute. A FIT releases nothing by itself. Control (C-R1 to C-R6, V2 and the like). A check built to fail if the instrument is wrong. A passing control is not a model result. Status words (positive, negative, diagnostic stop, blocked) are defined in the format page .

665.body: The integer path is built and its finite controls pass. Those are construction results, and they say nothing about language. Training moves the rank counts up but has not yet beaten the context-free count table. The best trained result in the rows is 463 of 14,287, against 6,300 for T2 and 1,226 for the unigram table (CHARTER.md, section 4.8). The main obstacle found so far is admission: a token outside the shortlist can never be chosen. Widening the shortlist at test time did not fix it (row of 15 October). Placing cells by address structure fixed it at the start (1,351 against 127 of 3,847), but training then pushed target cells out of the shortlist (the A8 row). Six of the 30 rows are blocked by tooling or build faults and are not results about the model. The row-parallel kernel (about 56x faster proposals with identical losses) is the largest measured speed change. The next step recorded in the A8 row is a choice among three diagnoses by the PM: an acceptance rule that refuses moves which eject a target cell, a per-checkpoint cell census, or a finer checkpoint cadence. Each new training run needs a reviewed sheet and a typed owner release.

668.body: This notebook records tests of one idea: give every token a fixed starting vector built from numbers rather than from random noise. Each token gets a prime number by its rank, and the phases of the Riemann zeta zeros, read at the logarithm of that prime, turn the prime into an eight-dimensional integer vector. The one result so far shows that the vectors are distinct and the GPU code accepts them. It does not show that the vectors help the model read. flowchart LR A["Token id v"] --> B["Prime by rank:<br/>p = prime number v+1"] B --> C["Zeta phases:<br/>gamma_k times ln p, mod 2 pi"] C --> D["Quantize to integers<br/>(29-bit phase, 30-bit unit vector)"] D --> E["Nearest E8 root cell,<br/>balanced over 256 cells"] E --> F["Integer codebook table<br/>read by the GPU model"] How one token becomes one table row. The steps are the construction described in the record linked below; the table is built once, offline, on the host. Background: primes and zeta explains the phases, and the prime-zeta codebook page gives the mechanism's status. The line page for the model that reads this table is discrete attention .

673.body: This notebook tracks whether conversation can be stored so that it lasts across sessions and comes back exactly as it went in. The idea is to fold text into a deduplicated store of small records and rebuild the bytes from them, with a hash check that proves nothing changed. 68.body: In one paragraph. UOR-R4 uses a lot of words that come from three places: language models (token, softmax, BPB), geometry (quaternion, E8, icosian) and the project's own rulebook (FIT, KEEP, PARKED). This page defines each one in a sentence or two and links to the page that explains it properly. Words are in alphabetical order. If you meet a code name such as K16 or A8 in a record, look for it here too. The project is pre-alpha: 0 of its 8 milestones are complete and no model holds a useful conversation yet ( STATUS ). flowchart LR subgraph model["The model, in the order text flows through it"] direction LR T["Text"] --> TK["Tokens<br/>(tokenizer, BPE)"] TK --> AD["Address<br/>(codebook, E8, prime)"] AD --> RD["Read<br/>(Route, Flock, Relation)"] RD --> AM["Admission<br/>and writer"] AM --> NX["Next token<br/>(top-1)"] LS["Loss and learning<br/>(hinge, counterfactual move)"] -.-> AD NX --> EX["Export<br/>(UORLUT01, export gap)"] EX --> SV["Serving<br/>(D11, WASM, tokens/s)"] end subgraph rules["How the work is judged"] direction LR CH["Charter and D-entries"] --> FT["FIT sheet"] FT --> RL["Owner release"] RL --> NB["Notebook row<br/>(KEEP, PARKED)"] end Where each family of terms sits. 693.body: UOR-R4 is trying to build a fast language model that runs on an ordinary laptop and does not use the expensive machinery inside today's chat AIs. A short rulebook, the charter , keeps every contributor pointed at that goal. This page explains what the charter says, why each rule exists, what the project's labs may and may not do, and who makes which decision. It is a guide to the charter, not a replacement: if the two ever disagree, the charter wins. flowchart TD idea["Idea or experiment"] --> rules{"Inside the constraints?<br/>Geometry only, no squashing,<br/>no matmul"} rules -- "No" --> owner["Only the owner can<br/>change the charter"] rules -- "Yes" --> need{"Needs GPU training or evaluation,<br/>or will a milestone claim rest on it?"} need -- "No: builds, kernel tests,<br/>host checks" --> doit["Just do it"] need -- "Yes" --> sheet["Pre-registration: one-page sheet<br/>bar, noise, controls, seeds,<br/>cost, what each outcome decides"] sheet --> fit{"FIT review by someone<br/>other than the author"} fit -- "Not fit" --> sheet fit -- "FIT" --> release["Owner release:<br/>one per sheet, typed by Casey"] release --> run["Run on the GPU via uor-pod"] run --> row["Notebook row: date, what ran,<br/>number, bar, verdict, artifact"] doit --> row How work moves from an idea to a recorded result. Only the Yes branch that needs GPU spend or a milestone claim goes through a sheet, a review and an owner release.

694.body: The owner's stated goal behind every ban, in his own words from 18 October 2026, is "to ban expensive operations" and to optimise for "fast local ai that can train fast and run fast" and reaches "almost frontier level capability" (CHARTER.md §1, from decision D37). Each rule removes a cost that a dense neural network pays, or protects the evidence that tells the project whether its geometric replacement works. When a case is unclear, the charter says to choose what trains and serves fastest on a laptop through the geometric path, and to write the choice down. The project's headline metric is tokens per second: how fast the model reads and writes text, with decode speed and context speed measured separately. A small quality gap is acceptable (CHARTER.md §1). The project is pre-alpha, 0 of its 8 milestones are complete, and no model holds a useful conversation yet (STATUS.md; see the mechanism board ). These are rules, so the labels "proof", "measurement" and "hypothesis" from docs/formal_vocabulary.md do not apply to them. The "why" given for each rule below is the reason the charter itself states. It is not a measured result.

695.body: The charter's section 3 lists thirteen technical constraints. Here they are in everyday terms. Terms are defined in the glossary . # Rule What it means in practice Why the charter gives 3.1 Geometry only Every mechanism, training signal and fix comes from the project's geometry (prime addresses, rotations, E8/H4 structures). The flock rule for attention looks at about 7 nearest neighbours, not a dense teacher. The bet is that geometry replaces expensive dense operations. 3.2 No squashing functions No softmax, log-softmax, cross-entropy, softplus, sigmoid, tanh or GELU anywhere, including in losses, sampling and comparators, and including renamed or lookup-table versions. They are expensive and hide a dense global normalisation. 3.3 No matrix multiplication No dense matmul in training, evaluation, tooling or serving, including wrappers and hand-written loops. A geometric feed-forward block is allowed; a dense MLP is not. Matmul is the cost the project exists to remove. 3.4 Presence counts Banned code may not sit in any compiled or loaded module. NVRTC (runtime GPU compilation) is banned. The checks uor-harness ratchet d23 and d25 only ever tighten. Code that is present eventually runs. 3.5 Research compute is GPU-only Training, evaluation, qualification and reference runs use the GPU. Spend GPU only where a run can change a decision. Host runs gave wrong timing and wrong evidence, and the GPU is where the speed is. 3.6 Serving is integer, on your device The shipped model uses no float, transcendental, multiplier or integer-divide instruction. Running it on a laptop CPU, in a browser (WebAssembly) or on Apple silicon is allowed, and so is measuring its speed and energy. Panel scoring, qualification and milestone evaluation of an exported artifact remain GPU research compute; only product serving and measuring its tokens/s and energy run on client devices. The product is fast local AI on ordinary hardware. 3.7 Float only offline, with an export gap Float training is legal offline in a separately scanned module. Every float candidate reports how much accuracy it loses when exported to integers; a loss above the two-seed noise band disqualifies it. Float trains faster, but only the integer artifact ships. 3.8 Zeta exception Float is allowed for complex-plane zeta-zero parts and prime log-phases. Everything downstream is discrete. Zeta phases are complex numbers by nature. 3.9 Efficiency is measured Report sparse access, bytes per token, bounded candidates and exact memory together. Unmeasured efficiency is not efficiency. 3.10 No neural comparisons No neural comparators, controls, teachers or graders until the owner says the model works end to end. Panels are graded by deterministic checks. The one exception is a one-time donor pass (D41) with binding conditions. A neural comparator would hide a dense model behind the geometry. 3.11 Rust first New code is Rust, built on the uor-foundation crates. Python only where Rust cannot do the job. One fast, checked language keeps training and serving on one path. 3.12 Exact identity stays separate from address One shared vector writer serves input, carry and output. Every artifact binds its data, seed, configuration and parameters. One representation avoids translation costs, and exact identity cannot be recovered from a geometric address. 3.13 Hygiene Typed errors instead of panics, no committed binaries, corpora or secrets, and API keys are never read or printed. It keeps the repository small and the keys out of it. Source: CHARTER.md §3; the first column gives its clause numbers.

696.body: A lab is any contributor, human or AI, working under the charter. The rules in sections 3 and 5 give these limits. Labs may: Choose their own work from NOW.md, post a one-line intent note, claim a branch and carry on unless redirected (CHARTER.md §5.3). Build, run finite kernel tests and run host checks without any pre-registration (§4.5). Train in float offline once a sheet, FIT and typed release exist (training is currently held; §3.7, §4.5, §5.1), and report the export gap on the same evaluator. Serve the integer model on a user's device and measure it (§3.6). Review their own pull request at the exact head, from a fresh context (§5.5), and use a fresh-context subagent as the non-author FIT reviewer (§4.5). Labs may not: Use a banned operation anywhere, including in comparators, or in renamed form (§3.2, §3.3). Run research compute on the CPU, or spend GPU on work that cannot change a decision (§3.5). Start GPU training or a milestone-bearing run without a sheet, a FIT review and a typed owner release (§4.5, §5.1). Use a neural comparator, teacher or grader, apart from the single D41 donor pass (§3.10). Type an owner release themselves. Casey types it personally with UOR_LAB unset; labs only stage the commands (§5.1, from D40). Cancel a healthy run because a self-set budget ran out, or touch another session's GPU or files (§5.4). Stop a mechanism. That needs the owner (§4.1). Delete research. Negatives, unique source and other labs' work go to the archive unchanged (§4.7). Exceed 4 pods or $8 per hour across all labs (§5.4).

698.body: Section 4 of the charter is about not fooling ourselves. A negative closes one configuration, never a mechanism. Mechanisms carry one of three statuses: ACTIVE (on the model path), READY (built and tested, not yet trained in) or PARKED (a tested form failed or broke a rule; the reopen conditions are listed). There is no "retired" status for a mechanism (§4.1). Rules can be retired; mechanisms cannot. Instrument before verdict. If a check fails, first ask whether the measuring tool or the mechanism is at fault. A broken instrument is a fix, not a negative (§4.2). Power. A decisive run uses at least 2 seeds or at least 200 fresh rows, with bars no narrower than the measured noise, and reports a fresh transfer number with every development gain (§4.3). Controls and pivots. Compare against lawful non-neural baselines such as count tables. After three results on one line that do not move its headline number, write a pivot note: stop, or run one decisive experiment (§4.4). Claims. Write "measured X on Y against Z". A test pass is not trained capability, and NOT_RUN is not a pass (§4.6). The first-milestone closing bar. For milestone M1, the integer model's top-1 accuracy through the D11 export must beat both the unigram table (1,226 of 14,287) and the T2 successor table (6,300 of 14,287) on the same development panel, on each of two seeds, with tokens per second reported (§4.8).

7.body: A language model reads text and guesses what comes next. First a tokenizer cuts the text into numbered pieces called tokens . A token is a word or part of a word. UOR-R4's tokenizer has 4,096 pieces ( tokenizer ). The model then looks at the pieces so far and predicts the next one. Given "the cat sat on the", a good model puts "mat" near the top of its list. It appends its guess and repeats. Everything a chat assistant does, answering, summarising, writing code, comes from running this one loop many times. So a model is only as good as its next-piece guesses, and only as fast as one turn of the loop.

70.body: A8. The nickname of the address-structured cells table, the starting table of the current model, and of the training run that began from it. At zero training it let the reader reach 1,351 of 3,847 copy-successor targets, against 127 for the plain PrimeZeta start ( measurement ). Learning then eroded that gain, and the first training run stopped at its first checkpoint. See address cells . ACTIVE. A mechanism status: the mechanism is on the current model path. See mechanism status . Address. A token's place in the model. It is 4 blocks of 8 whole numbers, and each block is one of 16 fixed points of the E8 lattice. Exact token identity is kept separately from this geometric address. (A token's prime address, defined below, is a different thing: its exact name as a prime number.) See the model, end to end . Admission. The shortlist step before the model picks a word. The 4,096 words sit in 256 cells, and the model opens only the few cells nearest to what its read points at. A word in an unopened cell can never be chosen, so admission caps everything before it ( proof , by construction). See admission . Artifact. A saved model file together with the data, seed, settings and parameters that made it. The charter requires every artifact to bind all of these. See charter , section 3.12. Attention. The step in which a language model decides which earlier words matter. A transformer compares the newest word with every earlier word. UOR-R4 replaces it with three cheaper reads: Route , Flock and Relation . See transformer vs geometry .

71.body: Bar. A pass line that is fixed before a run, so the result cannot be bent to fit afterwards. Bars are never narrower than the measured noise. See the rules . BPB (bits per byte). A score of how well a model predicts text: the average number of bits it needs for each byte. Lower is better. The older milestone bars use it (M4 asks for 0.90 or less). The current discrete model has no probabilities, so it cannot produce BPB, and on 19 October the owner replaced M1's BPB bar with a top-1 comparison. See rank-margin and charter , section 4.8. BPE (byte-pair encoding). The way the tokenizer builds its pieces. It starts from the 256 single bytes and repeatedly glues the most common neighbouring pair into a new piece. The pinned tokenizer has 4,096 pieces: 3 special ones, 256 bytes and 3,837 merges. See tokenizer and data and tokenizer . BVG-K (batched verified coordinates). A faster version of the learning step. It scores K table entries in one GPU launch and commits them together only if their joint loss beats the best single move. Scoring was about 16 times faster at K=16 ( measurement ), but it has never run as a learning law. See training .

712.title: UOR-R4 Charter

713.body: Build the UOR-R4 Geometric Language Model : a fast language model that is not a transformer. It predicts text with geometry (prime addresses, zeta phases, E8/H4/icosian rotations, SpiralCore/FBS routing) and exact memory, on an ordinary laptop or in a browser. Conversation with durable memory first, then coding and reasoning, on one model [AGENTS:mode, D19, AGENTS:both-lines]. Pre-alpha; no capability is established. The owner's rule: "USE GEOMETRY. THAT IS THE END OF IT. NEVER USE ANYTHING ELSE." [OWNER:0] The owner's goal behind every ban (18 Oct, verbatim): "my goal with all of these bans is to ban expensive operations and to always optimize for what is best for the project goal... fast local ai that can train fast and run fast and reach almost frontier level capability ... we have so many mechanisms, at this point we just need to stitch the right ones together and optimize all of the things that aren't, which will likely be found in the details" [OWNER:26, D37]. When unclear, choose what trains and serves fastest locally on the geometric path, and write it down [D37:why-bans]. The lead metric is tokens per second (decode, and context separately); a small quality gap is acceptable [OWNER:5].

Desktop client: a Tauri app sharing the web UI, the native integer model with D19 memory, offline, on M1-class laptops; spec only [renorm decision 8]. Legacy crates are repaired, not archived: uor-r4-graph-compiler, uor-r4-graph-certify, uor-r4-api, uor-r4-proof-model and the root crate are repaired to build on the current core; repairing restores the build only, and their mechanisms (r4g1-graph, native-geometric) stay PARKED. 714.title: 2. Products

715.body: Geometry only. Every mechanism, training signal and fix comes from the project's geometry; keep R4/S3, Hopf and paired-H4/icosian roles distinct (E8 = H4 ⊕ φH4, fixed). Flock reads use local rules (~7 nearest neighbours), not a dense teacher. Why: the bet is that geometry replaces expensive dense operations. [OWNER:0, OWNER:6, D20, D32:hamming-one-factor, AGENTS:typed-geometry, AGENTS:e8-shorthand] No squashing functions. No softmax, log-softmax, cross-entropy (implicit softmax), softplus, sigmoid, tanh, GELU or normalized exponential, anywhere: runtime, losses, gradients, sampling, teachers, surrogates, comparators, including renamed or table forms. Why: they are expensive and hide a dense global normalization. [D23, D25, OWNER:1, HR:no-squash] No matmul. No dense matrix multiplication or GEMM anywhere: training, evaluation, instruments, serving and tooling, including wrappers and hand loops. A geometric feed-forward block (Hamilton gate and projections) is allowed; a dense MLP is not. Why: matmul is the cost the project exists to remove. [D25:no-matmul-anywhere, D30, OWNER:2, OWNER:14, HR:no-matmul] Presence counts. Banned code may not exist in any compiled or loaded module or vendor path; NVRTC is banned; CUDA is prebuilt by nvcc. Ahead-of-time nvcc kernel builds run on the GPU pod (authorized by D30); the laptop runs CPU-only builds and static checks. The ratchets uor-harness ratchet d23|d25 only go down. Why: code that is present eventually runs. [D29, R5, OWNER:no-nvrtc, HR:banned-module] Research compute is GPU-only. Training, evaluation, qualification, and model and parity reference execution run on the GPU; a host fallback is a defect to fix with a kernel. Spend GPU only where a run can change a decision. Why: host runs gave wrong timing and wrong evidence, and the GPU is where the speed is. [D24, OWNER:4, OWNER:20, HR:gpu-only] Serving is integer, on the user's device. The exported artifact has no float, transcendental, multiplier or integer-divide instruction (D11 R1–R5); the frozen runtime does no steady-state allocation, and a dense model disguised as lookup tables is excluded. Serving it on client devices (CPU, browser WASM, Apple silicon), including measuring tokens/s and energy, is the product and is allowed; D24 does not apply, and D36's browser-as-CPU clause is replaced. Panel scoring, qualification and milestone evaluation of an exported artifact remain GPU research compute (§3.5); only product serving, and measuring its tokens/s and energy, run on client devices. Why: the product is fast local AI on ordinary hardware. [D11, D36, D39:float-horizon, HR:serving-integer, AGENTS:frozen-tla; owner 19 Oct] Float only offline, with an export gap. Float forward, gradients and optimizers are legal offline, in a separately scanned module, never in the discrete crate. Every float candidate reports its export gap on the same evaluator; a gap above the two-seed noise band disqualifies it. The D32 discrete path stays active; its qualification uses exact arithmetic. Why: float trains faster; only the integer artifact ships. [D37, D39:export-gap, R13, HR:float-offline, KIMI:d37] Zeta exception. Float is allowed on the complex plane for zeta-zero parts, prime log-phases and the C4→R4/C8→R8 phase maps; everything downstream is discrete. Why: zeta phases are complex numbers by nature, and the bans target expensive operations, not geometry. [D32:zeta-exception] Efficiency is measured. Report sparse access, bytes/token, bounded candidates, multiplier-free kernels and exact memory together, naming D5-a (residency) or D5-b (per-token sparsity, the end state). Why: unmeasured efficiency is not efficiency. [I1-I5, D5, D38] No neural comparisons (comparators, controls, teachers, graders) until the owner says the model works end to end; panels are graded deterministically. Sole exception: D41's one-time distill-d1 donor pass, on its binding conditions: the student consumes hard targets only (no logits, probabilities or distributions), the donor never executes in student preparation, training, evaluation, serving, grading or any panel, a generation receipt is bound at generation, and a typed D40 owner release is required at dispatch. Why: a neural comparator would hide a dense model behind the geometry, against geometry only. [D28, OWNER:memory-no-transformer, D41] Rust first , building on the uor-foundation crates; Python only where Rust cannot; no ad-hoc scripts. Why: one fast, checked language keeps training and serving on the same geometric path. [D27, OWNER:20, HR:rust-default] Exact identity stays separate from geometric address ; one shared vector writer serves input, carry and output; every artifact binds its data, seed, config, parameters and format. Why: one representation avoids translation costs, and exact identity cannot be recovered from a geometric address. [POLICY:shared-vectors, AGENTS:shared-vector, AGENTS:artifact-determinism] Hygiene: Result errors at library boundaries; no unwrap/expect/panic on recoverable paths; keep forbid(unsafe_code) in portable runtime and format crates; no committed binaries, corpora or secrets; never read or print API keys. Why: hygiene keeps the repository small and fast to clone, and keeps keys out of it. [AGENTS:errors, HR:no-artifacts, HR:no-credentials, AGENTS:no-keys]

716.body: A negative closes a configuration, never a mechanism. Mechanism statuses are ACTIVE (on the model path), READY (built and tested, not yet trained in) and PARKED (failed or broke a rule; reopen conditions listed). There is no terminal status. Stopping a mechanism needs the owner. [D22, D12, D2, POLICY:gates-promote, renorm decision 5] Instrument first. Classify a failing check as instrument or mechanism before calling anything; an instrument defect is a fix, never a negative. No target is set from a vacuous instrument; no single number rules out a line. [D31, R12, R14, D39:gcap] Power. Decisive runs use ≥ 2 seeds or ≥ 200 fresh rows, with bars no narrower than measured noise, the mechanism trained in, and a fresh transfer number with every development gain. [D22:power, D22:transfer, D17] Controls and progress. Compare against lawful non-neural baselines (count tables). After three results on a line that do not move its headline, write a pivot note: stop, or one decisive run. [D21, D6, D9, POLICY:progress-control] Pre-register only where it decides spend. 72.body: Carrier. The small integer block the model passes along: 8 whole numbers drawn from a 16-root orbit of E8, moved by 64 exact signed actions. Four carriers make one token's vector. See SpiralCore and architecture . Cell. One of the 256 drawers that admission opens. A word's cell is the pair of roots of its first and last block, so the grid is 16 by 16 and each cell starts with 16 words (training can move words between cells). See admission . Charter. The project's short rulebook, adopted by the owner on 19 October 2026. It replaced the older stack of instructions and numbered decisions. Only the owner changes it. See CHARTER.md and the rules in plain language . Codebook. The table that gives each of the 4,096 tokens its starting vector. In the current model it is built by a fixed recipe, not drawn at random: see PrimeZeta and A8 . See data and tokenizer and architecture . Control. A run identical to the one being tested except for the one thing under test. Controls here must be lawful non-neural baselines, such as count tables. See the rules . Counterfactual move. One step of learning. The machine picks one table entry and tries all 16 of its legal states (staying put plus 15 rotations), counts the mistakes after each on a batch of 64 examples, and keeps the best only if it strictly beats staying put. There are no gradients. See discrete learning and training .

721.body: Every equation and every normative mathematical statement in repository documents MUST carry exactly one of these role labels, written inline in bold (**Definition**, **Objective**, **Guarantee**, **Assumption**, **Empirical Criterion**): Label Meaning Where it may appear Definition Introduces an architectural object or mathematical term. True by convention; never "proven". Anywhere Objective A quantity the offline compiler attempts to optimize. Never a runtime invariant, never a theorem. Compiler-side docs/code only Guarantee A structural property of the compiled artifact or runtime. Requires a claim status from §2 and a proof artifact, witness, test, or explicit Unproven record. Artifact spec, runtime docs, proof model Assumption A condition a proof or certificate requires but the implementation does not itself establish. Proofs, certificates Empirical Criterion A measured property with a declared distribution, protocol, sample count, and uncertainty. Never stated as a proof. Certificates, evaluation docs Design aspirations are not theorems: an optimization target (arg max …) is an Objective , and a measured approximation (P_θ(a|c) ≈ P_θ(a|Z(c))) is an Empirical Criterion until the protocol behind it is declared.

722.body: Every Guarantee and every Empirical Criterion MUST also carry one of these statuses. The statuses are the machine-readable vocabulary of the proof-status matrix (crates/uor-r4-proof-model/src/proof_matrix.rs); the mapping is normative. Status Meaning ProofStatus mapping Structural Established by construction or by a named machine-checked test, fuzz target, or formal proof artifact that has actually run for the declared evidence. Verified Witnessed Established per execution by a bounded, replayable witness an independent verifier replays without the teacher. Verified (witness path) Empirical Measured on a pinned corpus with protocol, confidence intervals, and provenance identifiers, per docs/transformerless/EQUIVALENCE_AND_EMPIRICAL_PROTOCOL.md. DifferentialPass Assumed Required by a proof or certificate but not established by the implementation. recorded as an assumption entry Unproven Asserted as a goal but currently without evidence. Unverified (blocks verify_all) ExecutableSpec in the proof matrix means the obligation has a runnable specification but no activated binding check yet; documents must label such claims Unproven (or Assumed where applicable), never Structural .

723.body: The prohibited phrases are "machine-verified" , "machine verified" , "exact equivalence" , "exact teacher equivalence" , and "provably equivalent" . They are prohibited in normative documents (docs/**, crate READMEs) unless the same line links a proof artifact or certificate, or the phrase is explicitly disavowed on that line. The uor-r4-claim-wording gate enforces this when explicitly activated (see §6). The project does not claim exact teacher equivalence (disallowed per this rule), does not claim human-level reasoning, and does not treat plausible language output as evidence of coherent internal state transitions.

726.body: Avoid (unqualified) Use instead Rule "intent" Future-state optimization : belief = estimated current state, goal = desired future-state subset G ⊆ S, constraint = forbidden subset F ⊆ S, action = transition operator, plan = bounded trajectory π = (a_0, …, a_n) with T^π(s_0) ∈ G and T^π_i(s_0) ∉ F for all intermediate i ( Definition , PDF §12). Unqualified "intent" is informal prose; it must not appear in a labeled statement. "semantic atom" Semantic region — multiresolution, overlapping, proof-addressable; explicitly not an atom (glossary). "Semantic atom" is prohibited in normative text. "equivalence" Qualified forms only: byte reproducibility (identical pinned inputs ⇒ identical artifact bytes) or behavioral equivalence (an Empirical Criterion , valid only on the declared distribution, per the equivalence protocol). Unqualified "equivalence" is informal; "exact equivalence" hits the §2.1 wording rule. "reasoning" Precise mechanisms: typed state transitions , graph navigation , bounded planning (trajectory evaluation over T). Bare "reasoning" is informal; plausible language output is never evidence of it (§2.1). "transformerless" Zero source-attention calls and no dense full-prefix Q·K matrix/softmax kernel on the exact promoted decoder path; the replacement uses bounded geometric support shown load-bearing by disabled/permuted interventions. Does not imply multiplication-free, integer-only, allocation-free, coherent, or production-ready. Name retained source components and the checkpoint/scope. "geometric intelligence" Name the measured mechanism: geometric support change , memory-causal logit effect , student-prefix rollout , or another declared empirical result. Geometry being present or visually structured is not evidence of intelligence. Existing documents predate this convention. Their already-qualified uses ("behavioral equivalence", "not semantic atoms", "equivalence-tested") conform; unqualified uses are hereby marked informal and are migrated opportunistically, not by wholesale rewrite.

73.body: D-entries (D11, D22, D37 and the rest). Numbered owner decisions, from D0 to D41, that used to be the project's rulebook. The charter now holds the rules that still bind, and the decision map says what became of each decision. The ones you will meet most are D11 , D22 and D37 . D11. The serving contract: the finished model runs with whole numbers only. It has five rules. Two of them are that the served program uses no floating point and no multiply or divide instruction. See serving and export . D19 object store. A store that keeps bytes exactly, in a tree of fingerprinted pieces, so repeats are stored once and any range can be checked. It is built and tested (20 integration tests pass in the delivery record, 60 after later work), but no model uses it yet. See object store . D22. The owner's rule that a negative result closes one tested configuration, never a mechanism. Stopping a mechanism needs the owner. This is why no mechanism has a "retired" status. See the rules and decision map . D24. The owner's rule of 12 October 2026 that no model compute runs on the CPU: training, evaluation and every research measurement of the model are GPU work. Serving the exported D11 integer artifact on a client device is the product, not research compute (charter 3.6). See the rules . D37. The owner's rule of 18 October that floating point is legal in offline training. Softmax-like functions and matrix multiplication stay banned, and every float-trained candidate must report its export gap. See training . DEV panel. The set of 14,287 development rows used to score models while they are being designed. A model's first guess is right on some number of them (see top-1 ). The "fresh" panel is a separate sealed set, scored once after the design is chosen. See K16 outcome . Diagnostic stop. A run ended early on purpose, by a stop rule written down beforehand, so the cause can be found. It is not a negative result and not a failure of the mechanism. See research notebooks .

732.body: Registered source tokenizers are selected by CLI/API fields, not environment variables. CLI commands that accept --source also accept the atomic pair --tokenizer-family FAMILY --tokenizer-version N. Both flags must be present or absent. When absent, discovery succeeds only when the source directory has one unambiguous supported definition; a directory containing both tokenizer.json and spiece.model requires the explicit pair. Unknown pairs and any attempt to combine a registered adapter with legacy --checkpoint input fail closed. For raw SentencePiece sources, use family sentencepiece-unigram. Version 2 is the current, reference-correct adapter; automatic discovery of one unambiguous spiece.model selects it. Version 1 remains registered only as the immutable published behavior whose unknown id decodes to the literal model surface <unk>. N is part of the semantic identity, not a compatibility range: consumers do not substitute a newer or older version. Both versions read the pinned 32,000-piece spiece.model; neither applies the T5 Hugging Face wrapper's 100 sentinel tokens or EOS-appending post-processor. The host adapter performs text normalization and encoding. The deployed tagged tokenizer.bin is decode-only and carries the complete adapter binding (family, version, source-model CID, and policy digest). Serving requires a matching host encoder for prompt text. Missing/mismatched identity, unavailable encode, invalid token ids, and decode failures are errors; an explicitly tagged tokenizer does not fall back to a legacy tokenizer. SentencePiece observation records have no original-source byte anchors because normalization and unknown collapse do not preserve a total input-offset map.

738.body:
These knobs drive the teacher-free R4G1Runtime evaluator. Worker partitions are deterministic and reductions are replayed in canonical position order, so changing the worker count changes wall time but not report bytes. Once an evaluation phase launches it writes monotonic progress plus its phase terminal; a missing control, timeout, or absent identity is UNAVAILABLE/skipped and cannot authorize production. Variable Meaning Default R4_DEPLOYED_QUALITY_MODE full selects the complete held-out census; every other value selects the deterministic sample sample R4_DEPLOYED_QUALITY_POSITIONS Sample size when mode is not full 6,000 R4_DEPLOYED_QUALITY_WORKERS Evaluation workers. Results are canonically ordered after parallel execution available logical CPUs R4_CERTIFY_R4G1_BUDGET_SECS Cheap readiness-probe wall-clock budget 120 R4_CERTIFY_R4G1_EVAL_BUDGET_SECS Sample/census wall-clock budget 3,600 The historical certify-C diagnostic above and this normative command share the two budget variable names but retain distinct defaults: 600 seconds for the non-binding diagnostic, 3,600 seconds for r4 deployed-quality. Explicit CLI flags override their environment variables. Every invocation against a valid, non-symlink bundle root first creates evidence/deployed_quality_invocation_terminal.jsonl. The create-once JSONL journal is synced after its started row and again after exactly one completed, failed, or best-effort interrupted terminal row, so argument, bundle-discovery, cross-surface, witness, sample-gate, projection, and evaluator failures are all durable. A synced started row without a terminal row means the process was externally interrupted or otherwise unresolved; signals, power loss, and SIGKILL cannot be guaranteed to run cleanup code. An absent, symlinked, or non-directory bundle cannot safely host in-bundle evidence and therefore fails before journal creation. Reusing the same staged bundle is refused rather than overwriting its first invocation. The invocation journal is local, non-semantic evidence. It is excluded from the generation CID, production admission, and release archives, as are the resource sidecar and terminal transcript described below. Phase progress and phase terminal files under graph/ remain authoritative only after that phase actually launches. Production admission accepts only a schema-2 release-bundle.json whose component digests and compiler/selector identities reproduce from the loaded graph, teacher artifact, corpus pair, tokenizer, tokenizer adapter, score report, cover report, and deployed-quality report. A sampled report remains research evidence even when all measured rows are favorable. The release CLI exposes the same contract directly. --mode full cannot bypass the cheap instrument: it first runs the exact 6,000-position prefix of the canonical label-free, story-distributed order on the same bundle/evidence generation. Any structural, reachability, non-futility, planted-control, cross-surface, or witness falsifier emits STOP: and returns without starting the census. PROCEED: launches the census. A typed INCONCLUSIVE: extends the same immutable nested order to 18,000 positions; if that interval still overlaps the gate, it can launch only the census and only when the measured reachable ceiling remains sufficient. Before any census launch, the authorizing stage's measured throughput is scaled to the full population; a projection beyond the configured evaluation budget or one hour refuses launch and requires a revised run contract. No sample report can authorize production admission. cargo run --release -- deployed-quality \ --bundle .uor-models/compiled/<model>-staging \ --compiler-revision <full-40-character-revision> \ --mode sample --positions 6000 --workers 8 For a canonical run, wrap the command so host identity, effective workers, wall time, peak child RSS, free storage, bundle growth, exit status, and every graph evidence-file size are durable even when the evaluator fails. A create-once JSONL beside the summary samples the complete child process tree's CPU share, RSS, process count, host-memory headroom, and filesystem headroom every five seconds. The wrapped evaluator still streams its phase counters, throughput, and ETA. On the canonical macOS host, /usr/bin/script -e -F preserves that stream in a separate terminal transcript and propagates the child exit status; require a new transcript path before launch just as the wrapper requires a new sidecar. The resource summary, live-sample JSONL, and transcript are explicitly non-semantic and are never admission inputs. The inventory snapshot is captured when the child exits. If the live-sample JSONL is placed inside the bundle it is therefore present in that snapshot; the subsequently written resource summary and the outer transcript's final trailer are not. Both resource paths are append-only: the wrapper refuses to overwrite either one, and it verifies that its --bundle exactly matches the wrapped command's --bundle (evaluation) or --bundle-root (graph emission) before launch. It also records --workers or --jobs as the effective requested worker count. Use --samples-output to select the JSONL path; otherwise it is <output>.samples.jsonl. test ! -e .uor-models/compiled/<model>-staging/graph/deployed_quality_full.log

S private sequence states must share one immutable weight allocation and advance in one physical exact batch; the one W-thread pool must schedule disjoint output rows without nested oversubscription. Every output row must keep the pinned uor-matmul dot reduction intact; splitting or reassociating the reduction dimension is not permitted. Results return to canonical prompt/position order before metrics are reduced. The 36 logical teacher-forced positions are executed once in six physical batches with registered widths 8, 8, 8, 7, 4, 1. That transcript retains each canonical lane at its distinct final teacher-forced prompt prefix (lengths 5, 6, 5, 4, 3, 4, 5, 4 for the pinned tokenizer), rather than truncating different prompts to a colliding common prefix. S4 clones the templates, appends the already-computed teacher next token to each logical seed, and times only new causal continuation steps. Exact batches carry the per-lane sequence positions explicitly, so variable histories do not serialize the cohort. There is no duplicate live-teacher prefill and no independent full-model S4 warm-up. Preparation, decode, and one-shot elapsed time remain separate evidence fields. Before measurement, the harness reserves the bounded model-wide batch buffers, exact input/output transpose buffers, and one exact scratch slot per dedicated worker, then exercises the worker pool/backend with a tiny known product. Its elapsed time, retained capacity, capacity-growth event count, and actual added capacity bytes are recorded as excluded preparation. Measurement counters are reset without discarding those buffers. Every transcript and S4 physical forward must subsequently report zero workspace-growth events and bytes; otherwise the run fails rather than presenting allocation churn as steady-state throughput. Conditional source, artifact, store, graph, tokenizer, or corpus evidence is reported as AVAILABLE, UNAVAILABLE, FAILED, or NOT_RUN. An absent fixture is never a parity PASS merely because the enclosing test executable returns success. The progress/event/report schema and the launch gate are specified in the #932 run record . The report's required events object binds the sibling file_name, full-byte content_cid, byte_len, record_count, final_record_number, final_event, final_status, final_qualifies_full_run, and non-cyclic report_body_cid. FINAL is synchronized before the report is atomically committed, carries sequence == final_record_number == record_count, and must be the last JSONL record. Admission validates the current sidecar before teacher weights load; missing, truncated, appended, or tampered bytes refuse the run. Schema /1 bytes describe the superseded fixed-sweep design and remain historical evidence. Schema /2 binds the adaptive candidate set, fastest-exact selection policy, and the complete registered admission shape: 36 transcript logical forwards in batch widths 8, 8, 8, 7, 4, 1; eight continuation tokens across eight lanes; 100 logical forwards in 14 physical shared-weight batches; zero-based maximum sequence position 13; and private-state capacity 14. A smaller operator cap may produce diagnostic evidence but cannot qualify the binding suite. reference_workers names the first measured exact candidate, equal_to_reference binds every candidate's raw trace to it, and the cheap worker-pool/backend prestart is recorded separately and excluded from timed forward rates. CPU and RSS fields are diagnostics: they must be structurally valid and truthful, but a platform-reported UNAVAILABLE value does not by itself refuse exact admission. A later change to field meaning, type, requiredness, units, or artifact partition requires another schema id rather than reinterpreting an existing record.

74.body: E8. A famous lattice in eight dimensions with 240 "root" points. The project builds a pairing of the 120 icosians with a golden-ratio-scaled copy of themselves and gets these 240 roots. The current model uses only a 16-root piece of E8, not all 240. See E8, H4 and the 600-cell . Embedding. In a transformer, the learned list of decimals that stands for each token. UOR-R4's counterpart is the constructed integer codebook . See PrimeZeta . Exact memory. The idea of writing a fact once under an exact name (a prime-based address) and reading it back exactly, instead of smearing it across weights. The trained forms tested so far missed their bars, so the mechanism is PARKED. See exact memory . Export gap. The quality lost when a model trained with decimals is snapped into the whole-number file that ships. It is the served score minus the float score on the same evaluator. A float candidate whose gap exceeds the two-seed noise band is disqualified. Nobody has measured it for a model built under today's rules, because none has been exported. See serving and export .

744.body: Normative Invariant (verbatim) : Parallel execution may change compilation time, but must not change the canonical graph artifact produced from the same pinned inputs, compiler version, configuration, and target-independent compilation mode. All R4 compiler pipeline stages (whether Parallel-Safe, Parallel with Deterministic Merge, Bounded Parallel, or Sequential Canonical Finalization) must conform to this invariant.
744.breadcrumbs: Canonical artifact byte equality » 1. Primary Invariant Statement
744.title: 1. Primary Invariant Statement

745.body: To enforce strict byte-identical canonical outputs across sequential and parallel multicore executions, the R4 graph compiler mandates the following mechanisms: Stable Input Ordering & Shard Numbering : Observations, traces, and samples are partitioned into deterministic shards based strictly on content-addressed IDs or stable positional indices. Dynamic worker scheduling order or thread dispatch timing must never dictate shard numbering. Stable Candidate Ordering & Tie-Breaking : At every candidate selection point (e.g., region induction, XOR-polynomial candidate ranking, routing program selection), tie-breaking must follow a deterministic total order. For candidate scores, ties are broken strictly by candidate ID / content hash (ScoreQ fixed-point score descending, then candidate ID ascending). Deterministic Reductions & Sorting : Parallel map-reduce operations must partition reductions by content-addressed key and perform deterministic ordered merges. All canonical outputs (nodes, edges, regions, certificates) must undergo stable canonical sorting prior to binary encoding into R4G1 format. Floating-Point & Summation Policy : Order-sensitive floating-point parallel reductions are strictly forbidden for canonical output calculations. Compiler stages computing canonical graph quantities must use fixed-order summation or integer/fixed-point accumulator types (ScoreQ, saturating integer arithmetic). Compiler-internal float heuristics (e.g., loss diagnostics) may use floating-point operations provided canonical topology, IDs, offsets, and binary payload bytes do not depend on summation order. Random-Seed Policy : All pseudo-random processes (such as clustering initialization or randomized graph exploration) must consume pinned random seeds recorded in the compile report. Seed generation and PRNG state transitions must be positionally deterministic and independent of thread scheduling or multicore worker counts. Thread-Count Invariance : The compiled graph topology, node/edge IDs, section offsets, payload bytes, content CIDs, and performance/verification certificates must be 100% bit-identical across any thread count \(N \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, \dots\}\).
745.breadcrumbs: Canonical artifact byte equality » 2. Required Execution & Reduction Mechanisms
745.title: 2. Required Execution & Reduction Mechanisms

746.body: The following implementation patterns are explicitly forbidden within the R4 graph compiler pipeline: Forbidden Pattern 1 : Assigning canonical node or edge IDs during unordered parallel discovery. Forbidden Pattern 2 : Using thread completion order or worker arrival sequence as semantic ordering. Forbidden Pattern 3 : Mutating or appending to shared global graph data structures from parallel worker threads. Forbidden Pattern 4 : Iterating over non-deterministic hash map key orders to emit canonical output structures. Forbidden Pattern 5 : Order-sensitive floating-point parallel reductions feeding canonical graph attributes. Forbidden Pattern 6 : First-finished-candidate-wins race conditions in candidate selection.

747.body: The compiler crate (uor-r4-graph-compiler::reproducibility) provides ParallelReproducibilityHarness. The harness executes: \[\text{Harness}(\text{inputs}) \implies \text{Artifact}_{\text{seq}} \equiv \text{Artifact}_{\text{par}, N=1} \equiv \text{Artifact}_{\text{par}, N=2} \equiv \text{Artifact}_{\text{par}, N=4} \equiv \text{Artifact}_{\text{par}, N=\text{max}}\] The harness asserts: ArtifactBytes(seq) == ArtifactBytes(par, N) (100% byte equality) Digest(ArtifactBytes(seq)) == Digest(ArtifactBytes(par, N)) (BLAKE3 digest parity) The proof model (uor-r4-proof-model::structural_guarantees) currently provides an executable-spec check via verify_parallel_reproducibility_compliance; end-to-end compiler artifact-byte parity remains validated by compiler-path tests.

75.body: FBS. The project's name for the three-branch tree that holds earlier words in order. The tree is built by SpiralCore and gives the context at most 243 positions (\(3^5\)). See SpiralCore and SpiralCore/FBS projection . FIT (TEST FITNESS: FIT). The verdict of a review, by someone other than the author, that a pre-registered test is fit to answer its question. A fresh-context subagent counts as a non-author. A FIT releases nothing by itself: the owner still has to release the run. See the rules and training . Float. Decimal (floating-point) arithmetic. Allowed in offline training under D37 , never in the served model. See serving and export . Flock read. An attention replacement modelled on a starling flock. The model picks about seven of the nearest earlier positions, rotates what each knows into its own point of view, and moves toward their consensus. Nothing is normalised and no weight is multiplied. It runs inside every Relation run, but its own value has never been isolated. See Flock read . Fresh panel. Rows that were never seen during design and stay sealed until a run is registered to score them. Every development gain must also report a fresh number. See the rules .

76.body: H4. The symmetry group of the 600-cell, a regular solid in four dimensions. Its 120 roots are the icosians . See E8, H4 and the 600-cell . Hamilton gate. A gate for a feed-forward layer that turns the gate signal into a rotation in four dimensions and rotates the value by it, so no sigmoid is needed. A rotation keeps a vector's length, so the gate steers a signal rather than switching it off. It is built and tested (READY), and has never been trained. See Hamilton gate . Hamming distance. The number of positions at which two bit strings differ. It costs one XOR and one bit count. The model uses it as a tie-break inside its reads. See VSA and Hamming distance . Hinge loss. A loss that asks only whether the right answer beats its strongest rivals by a fixed gap. If it does, the loss is zero. If not, the loss is the shortfall. It needs no probabilities. The live version is an integer hinge. See rank-margin . Hold. An owner order that stops a kind of work until the owner lifts it. Training, the second milestone's training and rental, and Stage B are all on hold. A FIT review lifts none of them. See charter , section 5.1. Hopf map. A map that takes a point on a four-dimensional sphere (a unit quaternion) to a point on an ordinary sphere. It forgets one angle, called the fibre, so many states cast the same shadow. The kept-fibre idea is built as a helper but is not part of the current read, and the mechanism is PARKED. See the Hopf map and the kept fibre .

778.title: MSA: Modular Structural Arithmetic

779.body: Structural Arithmetic (SA), 10 pages. SA starts from ordinary arithmetic (Peano-style axioms for successor, addition and multiplication) and adds three named constants: \(\gamma=24\) (the generator), \(\mu=48\) (the mediator) and \(\varepsilon=96\) (the manifestation). Each doubles into the next, \(\delta(\gamma)=\mu\) and \(\delta(\mu)=\varepsilon\), which the paper calls the doubling cascade. It also states the "fundamental equation" \(\mu\times\mu=\gamma\times\varepsilon\). Numbers are classed by role as generators, mediators or manifestations, with axioms about how the roles are closed under operations such as greatest common divisor and least common multiple, and an induction schema over the structures built this way. Modular Structural Arithmetic (MSA), 6 pages. MSA is described as a conservative extension of SA: it adds reduction modulo a number \(p\) and asks which moduli keep the structure intact. Three predicates carry the idea: \(\mathrm{DP}(p)\), doubling-preserving: the reduced doubled constant equals the doubled residue, with no second reduction (for example mod 7 it fails: \(2\times6=12\) is not 5). \(\mathrm{RP}(p)\), role-preserving: the three constants stay distinct mod \(p\). \(\mathrm{SP}(p)\), structural-preserving: both of the above. The paper then states special cases as axioms. For example, mod 11 the constants become 2, 4 and 8 (the "11-theorem"), and mod 7 they become 3, 6 and 5, which sum to a multiple of 7 (the "7-vanishing"). It also axiomatizes a "modular resonance" and a resonance period. Checks anyone can do by hand (proof, by arithmetic). \(48^2=2304=24\times96\); \(24,48,96 \bmod 11 = 2,4,8\); \(24,48,96 \bmod 7 = 3,6,5\) and \(24+48+96=168=7\times24\). These confirm the numerical facts the axioms state. They do not show that the axiom system is consistent or that its larger claims, such as the characterization of doubling-preserving primes (axiom MSA9), hold; the papers present these as axioms, and this page has not checked that they follow from the others.

786.body: Prime numbers look random, but their running count wobbles around a smooth curve in a way that has long been tied to the zeros of the Riemann zeta function. This project asked whether that wobble (the Chebyshev residual \(\psi(x)-x\)) carries a structure that can be recovered and used to predict where primes fall. It is a pile of research notes, slide decks, simulations and scripts. Its own README calls it a late, concluding collection of the prime-router studies; the ancestry runs from the AI-Research workspace to a Python prime router, to this program, to the Rust model. The model's ideas about prime addresses and zeta phases draw on it. It is not a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, and not evidence that the language model works. flowchart LR A["Primes up to x"] --> B["Residual: psi of x minus x"] B --> C["Detrend, resample on a log grid"] C --> D["Hilbert transform: phase of the signal"] D --> E["Look for stable frequencies and compare with zeta zeros"] E --> F["Time-ordered 70/30 split: predict the held-out part"] E -.-> G["Idea the model draws on: prime log-phases and zeta zeros as fixed phases"] The program's pipeline as its own notes describe it. The dashed arrow is a transfer of an idea, not a transfer of a result.
786.breadcrumbs: Side projects » Prime Analysis: the Prime Phase and Chebyshev psi spectral program » Prime Analysis: the Prime Phase and Chebyshev psi spectral program
786.title: Prime Analysis: the Prime Phase and Chebyshev psi spectral program

787.body: Let \(\psi(x)=\sum_{n\le x}\Lambda(n)\) be the Chebyshev function, where \(\Lambda\) is the von Mangoldt function. The explicit formula writes the residual as a sum over the non-trivial zeros \(\rho=\tfrac12+i\gamma\) of the zeta function: \[\psi(x)-x \;=\; -\sum_{\rho}\frac{x^{\rho}}{\rho}\;+\;\text{small terms}.\] Each zero contributes an oscillation whose frequency is set by \(\gamma\). The program treats the residual as a signal and asks whether those oscillations can be seen and extrapolated. The notes describe a fixed ("fingerprint-locked") pipeline: causal detrending (no use of future data), resampling on a uniform log grid, analytic phase through a Hilbert transform, and time-ordered 70% train / 30% test splits so that prediction is judged out of sample. The program also developed a geometric side: the R4 Prime Router, Hopf-base sector discretization, and an H4 x H4 coupled field. Those briefings are one source of the model's prime-routing language.

8.body: A transformer is the design behind almost every modern language model (background: Vaswani et al., "Attention Is All You Need", 2017, arXiv:1706.03762). One turn of its loop looks like this: flowchart LR t["Token"] --> e["Embedding:<br/>a long list of decimals"] e --> a["Attention:<br/>compare with EVERY earlier token<br/>(softmax)"] a --> m["Feed-forward:<br/>multiply by large learned grids<br/>(matrix multiplication)"] m --> o["Output:<br/>score EVERY word in the vocabulary<br/>(softmax)"] o --> n["Next token"] m -. "repeat for many layers" .-> a One turn of a transformer. The three expensive operations are named in brackets. Three operations carry most of the cost: Matrix multiplication. Each token is carried as a long list of decimal numbers. Every layer multiplies that list by large learned grids of numbers. Nearly all of the arithmetic is here. Attention. To decide what matters, the newest token is compared with every earlier token. The work grows with the length of the text, and the model keeps a stored copy of every earlier position. Softmax. Scores are turned into probabilities with exponentials and a sum over everything, once inside attention and once over the whole vocabulary to choose the next word. The project bans two of the three outright, softmax-like squashing functions and matrix multiplication, anywhere: training, evaluation, tools and serving ( charter , sections 3.2 and 3.3). All-pairs attention is not banned as an idea; it is replaced by bounded reads of a few nearby tokens. The reason, in the owner's words: "my goal with all of these bans is to ban expensive operations" ( charter , section 1).

80.body: M1 to M8 (milestones). The eight GitHub milestones that define the road to an alpha release. None is complete. In plain words: # Meaning M1 It predicts text (a saved discrete model beats both count tables through the integer export) M2 It answers from memory (at least 256 of 512 development replies, and 40% on a fresh panel) M3 It remembers across sessions M4 It is served: exported to UORLUT01 and run from the command line M5 It is cheap on a laptop, with the cost measured M6 It reasons and codes M7 It runs the same in a library, a command line and a browser M8 It is released as one checksum-pinned file Source: language model and where we're going . Matmul (matrix multiplication, GEMM). Multiplying a long list of numbers by a large grid of learned numbers. It is nearly all the arithmetic of a transformer, and the project bans it everywhere: training, tests, tools and serving. A geometric feed-forward block is allowed. A dense one is not. See charter , section 3.3. Mechanism. One geometric replacement for one part of a transformer, such as the read, the loss or the optimiser. The project tracks 27, each with its own page. See the mechanism board . Mechanism status (ACTIVE, READY, PARKED). The only three statuses a mechanism can have: ACTIVE : on the current model path (10 mechanisms). READY : built and tested but not yet trained into a model (4). PARKED : the tested forms failed or broke a rule, and the page lists what would reopen it (13). There is no "retired" status, by D22 . Source: mechanism board . MLP (feed-forward layer). The block in a transformer that processes each token after attention, usually with big grids of multiplications and a gate. UOR-R4's candidates are the Hamilton gate and the SpiralCore/FBS projection ; neither has been trained.

800.body: This project is an attempt to write a proof about prime numbers in a proof assistant called Lean 4, where a computer checks every step. The goal was to connect how primes are spread out to the Riemann hypothesis, a famous open problem about the zeros of the zeta function. The result is a scaffold: a chain of statements with the pieces needed to prove them, plus 185 Python scripts that probe whether the needed inequalities hold. The Riemann hypothesis is not proved here, and nothing in this folder is evidence about the language model. flowchart TD P["Python probes: a1 to a4, o1 to o5, k1, tau12, fixed_error_psi"] --> C["Constants and majorant checks"] C --> L["Lean files: PrimeRiemannBridge spine, 17 files (plus 6 scratch probes)"] L --> T["Theorem chain: O1 to O5, L1 to L3"] X["Pinned in lake-manifest.json: mathlib and its own dependencies, Lean v4.28.0"] --> L T -.-> G["Goal: bridge to the Riemann hypothesis, not reached"] Probes feed constants into the Lean spine. Mathlib is pinned, not copied; the project README also names Lean-RH, PhysLean, Carleson and PrimeNumberTheoremAnd, which are not pinned and not imported. The last arrow is the goal, not a result.

801.body: formal/lean/: the PrimeRiemannBridge theorem spine. The folder holds 23 .lean files: 17 spine files plus 6 small scratch probes (dot-prefixed .codex_* files, a few lines each). The project README states no axioms; a search of the 23 files finds no axiom declaration (two comment lines only). It comes with lakefile.toml (which requires only mathlib), lake-manifest.json (mathlib and its transitive packages), a Lean v4.28.0 lean-toolchain, and three verification scripts. 185 Python scripts at the top level: probes, ledgers, majorant checkers and proof-obligation tooling, grouped by prefix (a1 to a4, o1 to o5, k1, tau12, fixed_error_psi, spinning_top, build_*). data/: reference data (19 JSON files: 12 arXiv listings and 7 zeta-zero tables from LMFDB and Odlyzko; sizes not re-checked here). A "majorant" is an upper bound that dominates the quantity being studied; most scripts check numerically that such a bound holds in a range, or turn a bound into a constant for the Lean files. A numerical check in a range is not a proof for all numbers. Casey Allard started this as a standalone local project. It was never part of the AI-Research or Prime-Analysis repositories (research/riemann-lean/README.md). The external Lean dependencies are fetched with lake exe cache get or lake update; their sources are not stored here because they are third-party, large and regenerable.

807.body: SpiralCore is a set of geometry ideas (by Matthew) that the language model borrows: a fixed graph of rotations in eight dimensions, with exact bookkeeping of the path taken between two points. This project poses a different question about the same family of ideas: could they help move and shrink data across a network? That question is posed here, not yet tested: the code that exists uses plain zlib framing with no SpiralCore routing. The folder also keeps two SpiralCore references. It is a side project. It is not wired into the model's training or serving, and nothing here is evidence that the model works. flowchart LR A["App or unmodified program"] --> B["Wire layer: UORADP01 framing, zlib or raw per direction"] B --> C["Network"] C --> D["Wire layer at the far end"] D --> E["Service"] R1["Reference: SpiralCore v68 HTML"] -. "consulted" .-> M["Model mechanism: SpiralCore/FBS projection"] R2["Reference: Atomic Ternary FBS r3.1 PDF"] -. "consulted" .-> M R1 -. "future: not built yet" .-> B Left: the wire transport that exists today. Right: the two preserved references, which were consulted but are not the build source of the model's mechanism (that follows a v63 reference and a hosted v69 file). The dashed line from the reference to the wire layer is a plan, not code.
807.breadcrumbs: Side projects » SpiralCore: networking protocols and compression » SpiralCore: networking protocols and compression
807.title: SpiralCore: networking protocols and compression

808.body: The project has two parts that arrived at different times. 1. The wire transport exploration (code). One framing for compressed traffic, exposed four ways: a pair of proxies (a plain app talks to a local edge, the edge talks compressed to a gateway, the gateway talks to the service), a socket library the app links directly, a process interposer that makes unmodified programs use the wire (on macOS through DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES, on Linux through LD_PRELOAD), and opt-in multiplexing of several streams over one connection (UORADM01). The framing starts with a UORADP01 handshake, then length-prefixed frames with a raw-flag bit, so each direction can send zlib-compressed or raw data. There are 36 tool files (16 Python, 17 shell, 3 C) and a Rust crate, wire-rs, that is not part of the model's Cargo workspace. This work currently sits at spiralcore-base/wire (82 files). It was copied from a separate review repository at commit 032d903, which keeps the full history. It will move into this folder. 2. The owner-supplied references (documents). Two sources the owner brought in on 13 September 2026, preserved byte for byte: Source What it is SHA-256 Spiralcore_Dodecahedron_IP_Schema_v68.html (about 1 MB) An executable reference: prompt-trace handler, address functions, E8 addressing and operator routing, a Bell-tone codec, breadth-first search, orbit tracing and a Kuramoto phase solver 2a45c2e5f46c8c36bf7801da1d1e12ee9e2ed8b3da488ff54c20a6ac6c2ceab0 atomic-ternary-fbs-reference-r3.1.pdf (about 3 MB) "Atomic Ternary FBS Formal Consolidated Reference", revision 3.1 917cb942811971d63cbe499f3a1641d3360c4dde7ebdc6b87e298c3cf1bbd747 Also kept: provenance.json (original paths, byte counts and hashes) and a plain-text extract of the mathematics. The scripts in the HTML file were not executed during import, and its embedded fixture claims were not re-run (research/spiralcore-v68/README.md).

809.body: The HTML reference defines a fixed graph of rotations over the 16 roots of one E8 anchor orbit, and a search that returns an ordered history between two roots. The model's SpiralCore/FBS mechanism follows a related convention (the v63 reference, implemented in crates/uor-r4-core/src/spiralcore_operator.rs, and a hosted v69 file reviewed on 9 October), not this v68 file. The idea is the same family: an output block picks one stored atom and moves it along a short path of signed coordinate swaps (see the mechanism page and the geometry explainer ). The wire transport does not use any of this yet. Its framing is plain length-prefixed zlib, chosen for interoperability.
