814.body: This project tries to prove, with a proof assistant called Lean 4, that one specific small program is the best possible program of its kind. The program is a matrix-multiplication kernel (GEMM) written for WebAssembly, the portable code format that runs in browsers. "Best possible" has a precise meaning set by the project: lowest score on a fixed cost formula, among every program that does the same job. The proof is not finished . The project's own result today is the honest answer "incomplete". It is a side project: it does not train, serve or test the language model, and the model's own rules forbid dense matrix multiplication, so this work is unrelated to how the model computes. It is outside every model build and every loaded path; whether the model ratchet's scan scope covers this folder was not checked for this page. flowchart TD A["Authority: pinned UOR-GNAF draft.2 spec and the fixed claim WGG-GO-1"] --> B["Lean model of WebAssembly: encode, decode, step, cost"] B --> C["Cost objective: 36 charged coordinates, weight one each"] C --> D["Proved: a best program exists if any program exists"] D --> E["Still to show: a concrete program exists, and it equals the committed binary"] E -.-> F["Release theorem: global optimality. Not established"] The proof structure. Solid boxes are done; the last arrow is the goal, which has not been reached.

815.body: It is a Lean 4 library of 141 files (about 3.4 MB) with a normative specification (SPEC.md), an obligation ledger (CERTIFICATION.md), a claim registry (model/claims.json), pinned copies of its authority documents under authority/, fixtures, tooling and its own licences (Apache-2.0 or MIT, at your option). It currently lives at proofs/wasm-gemm-gnaf and moves to this folder. "GNAF" is the name of the authority document the project follows, UOR-GNAF version 1 draft 2, whose text is pinned by a SHA-256 hash. The requested claim, GlobalOptimal, ranges over all finite byte sequences that decode and validate as a WebAssembly module under the chosen profile. It does not range over a hand-picked family of kernels.

815.title: What the project is

816.body: The project defines a cost vector with 36 charged coordinates and a canonical score, the weight-one sum of those coordinates. It models the binary format and the step relation of a subset of WebAssembly, and shows that its cost instrumentation does not change what a program computes. One key fact: each coordinate is at most the score, so every set of programs below a given score is finite. That lets a minimum exist. With that, the project proves that if some valid program exists, a lowest-scoring one exists and satisfies the optimality statement. What is left is not a bound but an exhibition: build one concrete program with proofs that it qualifies, then show the committed binary is the program the minimum selects.

82.body: Orbit. A set of points that one group of moves carries into one another. The model uses a single orbit of 16 E8 roots, each a signed rearrangement of (2, 2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0). See E8, H4 and the 600-cell . Owner. Casey Allard, the project lead. He sets the charter, the holds, the spending and the milestone bars, and personally types each run release. Owner release. The typed phrase by which the owner personally lets one pre-registered run start. One release covers all arms and seeds of one sheet. No lab types it. See charter , section 5.1.

83.body: PARKED. A mechanism status. See mechanism status . PM seat. The project-manager role: it sequences work and keeps NOW.md . Kimi holds it, with a cover lab named by the owner. See the rules . Pre-alpha. The project's honest stage. Parts are built and tested, but 0 of 8 milestones are complete and no model holds a useful conversation. See STATUS . Pre-registration (sheet). A one-page plan, written before a run, that states the bar, the noise, the controls, the seeds, the cost and what each outcome would decide. It is needed only before GPU training or evaluation and before any run a milestone claim rests on. See the rules . Prime address. The exact name of a token: the (id + 1)-th prime number, so no two tokens collide. For example the 4,096th prime is 38,873. It is kept separate from the geometric address . See primes and zeta phases . PrimeZeta codebook. The table that turns each token's prime into eight angles taken from the Riemann zeta zeros, and the angles into a starting vector. It gives all 4,096 tokens distinct vectors ( measurement ). The distinctness comes from a cell-balancing step, not from the angles; whether the zeta angles help at all has not been tested. See prime-zeta codebook .
83.title: P

84.body: Q1. The first checkpoint of a full-length run, at 4,096 of its 16,404 batches; Q4 is the last. The 18 October dose with Relation was stopped at Q1 when admission collapsed. See admission . Quaternion. A four-part number \(w + xi + yj + zk\). Multiplying by a length-1 quaternion turns a point in four dimensions without stretching it, and every such turn can be undone. Quaternions of length 1 form the 3-sphere. See quaternions and rotation .
84.title: Q

85.body: Rank-margin. The project's loss: the right token must outrank its strongest rivals by a fixed margin. See hinge loss and rank-margin . Read. The step in which the model looks back at earlier text to decide what matters for the next token: the project's bounded replacement for attention. There are three: Route , Flock and Relation . Reach. For one test position, whether the right next token is among the candidates the model opens at all; counted over the 14,287 positions of the DEV panel. A model cannot guess a token it never opens, so a low reach caps the top-1 score, but a high reach alone is not skill (variant R of K16 reached 12,000 positions by opening almost the whole vocabulary). READY. A mechanism status. See mechanism status . Relation read. A Flock read plus the ability to follow simple links between positions, such as "the word right after the earlier copy of this word". This is how copying is meant to work. It has trained twice, and both runs stopped before a verdict. See Relation read . Root. One of the fixed points of E8 used as a block value. See orbit . Route read. An attention replacement that walks a small tree of addresses, stepping toward the nearest branch at each level, and picks up one earlier word at the end. It never scores the whole history. It is the base read of every trained discrete model, but its own contribution is unattributed. See Route read . Rung 0. The first full-length run on the discrete path (seed 1, 16,404 updates, scored on the 14,287 development rows). Its bars were unreachable because only 1,920 targets were admitted, which pointed the work at admission . See route read .
85.title: R

86.body: Seed. The starting number of a random draw. A decisive run uses at least two seeds, so a result is not one lucky draw. See the rules . SiLU. A smooth squashing curve used as an activation in the older decimal stack. It is built from a sigmoid, so it falls under the ban on squashing functions. Softmax. A function that turns a list of scores into probabilities with exponentials and a sum over everything. Transformers use it inside attention and again to pick the next word. The project bans it, and every softmax-like squashing function, anywhere in the model, its training or its comparators. See charter , section 3.2. SpiralCore. An exact-geometry source credited to Matthew. From the octonion multiplication table it yields moves that shuffle the eight coordinates and flip some signs. Each move can be undone exactly. The integer form is the core of the current model. See SpiralCore . Studio. The single-page interface meant to be the shell of both the web and desktop clients. It is not yet connected to the new engine. See web client .
86.title: S

87.body: T2. A table built from the training text. It looks up the last word and returns the next word seen most often after it. It gets 6,300 of the 14,287 DEV first guesses right, and it is one of the two count tables a trained model must beat ( measurement ). See host diagnostics . Ternary. Used in two ways here. A ternary weight or gate takes one of three values: −1, 0 or +1. A ternary tree has three branches per node. Dense ternary weights are PARKED because every weight is still touched for every word. See ternary and XOR . Token. One numbered piece of text, a word or part of a word. The model never sees letters. See tokenizer . Tokenizer. The component that cuts text into tokens and turns tokens back into text. The pinned one has 4,096 pieces (identity d36d3e87). See tokenizer . Tokens/s (tokens per second). How many tokens the model reads or writes per second. It is the project's lead metric, with decode speed and context speed reported separately. It has never been measured for the current model. See charter , section 1. Tauri. A toolkit that wraps a web page as a desktop app. The planned desktop client would use it to share the web interface. Top-1 (and top-8). The number of DEV rows on which the model's first guess (or any of its first eight) is the right next token, out of 14,287. M1 requires the top-1 of the model, through the integer export, to beat the unigram and T2 tables. See charter , section 4.8. Transformer. The design behind almost every modern language model. Its cost sits in three operations: matrix multiplication, attention against every earlier token, and softmax. UOR-R4 is not a transformer. See what is UOR-R4 and transformer vs geometry .
87.title: T

88.body: Unigram. A table of word counts that ignores context and always guesses by overall frequency. It gets 1,226 of the 14,287 DEV first guesses right. The best trained discrete model got 65 and 463 ( measurement ). See K16 outcome . UOR. Short for Universal Object Reference, the foundation named as copyright holder in the project's MIT licence ( LICENSE ). A "UOR address" in this project is the prime-based name described under prime address . UORLUT01. The container format for the finished model: one file of 4-bit codes and small integer tables, pinned by checksum. It is what the engine serves. See serving and export and releases and artifacts .
88.title: U

89.body: VSA (vector-symbolic architecture). A memory idea using long bit strings (4,096 bits per token) glued by XOR and compared by counting differing bits. It improved bits per byte by 0.014 to 0.023 on a banned CPU learner, so it is PARKED. See VSA and VSA and Hamming distance .
89.title: V

9.body: UOR-R4 replaces each expensive part with something cheaper: Transformer part UOR-R4's replacement A long list of decimals per token A short address : 4 blocks of 8 whole numbers, each block a fixed point on a geometric object Compare with every earlier token A local read (a "read" is the step that looks back at earlier text): look at a few nearby earlier tokens, found by their addresses Softmax over every word Admission : open a few "drawers" (called cells) of words near what was read, then pick the nearest word inside them Learned grids of decimals Rotations from a fixed, finite set, plus table look-ups A growing store of every past position Exact memory : write a fact once under an exact name, read it back exactly The finished model is meant to run with whole numbers only: adds, subtractions, comparisons and table look-ups, with no multiply instruction at all. This rule is called D11 ( charter , section 3.6). The lead measure of success is tokens per second on ordinary hardware ( charter , section 1). Whether these replacements can match a transformer's quality is the open question. It is a hypothesis . No measurement so far shows it, and the next page says which parts are built and which are missing: transformer vs geometry .

90.body: W2. The next queued test: FIT-reviewed and awaiting an owner release (cost about $0.91, estimated). It decides whether the wall is the model's representation or its learning law, and includes count-table arms the headline bars lack. See open questions . WASM (WebAssembly). A compact, sandboxed machine code that browsers run. The integer serving engine is built for it, with 7 of 7 serving functions free of multiply, divide and float instructions ( measurement ). See web client . Writer (shared vector writer). The one component that handles a token's vector on the way in, along the carry and on the way out, using the same format everywhere. It builds the cells and picks the nearest token among the admitted ones. See architecture .
90.title: W

91.body: Z[φ]. Pairs of whole numbers (a, b) standing for a + bφ, where φ is the golden ratio. They add and multiply with no rounding, so icosian coordinates can be kept exact. See golden integers . Zeta zero. A point where the Riemann zeta function is zero. The project uses a few fixed zeros as clock speeds: for a prime \(p\) the angle on channel \(k\) is \(\gamma_k \ln p\). It uses the numbers only and makes no claim about the Riemann hypothesis. See primes and zeta phases .
91.title: Z

93.body: UOR-R4 aims to ship one thing people can use: a small, fast language model that runs on your own laptop or in your own browser, with nothing sent to a server. The owner defined three products around it on 19 October 2026. The first is the model itself, saved as one file of whole numbers. The second is a web client that runs that file inside a browser tab. The third is a desktop client , an installable app that runs the same file natively and remembers your conversations. None of the three ships today. The project is pre-alpha: 0 of its 8 milestones are complete and no model holds a useful conversation yet ( STATUS , NOW ). Nothing is released until a trained model passes milestones M1 to M8. Labels used below: proof means derived from definitions or code, measurement means a recorded run with its artifact, hypothesis means an untested idea ( docs/formal_vocabulary.md , glossary ). One file in the middle, labelled "model artifact (UORLUT01, integer only)". Two arrows leave it. The left arrow goes to a browser window labelled "web client: WebAssembly in a tab, Studio shell". The right arrow goes to a laptop labelled "desktop client: Tauri app, native engine, durable memory, offline". Both clients share one user interface, drawn as the same Studio panel inside each. A dashed border around everything reads "on your device; no model server". One model file feeds two clients that share one interface. Everything inside the dashed line runs on the user's own device.

95.body: Local by design. The mission is "fast local AI": a model that trains fast, runs fast and approaches frontier capability on ordinary hardware ( charter , section 1). The lead metric is tokens per second. A product that needs a data centre would defeat the point. One file, many hosts. The served model obeys one contract, called D11: no decimal (floating-point) arithmetic, no multiply or divide instruction and no transcendental functions, only adds, shifts and table look-ups ( D11 ). A file that needs nothing more exotic than integer adds can run the same way in a browser, on a laptop processor or on Apple silicon. The charter says serving this file on the user's device is the product and is allowed. The rule that research compute must run on a GPU (D24) does not apply to it ( charter , section 3.6). One interface, two shells. The Studio, a single-page interface already in the repository, is the shell for both clients. The browser runs the engine as WebAssembly. The desktop app wraps the same page and runs the engine as native code, which should be faster (a hypothesis ; no side-by-side timing exists).

97.body: The products depend on the model, and the model depends on milestones. Roughly: M1 to M3 give a model that predicts text, answers from exact memory, and keeps memory across sessions. M4 exports that model through D11 and serves it from the command line. M5 measures its cost on a laptop, and M6 adds reasoning and coding on the same model. M7 makes the browser worker, the command line and the Rust library produce bit-identical tokens. That is the web client's gate. M8 is the alpha release: one versioned, checksum-pinned model file that meets every earlier bar. The desktop client has no milestone of its own yet. It rides on M3 for memory, M5 for laptop cost and M7 for the shared interface. The full definitions are in the project track .

99.body: The core product is a language model: a program that reads text and predicts what comes next, and so can hold a conversation. Most language models today are transformers that do billions of decimal multiplications per word. UOR-R4 tries a different route. It predicts text with geometry (prime-number addresses, rotations in four dimensions, exact look-up memory), and it ships as one file of whole numbers that an ordinary laptop or browser can run without a single multiply instruction. That file is meant to be the one thing every client loads. It does not exist yet. No trained model has been exported in that form, training is on hold pending review, and 0 of the 8 milestones are complete ( NOW ). Nothing ships until a trained model passes M1 to M8. Labels used below: proof (derived from definitions or code), measurement (a recorded run with its artifact), hypothesis (untested). See docs/formal_vocabulary.md and the glossary . flowchart LR T["Train on rented GPUs<br/>(crates/uor-r4-discrete)"] --> X["Export to one integer file<br/>UORLUT01"] X --> A["Audit: 0 multiply,<br/>0 divide, 0 float"] A --> S["Serve on the device<br/>(crates/uor-r4-integer)"] S --> C1["Command line<br/>uor-chat"] S --> C2["Web client<br/>WebAssembly"] S --> C3["Desktop client<br/>native"] The model's life in one line. Training happens once, offline, on a GPU. Everything after the export runs on the user's machine using whole numbers only.
